title: Alice Huang: Nvidia CEO's aide and 'spy' accused of smuggling microchips to China
description:

text:
The US is probing an alleged network involved in smuggling advanced AI chips to China, with investigators also examining suspected espionage and the possible gathering of sensitive commercial information for Beijing. The investigation has drawn attention to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the company's links to individuals under scrutiny.

At the centre of the probe is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. She is suspected of gathering commercial information for China and reportedly had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times.

But who is Alice Huang, and how did a business executive working in Singapore find herself at the centre of an intelligence investigation involving one of the biggest names in the global artificial intelligence industry?

WHO IS ALICE HUANG?

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese national who worked as a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company. While little has been reported about her personal life or early career, her professional position placed her in the middle of the global AI chip supply chain.

Megaspeed purchases computing equipment powered by Nvidia chips and operates as an intermediary, renting data centre capacity to businesses, including Chinese technology giant Alibaba, according to The New York Times.

The company's business model came under scrutiny as American authorities investigated whether firms operating through Southeast Asia were helping Chinese businesses circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips.

Alice Huang was a senior executive at Megaspeed during the period under investigation. Her position and the company's dealings with Nvidia reportedly brought her into contact with Jensen Huang, the company's chief executive.

According to The Guardian, American officials had previously suspected her of helping smuggle Nvidia chips to China. She was subsequently placed under surveillance.

WHY DID US INTELLIGENCE SUSPECT HER?

The investigation into Alice Huang was closely linked to concerns over the movement of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

The US government has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to Beijing, citing national security concerns. American officials suspected that Megaspeed was helping Chinese businesses obtain technology that they would otherwise struggle to access because of these restrictions.

According to The New York Times, scrutiny of Megaspeed dates back to late 2024. A US Commerce Department official who visited a data centre operated by the company in Malaysia reportedly found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising questions about whether the equipment was being installed at the facility or shipped elsewhere.

The investigation also extended to Megaspeed's business network. Its sister company in Malaysia purchased at least USD 4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius and cited by the newspaper.

US officials suspected that some of the chips acquired through the company's network were being diverted illegally to China.

The company's activities also attracted scrutiny outside the US. Singaporean authorities questioned Alice Huang in 2025 before releasing her, according to The New York Times.

The investigation, initially handled by the Commerce Department, was transferred to the Justice Department this year, administration officials told the newspaper.

HOW DID SHE DEVELOP A CONNECTION WITH JENSEN HUANG?

One of the most sensitive aspects of the investigation was Alice Huang's reported relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who is not related to her.

According to The New York Times, US intelligence agencies discovered that the two had developed a close relationship while investigating the businesswoman's suspected links to Beijing.

The connection reportedly emerged after intelligence agencies intercepted communications involving Alice Huang and an American citizen. A process known as unmasking subsequently identified the American as Jensen Huang.

Under US intelligence rules, the identities of American citizens may be disclosed through this process when their communications are incidentally collected during authorised surveillance of a foreign target.

The two were photographed together at a bar in Taipei in June 2024, following a technology trade show. The photographs, shared on LinkedIn by technology company NetThunder, showed Jensen Huang sitting alongside Alice Huang and other executives.

They were seen together again in May 2025, leaving a restaurant in Taipei after a business dinner with AI suppliers. According to The New York Times, Alice Huang waited behind as Jensen Huang spoke to journalists.

While the exact circumstances and beginning of their relationship remain unclear, these encounters became significant after American intelligence agencies examined her alleged activities and connections.

WHY DID HER CONNECTION WITH NVIDIA'S CEO RAISE ALARMS?

The concerns surrounding Alice Huang went beyond her association with a company suspected of helping Chinese businesses obtain restricted technology.

Jensen Huang is among the most influential figures in America's artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia's advanced chips are central to the development of AI systems, making the company a key player in the US effort to maintain its technological advantage over China.

He has also emerged as an important interlocutor for the Trump administration on technology, manufacturing, jobs and national security.

According to The New York Times, American intelligence officials were concerned that Alice Huang could have obtained information about Nvidia's business plans through her interactions with its CEO. There were also questions about whether such interactions could have given Beijing insights into Trump's thinking on advanced chip exports to China.

The issue was particularly sensitive because Jensen Huang had been lobbying the Trump administration to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China.

The newspaper reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about a year ago. However, officials did not believe that Jensen Huang knew that the businesswoman was allegedly gathering information for Beijing.

According to people familiar with the surveillance cited by the newspaper, Jensen Huang has not received a defensive briefing of the kind US authorities sometimes provide to Americans who may be targeted by foreign intelligence services.

WHAT HAVE NVIDIA AND MEGASPEED SAID?

Nvidia has rejected suggestions that its interactions with Alice Huang were unusual or that Megaspeed received sensitive company information.

In a statement to The New York Times, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said that meetings with customers were a routine part of the CEO's responsibilities.

"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Rizzo said.

He added that regional cloud customers such as Megaspeed received ordinary business information, not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets or information relevant to national security.

Rizzo also said Nvidia was confident that the US government would inform the company if it believed any individual posed a threat to American industry.

Megaspeed, meanwhile, said its current leadership was taking the allegations seriously. The company said it had appointed outside legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation and had informed the US government of its willingness to cooperate.

INVESTIGATION INTO ALLEGED CHINA LINKS CONTINUES

Alice Huang remains under surveillance by US intelligence agencies, according to The New York Times. Companies affiliated with Megaspeed have also continued purchasing Nvidia products this year, often through intermediaries.

The developments have placed her at the centre of a wider debate over the movement of advanced AI technology between the US and China, and the difficulties Washington faces in enforcing export restrictions through companies operating in third countries.

For now, the allegations against Alice Huang remain part of an ongoing investigation. Her reported association with Jensen Huang has added another layer of sensitivity to a case involving commercial interests, intelligence concerns and the growing technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

text:
DoorDash DASH agreed on Thursday, Oct. 29, to acquire Maplebear Inc. CART, doing business as Instacart, in a transaction valued at approximately $17 billion. The offer prices the target at $65 per share, with stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination, subject to proration. Usually, an acquired company's stock immediately climbs to approach the buyout price. Instead, Instacart shares hovered near $57, leaving a wide spread between the current price and the proposed payout.

This pricing gap suggests investors may anticipate a prolonged, difficult path to final approval. The companies estimate the transaction will not close until late 2027 or the first half of 2028. In the interim, Instacart has suspended its forward guidance and canceled its scheduled Nov. 5 earnings call. For investors analyzing this local commerce combination, the wide discount signals that Wall Street expects regulatory scrutiny before any shares change hands.

Price Checks and Missing Premiums

The deal's mechanics highlight two companies operating from different positions of strength. DoorDash reported a solid third quarter, posting GAAP earnings of $1.06 per share, above the 81 cents consensus. Revenue expanded 34% year over year to $4.62 billion, topping estimates and setting internal records for marketplace gross order volume.

This core business strength gives management the flexibility to pursue an aggressive expansion into grocery delivery. DoorDash plans to use cash on hand and debt financing to fund the cash portion of the deal, which reportedly makes up at least 75% of the total consideration.

On the other side of the table, Maplebear Inc. faces a more complicated picture. While third-quarter revenue grew to roughly $1.1 billion and gross transaction volume increased 15%, the company reported earnings per share of 60 cents, missing analyst estimates.

After the deal announcement, shares settled around $57.11, roughly 12% below the $65 offer. A discount of this magnitude in merger arbitrage can reflect significant market doubt about the probability of a successful close, not just the time value of money.

Too Many Cooks: The Federal Pushback

The skepticism priced into Instacart's stock price stems directly from the regulatory landscape. DoorDash currently holds a leading share of U.S. restaurant delivery, while Instacart is a major player in third-party grocery delivery. Bringing the two major U.S. delivery applications under one roof is likely to draw antitrust scrutiny from the Federal Trade Commission.

History provides a useful guide here. DoorDash previously explored acquiring Instacart in 2021 when valuations were substantially higher. Those preliminary talks largely dissolved because of potential opposition from antitrust regulators. The FTC has also scrutinized delivery platforms' pricing and fee practices.

Beyond federal regulators, the proposed merger is already drawing organized opposition. Advocacy groups like the American Economic Liberties Project have urged regulators to block the transaction, citing concerns over wage suppression and reduced leverage for the roughly nine million gig workers operating across both platforms.

Local officials in major metropolitan areas have echoed these concerns, warning that corporate consolidation could lead to higher consumer prices. DoorDash's recent string of smaller acquisitions, including platforms like Deliveroo and SevenRooms, along with its announced agreement to acquire Grubhub's campus dining business, illustrate its broader expansion through acquisitions.

The Long Road to Closing

If the deal survives the regulatory gauntlet, the strategic and financial rationale becomes clear. The ultimate goal is to build enough scale in local commerce to compete directly with retail giants like Amazon AMZN and Walmart WMT.

Management is targeting $500 million or more in combined operational efficiencies, driven by cross-selling capabilities and a broad delivery network. Combining restaurant logistics with grocery fulfillment could allow a single driver to complete multiple, varied orders in a single trip, improving unit economics for the platform while offering consumers a single local commerce destination.

The projected closing window stretches into late 2027 or early 2028. That 18-month to 24-month horizon introduces substantial execution risk. While waiting for regulatory clearance, business conditions, consumer spending habits, and interest rates can shift dramatically, potentially altering the fundamental value of the assets involved.

Instacart executives also reported share sales in late October, although the transactions occurred under prearranged trading plans. Chief Executive Officer Chris Rogers executed two major sales, offloading 24,060 shares on Oct. 23 and another 24,665 shares on Oct. 26. Additional filings show Chief Financial Officer Emily Reuter selling 50,000 shares on Oct. 23 and Chief Legal Officer Morgan Fong selling 18,390 shares on Oct. 22. All three transactions occurred under Rule 10b5-1 trading plans established months earlier, so the timing alone does not suggest advance knowledge of the deal.

Left at the Door: Evaluating Standalone Realities

For investors holding either stock, the current environment requires weighing the downside risks if regulators ultimately block the transaction. DoorDash may be better positioned to withstand a failed deal. The company is operating at record volumes, its international expansion through Wolt continues to gain traction, and its core restaurant delivery business generates enough cash flow to support ongoing logistics investments. If the Instacart acquisition stalls, DoorDash would still have its established delivery operations and ongoing expansion efforts.

Instacart faces a more precarious setup. The company's recent earnings miss and subsequent decision to suspend forward guidance leave the stock lacking near-term catalysts outside of the acquisition narrative. The company has made commendable strides in building a high-margin advertising business, but without guidance, the market struggles to price that future growth. If regulators successfully challenge the merger, Instacart shares could lose some or all of the remaining acquisition premium attached to the $65 offer.

Investors considering a position in Instacart are currently balancing the potential upside between its share price and the $65 offer against the opportunity cost of tying up capital for potentially two years, alongside the distinct risk of a regulatory block. Cautious investors might prefer to monitor the initial federal commentary and early shareholder votes before committing capital, as the true odds of completion will become much clearer once the regulatory review officially begins.

The big-picture story is still good for J&J What's interesting is that J&J increased its full-year revenue and earnings guidance even as it took that big quarterly charge.

text:
Johnson & Johnson(NYSE: JNJ) is a member of the highly elite club of companies known as Dividend Kings. It has increased its dividend annually for a huge 64 years. As you consider the $7 billion charge the company took in the third quarter of 2026, which pummeled its earnings, keep in mind its incredible dividend track record. This is a business that knows how to survive and thrive.

In fact, despite the weak quarterly earnings, J&J upped its full-year guidance. Here's a deep dive into what happened and what it means for conservative long-term dividend investors.

What's up with J&J's $7 billion charge?

To quote the company, "Results in the quarter were impacted by the proposed talc litigation resolution as well as expenses associated with the Firefly Bio transaction and Sail Biomedicines' collaboration amounting to approximately $7 billion." There are two pieces to consider here, one not so good and one that's much better.

The negative is the litigation expense. J&J spun off the business that used to make talcum powder, but it still faces exposure to the class action lawsuit alleging the company's talcum powder caused cancer. It has a potential settlement that will largely end the litigation, but it comes at a high cost. An initial payment of $3 billion is due in 2027, with the remainder of the proposed $5.5 billion settlement set to be paid in future years. That's a lot of money, but at least it could help bring to a close a legal headwind that has dogged the company for years.

Meanwhile, the remainder of the quarterly charge was for items that will help J&J grow over the long term: an acquisition and a partnership. Simply put, despite the legal distractions this healthcare giant faces, it remains focused on long-term growth.

The big-picture story is still good for J&J

What's interesting is that J&J increased its full-year revenue and earnings guidance even as it took that big quarterly charge. It highlights something that the company's status as a Dividend King hints at: J&J knows how to thrive through good times and bad.

Even the best-run businesses eventually go through difficult periods. Surviving those periods while continuing to reward investors with regular dividend increases is a distinction that sets J&J apart. In fact, it has the longest dividend streak of any healthcare company.

The truth is, you could actually view the talc settlement as a net positive as well, despite the huge cost. Removing that issue will make it easier for J&J to focus on the long-term growth of its business. And that growth could continue for decades, given the importance of healthcare in an aging society. It's also important to keep in mind that the company's revenues grew nearly 6% in the quarter, signaling that the core business remains strong despite the roughly 96% decline in GAAP earnings per share.

Notably, healthcare spending tends to be resilient to recessions, since it isn't usually optional. Getting the talc issue out of the way now, while the economy is still growing, spares the company from taking a huge charge when investors are worried about other issues, like a bear market. Don't underestimate the importance of the timing. In a bull market, investors are willing to overlook bad news; in a bear market, investors often pay extra attention to it.

J&J remains a fundamentally strong business

You don't need to dig too deeply into the one-time charge to understand that Johnson & Johnson is still a good company. The quarter was ugly, but the outlook remains bright. And if you are a conservative long-term dividend investor, this Dividend King remains as resilient as ever.

title: Why Blockchain Is Becoming Financial Infrastructure Rather Than Just an Investment Technology
description:
Plenty of people still see crypto only as an asset, and blockchain only as an investment technology.
The growing connection between established financial markets and blockchain technology has some visible examples.
Developments like this suggest the future of blockchain technology may be becoming less tied to the success or failure of any single cryptocurrency.
Pontes is therefore not another route for trading traditional assets with blockchain technology.
Still, the development of systems like Pontes suggests that some traditional financial institutions see potential in blockchain technology as infrastructure.
text:
Plenty of people still see crypto only as an asset, and blockchain only as an investment technology. For them, checking the XRP price today on an exchange such as Binance might be the main way they interact with the crypto market. But the technology underlying digital assets is starting to be used for more than that. Blockchain is increasingly being tested as infrastructure underneath financial markets, with potential uses in settling, issuing, and trading assets.

The growing connection between established financial markets and blockchain technology has some visible examples. On September 21, 2026, the European Central Bank (ECB) launched a new system called Pontes, which is designed to allow wholesale transactions in tokenized assets to settle using central bank money.

Developments like this suggest the future of blockchain technology may be becoming less tied to the success or failure of any single cryptocurrency. Many investors still focus on the price of XRP or whichever other coin they hold, while some financial institutions are exploring how distributed ledger technology could support the processes that run markets. The industry has also put down local roots, with a cryptocurrency mining company choosing Fayetteville for a regional headquarters.

Traditional Financial Infrastructure Is Moving On-Chain

Assets pass through several stages between being created and reaching an investor. Those stages include issuance, trading, custody, settlement and servicing, and each requires its own reconciliation processes, intermediaries and systems.

The ECB believes some of these stages can be combined and streamlined through tokenization. It describes the new Pontes system as a way to make financial transactions more efficient and faster by bringing different parts of an asset’s lifecycle together. In effect, the idea is to automate stages of a financial asset’s lifecycle using smart contracts and distributed ledger technology.

This is not a wholesale replacement of traditional financial infrastructure. Blockchain-based systems are being integrated within the infrastructure that financial markets and institutions already use.

Pontes reflects that approach. The ECB has said the financial institutions initially participating include Santander, BayernLB, Deutsche Bank and Société Générale, along with providers of market infrastructure.

What Pontes Does Differently

The main difference Pontes introduces is the type of currency that can be used for settlement. Tokenized financial assets would normally be settled using private crypto or stablecoin assets, but Pontes allows eligible transactions to be settled in central bank money. Central bank money is already a core piece of the settlement ecosystem the ECB uses.

According to the ECB, Pontes is the first initiative to make central bank money suitable for settling tokenized financial transactions. Its services are expected to expand over time, with additional functionality and longer operating hours phased in through 2028.

Pontes is therefore not another route for trading traditional assets with blockchain technology. It is a connection between established financial infrastructure and markets that exist on blockchain systems, and a step toward combining digital and traditional finance through shared infrastructure.

Washington is moving along a parallel track. In September, the SEC issued a five-year Innovation Exemption that lets qualifying venues trade tokenized U.S. stocks on blockchain-based systems, a sign that American regulators are also making room for this kind of market plumbing.

Tokenization Is Growing Beyond Experiments

Tokenization is spreading across a number of asset classes, though it is doing so gradually.

A report released by Binance Research in September 2026 showed an 85.2% increase in tokenized real-world assets since the beginning of the year, to a value of $34.18 billion on September 15.

The growth rate is high, but tokenized assets still represent a very small share of global financial markets. Despite rapid percentage growth, blockchain technology is far from transforming global finance, and financial institutions and other market participants are still adopting and testing it slowly.

Blockchain Could Change How Markets Operate, With Open Questions

It could, but whether and when is less certain. For blockchain technology to be used substantially across financial markets, several big questions need answers. Interoperability, custody, liquidity, regulation, and technological standards are all still under scrutiny, and many market participants have yet to see them satisfactorily resolved.

Still, the development of systems like Pontes suggests that some traditional financial institutions see potential in blockchain technology as infrastructure. In many cases, blockchain may be used not to replace traditional financial technology but to improve those processes and make them more efficient, connected and automated.

text:

GLP-1 Focus or Broader Peptide Exposure: Which ETF Has the Edge?

Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE:LLY) raised its full-year outlook after reporting third-quarter revenue growth of 39% from the prior-year period, driven primarily by demand for its Mounjaro and Zepbound incretin medicines and continued growth across international markets.

Chair and CEO Dave Ricks said revenue increased by nearly $7 billion compared with the third quarter of 2025, while revenue from key products rose by more than $6 billion. The company also cited doubled revenue from its oncology, immunology and neuroscience portfolio.

Eli Lilly's First Full Medicare Quarter: Is Volume Still Outrunning Price Cuts?

Lilly increased its 2026 revenue guidance to $91 billion to $92 billion and projected non-GAAP earnings per share of $35 to $36. CFO Lucas Montarce said the outlook reflects strength in U.S. demand, including uptake of the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program, as well as international Mounjaro performance.

Incretin growth drives results

Mounjaro and Zepbound generated more than $16 billion in combined third-quarter revenue, representing $6 billion of growth from the year-earlier quarter, according to Montarce. U.S. revenue increased 34%, primarily on higher volumes for the two medicines, partially offset by a 7% decline in price. Excluding a favorable adjustment to rebate and discount estimates, U.S. price declined 10%, he said.

→ Boeing Got Its MAX 10 Approval, But Q3 Delivered a Reality Check

Buy the Dip: 4 Stocks the Market Marked Down Too Far Ahead of Big Catalysts

Outside the United States, Mounjaro drove growth in several markets. European revenue rose 29% in constant currency, aided by volume growth and a $410 million one-time Jardiance milestone payment. Revenue in Japan grew 26% in constant currency, China revenue increased 62%, and revenue in the rest of the world rose 87% in constant currency.

Montarce said Mounjaro became the first medicine in China to surpass $1 billion in revenue during its first full year. Lilly's international incretin business increased 53% year over year based on IQVIA gross-sales measurements, and the company's share reached approximately 58%, up nearly four percentage points from the second quarter.

→ Johnson Controls Beats the Heat in AI Data Centers

The company said its Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program had enrolled more than 500,000 prescription fills since its July 1 launch. Ricks said approximately 20 million seniors have access to obesity medicines through the program, and seven of 10 new Bridge patients are starting on a Lilly obesity medicine. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities, said about 80% of people receiving treatment through the program are new to incretin therapy or had not used it previously.

Ricks said Lilly expects the program's early uptake and potential cost effectiveness to support continued access beyond 2027, though he noted that future arrangements would involve discussions with the administration and Part D carriers.

Foundayo launch expands oral market

Lilly said Foundayo, its oral obesity medicine, is gaining traction in the U.S. and four international markets. In the U.S., approximately four in 10 patients beginning an oral obesity medicine selected Foundayo, while the number of new Foundayo patients doubled sequentially in the third quarter.

Yuffa said Foundayo accounted for 45% of sequential growth in oral prescriptions from the second quarter to the third quarter. About 25% of patients are at one of the medicine's maintenance doses, according to the company.

Internationally, Lilly launched Foundayo in the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia and Mexico. Patrik Jonsson, president of Lilly International, said early launches were tracking in line with expectations and that oral medicines were bringing new patients into incretin therapy. Lilly expects regulatory action on Foundayo in U.S. type 2 diabetes during the fourth quarter and said it anticipates a broader global rollout in major markets during 2027.

Margins, spending and 2027 considerations

Third-quarter gross margin rose 80 basis points to 84.4% of revenue, supported by product mix and lower production costs, partly offset by lower realized prices. Marketing, selling and administrative expenses rose 14%, while research and development spending increased 23% as Lilly invested in its pipeline and acquired programs.

Non-GAAP performance margin was 54.2%, up 5.9 percentage points from the third quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP earnings per share were $7.48, including $4.57 of acquired in-process research and development charges, compared with $7.02 a year earlier, which included $0.71 of such charges.

For 2027, Montarce said Lilly expects continued incretin volume growth, a full-year contribution from the Medicare Bridge Program and a potential U.S. type 2 diabetes launch for Foundayo. He also said 2026 benefited from about $2 billion of one-time items, principally milestone payments and changes in rebate and discount estimates, that are not expected to recur.

Yuffa said Lilly expects commercial obesity-drug access to remain relatively stable in 2027, with expanded Medicare and Medicaid access representing the main opportunity for coverage growth. He said a changing mix toward Medicare, Medicaid and self-pay channels could pressure average net price, while the company expects to maintain a "modest and disciplined" approach to commercial pricing and access.

Pipeline, approvals and manufacturing investment

Lilly highlighted new U.S. approvals for weekly basal insulin Onswik and for tirzepatide to reduce cardiovascular risk in adults with type 2 diabetes. The Food and Drug Administration also approved pirtobrutinib for certain previously untreated chronic lymphocytic leukemia or small lymphocytic lymphoma patients, and approved imlunestrant with abemaciclib for certain advanced breast cancer patients.

Chief Scientific and Product Officer Dan Skovronsky said retatrutide reduced A1C by 2.2% and produced 20% to 21% weight loss in the TRANSCEND-T2D-2 study, compared with a 1.8% A1C reduction and 9.4% weight loss for 2-milligram semaglutide. Lilly also reported phase II results for EloraTZP, a combination of eloralintide and tirzepatide, showing 23.3% weight loss at 48 weeks in people with type 2 diabetes and obesity.

The company acquired AtaiBeckley, adding neuroplastogen programs for depression and other mental-health conditions, and Merida Biosciences, which is developing a phase I precision-immunology therapy for Graves' disease and thyroid eye disease.

Lilly also broke ground on a $6.5 billion manufacturing facility in Houston and a $5 billion facility in Richmond, Virginia. During the quarter, it paid $1.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $400 million of shares.

Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY) is a global pharmaceutical company that discovers, develops, manufactures and markets medicines for a range of medical conditions. Its major therapeutic areas include diabetes and obesity, oncology, immunology, neuroscience and cardiovascular health.

The company's portfolio includes Mounjaro and Trulicity for diabetes, Zepbound for chronic weight management, Humalog insulin, Taltz for inflammatory diseases, Verzenio for certain breast cancers and Kisunla for early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease.

text:
NEW YORK, Oct 31 — Nvidia’s US$3 billion (RM12 billion) investment in Meta’s share sale, announced Tuesday, is the latest addition to a portfolio of stakes, loans and guarantees that has made the chip giant what some analysts describe as the central bank of the artificial intelligence boom.

The galaxy of deals has helped keep demand running high for Nvidia’s processors, which power vast data centres around the world and are the central ingredient of the AI revolution.

That demand has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company by market capitalisation and turned chief executive Jensen Huang into AI’s kingmaker.

But the investments have raised a nagging question among some doubters on Wall Street: is Nvidia helping to inflate an AI bubble?

What is Nvidia investing in?

Nvidia has taken stakes in leading AI developers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI, now part of SpaceX.

It has also invested in “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent out computing power built on Nvidia chips.

Its bets extend well beyond the United States. In Europe, Nvidia has backed French AI developer Mistral and British self-driving startup Wayve. In Asia, it has teamed up with South Korea’s SK Group to build data centres.

Beyond equity, the company has offered financial backstops, acting as a customer of last resort.

In CoreWeave’s case, Nvidia committed to buy up to US$6.3 billion of unused computing capacity if no other customer takes it.

Nvidia also has around US$36 billion in cloud backstops and a guarantee of up to US$105 billion linked to an OpenAI data centre, according to US media.

Why is Nvidia doing this?

Experts say Nvidia’s enormous profits give it few better options.

“They’re essentially becoming a bank,” said Michael Cusumano, a professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management.

“Channeling it back to infrastructure investment tied to purchases of Nvidia equipment is a smart thing.”

He said the alternatives were less attractive.

Running its own data centers would put Nvidia in competition with its biggest customers “and that might also trigger a whole bunch of antitrust complaints,” Cusumano added.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia identifies parts of the AI ecosystem that are not investing enough and puts money into them to fill the gaps.

“It’s unprecedented, but it appears to be working,” he said.

Huang has defended the approach, arguing that frontier AI labs are the first generation of startups that need tens of billions of dollars to get started, not just millions.

Nvidia’s investments effectively give those companies more time to succeed.

Is it ‘circular’ financing?

Critics have compared the deals to the dot-com era, when companies inflated their growth by investing in startups that then bought their products.

“There is nothing intrinsically wrong with Nvidia helping its clients,” said Paulo Carvão, a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School.

“But the closer these relationships are, the harder it is for one to assess true sustainable demand.”

Luria said not all demand was equal.

“If Nvidia gives CoreWeave money to turn around and buy Nvidia chips, that’s not as good as Microsoft buying Nvidia chips because they have a customer in OpenAI that has a customer in an enterprise technology that’s willing to pay for it,” he said.

What are the risks?

The main concern is concentration. Two direct customers accounted for 22 percent and 14 per cent of Nvidia’s revenue in its 2026 fiscal year, according to the company’s annual report.

Carvão said the web of overlapping investments increases the risk of contagion if a weaker company such as CoreWeave runs into trouble.

“If AI demand disappoints, spending cuts could hit chipmakers, data-center builders and their financiers at once,” he said.

Those concerns have grown this month. Shares of several Nvidia-linked neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, fell at least 30 per cent in October amid worries about tighter credit for AI projects.

Carvão noted that the market for AI chips remains limited by supply. He estimated demand would keep growing for another 12 to 18 months before it begins to level off.

Cusumano said he expected high demand for Nvidia chips to continue for three to five years. — AFP

title: Tech needs legacy businesses to grow trillions into AI buildout - CNBC
description:
For now, they’re reliant on their legacy businesses — whether it’s online advertising, business software or e-commerce — to fund their artificial intelligence ambitions.
Earnings this quarter revealed new levels of strain on those core businesses and offered an early test of whether these companies can sustain extended bouts of spending.
Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, while Amazon’s outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet’s reached $9.07 billion.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% after the earnings report last week even though the company beat on revenue.
“Weakness in Search and YouTube revenue performance relative to expectations surfaces growing concern about AI displacement of the company’s largest revenue generators,” Woo said.
text:
Sebastien Bozon | AFP | Getty Images

The tech megacaps are collectively placing a multitrillion-dollar bet that their infrastructure spending will result in many years of profitable growth. But that’s all in the future.

For now, they’re reliant on their legacy businesses — whether it’s online advertising, business software or e-commerce — to fund their artificial intelligence ambitions.

Earnings this quarter revealed new levels of strain on those core businesses and offered an early test of whether these companies can sustain extended bouts of spending. Meta joined Alphabet and Amazon in reporting negative free cash flow, leaving Microsoft as the lone hyperscaler to remain positive in that realm.

Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, while Amazon’s outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet’s reached $9.07 billion. Microsoft’s cash generation declined dramatically for a second straight quarter, this time dropping 27% to $18.63 billion, and the company said it will now turn to the bond market as it continues to ramp up AI infrastructure spending.

Hyperscaler earnings over the past two weeks have coincided with intensifying concerns about the overall health and stability of the broader AI sector. Rising interest rates are making it costlier for companies to raise debt, putting pressure on cash-burning neoclouds that have become critical to the global buildout.

While the tech giants have a cushion not afforded to the neoclouds and other players, investors eventually need the historic rates of spending to convert into massive new revenue streams. Nerves are hitting the stocks this week, with Alphabet suffering its steepest drop ever on Thursday and Amazon sliding in extended trading after its report.

watch now

Amazon said growth slowed in both its retail and ad business. Online sales gained 2% year over year, decelerating from 10% a year ago and falling short of analysts’ estimates. The midpoint of Amazon’s revenue guidance came in lower than the $244.5 billion that analysts were expecting, a particularly disappointing figure for the quarter that includes the holiday shopping season.

Meanwhile, Amazon expects capital expenditures this year to reach $220 billion, and analysts project that number will top $280 billion next year, according to FactSet, as the company continues to produce negative free cash flow.

At Meta, investors have responded favorably to the company’s early success with its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, which present potential new sources of revenue outside of advertising.

But it will take time for these efforts to significantly impact the company’s overall business while it continues spending on data center and computing gear. Capex will reach as high as $145 billion this year, the company says, and analysts see it passing $210 billion in 2027, alongside a deepening cash flow hole.

Investors sent Meta shares down 7% after the earnings report last week even though the company beat on revenue. Meta followed its report by announcing on Monday that it’s planning to raise a total of $95 billion in stock to support its AI investments.

‘Borrowing from the for-now’

Alphabet’s report concerned investors the most.

The company’s core search business saw a third straight quarter of slowing growth and missed analysts’ projections, underscoring the challenges it faces with the rise of ChatGPT, Claude and other AI-powered bots and agents. YouTube-related advertising revenue also came in light.

Mark Mahaney, an analyst at Evercore, told CNBC’s “Closing Bell Overtime” on Wednesday that while Google’s strong cloud revenue was “good news” for the company, its decelerating digital advertising business represented “the overwhelming bad news.”

Forrester analyst Tracy Woo said in an email that “Alphabet’s massive capex investment in infrastructure buildout has been tolerated for now,” but the company “is walking a fine line,” due to the online ad sales misses.

“Weakness in Search and YouTube revenue performance relative to expectations surfaces growing concern about AI displacement of the company’s largest revenue generators,” Woo said. “The issue is less the current earnings miss and more the possibility that future AI spending grows faster than the cash generation of the franchises expected to support it.”

But not everyone is concerned. Bullish investors say that the tech leaders have long histories of operations, and legacy businesses that are dominant enough to prop them up for the foreseeable future.

Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, noted that Alphabet’s negative free cash flow of $9 billion is tiny relative to the company’s overall business. Its operating income topped $40 billion for the quarter.

Unlike AI model companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which are still unprofitable and spending billions of dollars a quarter on infrastructure, Alphabet has a strong balance sheet, Ballard said.

“They’re borrowing from the for-now in order to invest in the future,” Ballard said. “I think it’s OK, and they’re doing it in a responsible manner.”

Although the hyperscalers didn’t provide specific capex projections for next year, they all implied their data center spending spree will continue to grow, even if it means reporting some uncomfortable metrics.

“Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years, and you can spread the capex over 25 years?” Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Thursday’s earnings call. “Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”

text:
Oct 30 (Reuters) – S&P Global Ratings on Friday revised its outlook on Meta Platforms to “negative” from “stable”, citing significant uncertainty around the social media giant’s capital spending and free operating cash flow.

Big Tech has historically spent heavily on cloud computing, online advertising and e-commerce, but the AI boom has pushed capital expenditure to dizzying levels, stoking investor concerns about whether the sector can generate returns quickly enough.

Last week, Meta forecast annual capital expenditure between $135 billion-$145 billion after reporting a free cash flow deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter. Meta is also planning to tap public markets and sell $97.5 billion in stock to fund the AI buildout.

Meta’s ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers, S&P said, adding it was unclear when its revenue streams would generate material contributions exceeding their rising costs over the next few years.

S&P now forecasts Meta will generate FOCF deficits of $39 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027.

The agency said elevated spending could keep FOCF negative beyond 2028 and expects Meta to fund its 2028 cash shortfall entirely with debt.

“Given the lack of clarity around the company’s future capex and its very ambitious multi-year AI investment plans, we are less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated,” S&P said.

The ratings agency said it believes Meta’s leverage could rise to above 1.0x as early as 2027, which is S&P Global’s threshold for the “AA-” issuer credit rating.

“We respectfully disagree with S&P’s assertion about Meta’s AI monetization capabilities,” a Meta spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company sees “significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile.”

Meta’s leverage increased from 0.1x in 2025, primarily due to its strategy of leasing data-center capacity rather than issuing debt, S&P said.

“If capex remains elevated and continues to grow at a faster pace than we expect, credit profiles will continue to weaken and cash flows will be negative,” Naveen Sarma, US media and telecom sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said.

The company reported long-term debt of $80.92 billion as of September 30.

S&P on Thursday also lowered its outlook on Broadcom to stable from positive, saying the chipmaker’s rapid AI growth was increasing its exposure to a few big customers.

Earlier this year, S&P lowered cloud computing giant Oracle’s credit rating to “BBB-“, one notch above “junk”, due to its heavily leveraged balance sheet.

(Reporting by Vallari Srivastava and Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing by Pooja Desai)

text:
Italy’s second-largest bank, UniCredit, will see its chairman, Pier Carlo Padoan, stepping down at the end of his term in early 2027 for personal reasons, as the lender advances its takeover of German rival Commerzbank and prepares for a change in board leadership.

Padoan, 76, and the rest of UniCredit’s board, including Chief Executive Andrea Orcel, the key architect behind the Commerzbank acquisition, are due to complete their mandates in early 2027.

Shareholders will appoint a new board when they meet to approve the bank’s 2026 results.

The bank said Padoan would work closely with its nomination committee to identify a suitable successor.

“Padoan has been a source of sound counsel and wisdom, and I have greatly valued our partnership,” Orcel said in a statement.

Padoan, a former Italian economy and finance minister, joined UniCredit in April 2021, when Orcel took over as chief executive.

He secured a three-year reappointment in 2024, although the bank had previously considered a potential replacement amid strained relations with Italy’s centre-right government.

Padoan served as the European country’s economy and finance minister from 2014 to 2018 under successive centre-left administrations.

Padoan’s departure comes as UniCredit faces significant strategic decisions over the future of Commerzbank, where the Italian lender has built a stake of almost 50% despite opposition from the German bank and criticism from the German government.

UniCredit’s governance rules allow the outgoing board to present a list of candidates to replace it.

However, changes to Italian legislation governing how outgoing boards nominate successors have discouraged other companies, including insurer Generali, from presenting board slates, amid concerns that the new rules could produce unpredictable and potentially chaotic outcomes.

The leadership transition will coincide with a critical period for UniCredit’s German expansion, as Orcel seeks to secure savings at Commerzbank and move towards a potential full integration.

Talking about the current situation regarding the Commerzbank acquisition, UniCredit said the European Central Bank had authorised it to cross the 30% ownership threshold in the German major and increase its stake without an upper limit.

The approval followed a 45 billion euro (USD 50.51 billion) hostile takeover offer completed in July, which lifted UniCredit’s stake in the German lender to 48%.

The bank needed regulatory approval to take delivery of shares tendered in the offer and advance what could become Europe’s largest cross-border banking deal since the global financial crisis.

UniCredit said it expected to take control of Commerzbank by the end of the year, with around 50% of voting rights, after completing the remaining regulatory processes and conditions.

The Italian lender, which has operated German bank HVB since 2005, began investing in Commerzbank more than two years ago as Orcel pursued a takeover that several of his predecessors had also considered.

Despite resistance from Commerzbank and the German government, UniCredit secured enough shares to control ordinary shareholder resolutions while remaining below the 50% threshold that would require it to buy out minority investors in Commerzbank’s Polish subsidiary, mBank.

Orcel has asked Commerzbank to adopt his strategy to improve profitability from January while pushing back a full merger to 2029-2030.

The UniCredit chief has held discussions with German government representatives, who want Commerzbank to retain its Frankfurt headquarters, protect jobs, and continue lending to German businesses.

Once it has taken possession of the shares, Orcel has threatened to call a shareholder vote and install a new supervisory board and management team at Commerzbank without waiting for the German lender’s annual general meeting next year.

For UniCredit, the next phase will involve translating its growing ownership into operational changes and targeted savings while navigating political opposition and regulatory requirements.

text:
DoorDash announced on October 29 that it will buy Instacart for about $17 billion. Mergers and acquisitions usually happen for the benefit of shareholders, but to get the deals passed by regulators, companies say that they are for the benefit of consumers and employees. So it’s no surprise that the DoorDash announcement leads with benefits for consumers, delivery drivers, and local retailers.

Consumers And Drivers Will Get The Short End Of The Stick

Let’s be clear: DoorDash is buying a competitor and is using its inflated stock price to do so (its price-earnings ratio is a whopping 90+, in contrast to Amazon’s, which is around 20). DoorDash’s announcement called out several outcomes of the acquisition: more choice for shoppers, better exposure for stores, two memberships for the price of one, and more ways to earn for drivers and delivery personnel. Much of what is likely to happen is microeconomics 101:

Less choice for shoppers over time. Because DoorDash and Instacart have significantly overlapping businesses, both in grocery and in same-day retail, a merger gives the combined entity more leverage to deprioritize or even reject unfavorable consumers. In our experience, e-commerce companies are often highly aggressive with consumer acquisition in the face of competition, even losing money to win market share. Acquisitions buy the market share and limit consumers’ options and comparison shopping power.

Higher membership fees in the long run. DoorDash claims it will make “two memberships for the price of one.” Presumably, they will refund one membership for anyone who belongs to both programs. That may make sense if there isn’t much overlap. But we foresee instead that this combined entity will raise its membership fees over time, just as Netflix and Amazon have done. Promotional membership rates intended to thwart competition are unnecessary after merging with the primary competitor.

Lower pay for drivers and delivery people. On-demand delivery services often face bursts in demand: think of winter storms or the Super Bowl. Competing for good drivers during high demand periods often requires higher pay and surge prices. One platform creates a monopsony that benefits the combined entity, not drivers and delivery personnel. What about competition from Uber Eats or Amazon? Amazon’s central fulfillment model makes it a very different player that is not competitive with DoorDash at this time. Uber Eats is similar but smaller and could also benefit from lower driver fees (Uber’s stock rose slightly on the news of this acquisition).

The Real Beneficiaries Are The Shareholders

The benefits to shareholders, however, should be substantial. In order for a $17 billion acquisition to make sense, two brands with overlapping services and geographies will have to be combined. Combining order routing, consolidating marketing spend, supporting a single retail media network, and reducing headcount by consolidating similar overhead functions are all obvious outcomes. That’s why we expect the eventual merger of the two brands — even though the DoorDash CEO said in the press release announcing the acquisition that they will remain separate. We sometimes see CEOs do that to allay the fears of skittish employees and maintain stability while planning for changes to come.

Anticipate The Consolidation

As this all settles out, business leaders should:

Expect both companies to keep talking up local grocers, worker opportunity, and membership savings through a long antitrust review. Just remember whom the deal was designed to benefit.

Evaluate your agreements with both entities and be prepared for renegotiation, because the combined org will do the same.

Keep customer experience at the top of your priority list and make sure that changes don’t sully the experience in that last mile before your products are in your customers’ hands.

The company raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth target to 9% to 9.5% at constant currency, from its earlier estimate of around 8.5% to 9%. It maintained its operating margin target of 13.6% to 13.8%.

Chief executive officer Aiman Ezzat said, "Capgemini delivered another solid quarter, with growth of +11.7% at constant exchange rates and underlying growth close to Q2, once again outperforming the industry. In a stable demand environment, we continue to see strong momentum in North America and the United Kingdom, and a clear acceleration in France."

He also said clients were increasingly focused on deploying AI at enterprise scale, while addressing challenges related to governance, cost and security. This was driving demand for technology and data modernisation and the transformation of business operations with agentic AI.

Capgemini's third-quarter bookings stood at 5.4 billion euros, up 3.4% year-on-year at CC.

Among its business segments, Operations & Engineering recorded the fastest growth, with revenue increasing 26.9% in CC. Strategy & Transformation revenue rose 18.6%, while Applications & Technology, its largest business, grew 3.5%.

Financial Services revenue grew 17% year-on-year, while Consumer Goods & Retail increased 15.5%. Services recorded growth of 22.6%, followed by the Public Sector at 11.5%.

North America remained a key growth market, with revenue rising 18.3% at constant exchange rates. The United Kingdom and Ireland recorded growth of 25.2%, while France grew 4.9%. The rest of Europe grew 3.4%, and Asia-Pacific and Latin America increased 11.9%.

The company had 417,500 employees at the end of September, up 62,800 from a year earlier, primarily reflecting the integration of WNS employees.

text:
DoorDash has agreed to buy grocery delivery company Instacart in a deal valuing its equity at about $17 billion, bringing two major US delivery platforms under a proposed common owner.

The agreement, announced by both companies on 29 October 2026, offers Instacart shareholders $65 per share, a 26% premium to its closing share price on 22 October. At least 75% of the total consideration will be cash, with DoorDash shares accounting for no more than 25%.

The deal is expected to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. Until then, the businesses will operate independently. DoorDash says it intends to retain Instacart’s brand, app and enterprise technology products.

For supermarkets, the most important question is not the headline purchase price but how the merger would reshape the options available to retailers. Instacart supplies ordering, fulfilment, advertising and data technology to grocery businesses, while DoorDash operates a delivery marketplace and logistics network.

A retailer using these services may benefit from broader consumer reach and integrated technology, but could also face questions about pricing, data access and negotiating leverage. The companies have said local grocers will not be required to use an exclusive grocery delivery platform. That commitment will be important to examine as detailed terms and regulatory reviews develop.

The transaction could also strengthen the role of retail media in online grocery. Brands increasingly pay to reach shoppers on digital ordering platforms, so how advertising products and reporting tools are combined may matter to both supermarket operators and FMCG suppliers.

Instacart separately reported third-quarter 2026 results showing gross transaction value growth of 15% and revenue growth of 17%. Those figures show the scale of its existing grocery activity; they do not establish what the combined platform’s future pricing or market share will be.

Competition authorities will assess the transaction before it can proceed. Retailers should therefore avoid treating proposed integration plans as completed operational changes.

GTN has previously examined online shopping and delivery in its coverage of online grocery in Canada and the wider supplier landscape in retail technology market analysis.

The next milestones are Instacart shareholder approval and regulatory reviews in relevant markets.

name: Eli Lilly
title: Eli Lilly Is Now Worth as Much as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway. Can the Rally Keep Going?
description:
That's the real question investors need to ask when they look at Eli Lilly's (NYSE: LLY) roughly $1.1 trillion market cap.
Berkshire Hathaway vs Eli Lilly?
Eli Lilly has a GLP-1 problem, and it's working on it The problem isn't just the size of the company's GLP-1 revenues.
That incredible run is largely driven by the company's GLP-1 success, which has investors very excited about Eli Lilly.
When you bring it all together, Eli Lilly is working to diversify its business (at least moving it in the general direction of Berkshire Hathaway).
text:
Warren Buffett is no longer involved in running Berkshire Hathaway(NYSE: BRKA)(NYSE: BRKB), but the company he built is nothing short of impressive. With a roughly $1.1 trillion market cap as of this writing, it is a diversified giant with businesses spread across insurance, utilities, transportation, energy, retail, and manufacturing. And that doesn't even do justice to the company's scale.

So how does a company with just one big product compare? That's the real question investors need to ask when they look at Eli Lilly's (NYSE: LLY) roughly $1.1 trillion market cap. The answer isn't as clear-cut as it may seem when you consider what Eli Lilly is doing with the profits from its highly successful GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Here's what you need to know.

Berkshire Hathaway vs Eli Lilly? No comparison.

Warren Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway using his simple but highly effective investment approach. To sum it up, Buffett liked to buy well-run companies when they were attractively priced and then hold them for the long term. That allowed him to benefit from the businesses' growth over time, though he generally took a hands-off approach to day-to-day operations. Buffett let company managers do their job while he focused on continuing to build Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio of owned businesses.

The end result is that Buffett handed off a massively diversified company to his hand-picked successor, Greg Abel. If one business within Berkshire Hathaway were to falter, it wouldn't be a particularly big deal. In fact, Greg Abel used headwinds in the housing sector to augment the company's housing-related businesses when he bought Taylor Morrison Home in early 2026.

This is very different from Eli Lilly. The giant pharmaceutical company has achieved huge success in the emerging GLP-1 weight-loss niche. But its GLP-1 product lineup, which includes shots and pills, accounted for nearly two-thirds of the company's revenues in the first half of 2026. That makes the company look like a one-trick pony in comparison to Berkshire Hathaway.

Eli Lilly has a GLP-1 problem, and it's working on it

The problem isn't just the size of the company's GLP-1 revenues. The deeper issue is that drugs have limited patent protections. And once those patent protections end, generic versions of the drug can be sold. That normally results in material revenue declines in the branded drugs. There's some time to go before Eli Lilly has to worry about its GLP-1 drugs facing generic competition, but that competition will eventually come. That's just how the drug sector works.

Which is why it is so important that Eli Lilly is using its GLP-1 profits to expand its healthcare business in new directions. To put it simply, Eli Lilly has gone on a GLP-1-fueled acquisition spree, buying its way into new treatment niches that greatly improve its diversification. To be fair, many of the acquisitions involve drugs that are still in development, so some of this spending may prove to have been in vain. However, Eli Lilly's drug pipeline is robust and diversified, creating a stronger foundation than the huge dependence on GLP-1 revenue may suggest.

Can Eli Lilly's rally keep going?

Eli Lilly's stock has risen over 50% in a year, as of this writing. It is up 400% over the past five years. That incredible run is largely driven by the company's GLP-1 success, which has investors very excited about Eli Lilly. The stock's price-to-earnings ratio is 43x, which is well above the industry average of 27x. Eli Lilly looks expensive, relatively speaking.

When you bring it all together, Eli Lilly is working to diversify its business (at least moving it in the general direction of Berkshire Hathaway). But a lot is riding on the acquisitions it is making, and the GLP-1 patent clock is ticking. If you have a big gain in Eli Lilly, it might make sense to take some profits even if you don't sell your entire position. If you are thinking about buying the stock today, the rally could be more tenuous than you think, given Eli Lilly's huge exposure to just one category of drugs and the still unproven success of its acquisition program.

Mounjaro and Zepbound took Lilly past a $1.146 trillion market cap. I think the next leg of growth could come from somewhere else.

In Q2, Lilly’s Key Products in immunology, oncology and neuroscience grew 121% year over year. Our confidence is high. The rating rests on a streak of earnings beats, guidance that has gone up, and 83% bullish analyst opinion.

Steady Gains Follow a Blowout Quarter and a Busy October

Lilly shares rose 0.3% this past week. They are up 8.8% over the past month, 20.39% year to date and 56.79% over the past year. The 52-week range runs from $804.56 to $1,321.21.

Q2 revenue came in at $22.97 billion, up 47.7%. EPS was $8.38, well above the $6.58 estimate. Lilly also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $85 billion to $87 billion.

October’s news has mostly been about drugs outside weight loss. The FDA expanded Jaypirca’s label to cover previously untreated CLL/SLL. Lilly also presented olomorasib lung cancer data at ESMO.

On top of that, retatrutide produced more than double the weight loss of Ozempic’s highest approved dose in a head-to-head trial released today. Goldman Sachs and Bank of America both raised their price targets this month.

Why Bulls See $1,800 and Beyond

The bull case is $1,807.23. Lilly plans to file retatrutide for approval in Q1 2027. Foundayo, its oral GLP-1, could reach patients who do not want shots. Growth beyond weight loss is already visible: Ebglyss rose 131% and Jaypirca rose 56%.

In early data, the VERVE-102 gene editor cut LDL cholesterol by up to 62%. Lilly has also spent about $20 billion on acquisitions in 2026. Analyst ratings stand at 6 Strong Buy and 19 Buy.

Falling Prices and Revenue Concentration Are the Risks to Watch

The bear case is $1,317.78. Realized prices fell 13% in Q2. Mounjaro and Zepbound together bring in about 65% of revenue. Possible pharma tariffs and Medicare price negotiations add more pressure.

Still, volume grew 60%, and gross margin reached 85.8%. Reported earnings were also held down by $2.78 billion in one-time acquisition charges (acquired IPR&D). That spending is paying for the diversification described above.

Merck (NYSE:MRK) is a useful comparison because it is the cancer-drug leader Lilly hopes to become. Its quarterly revenue grew just 5.1%. Given how much faster Lilly is growing, I think the peer comparison makes our target look reasonable.

name: Microsoft
title: Are Microsoft's Voluntary Buyouts a Sign of What's to Come? - Harvard Business Review
description:
On October 26, Microsoft offered voluntary buyout packages to 60,000 employees—one quarter of its global workforce.
In the early 2000s, as people shifted from landlines to mobile phones, Verizon offered buyouts to 152,000 employees.
When did companies start using voluntary buyouts, and how have they changed over time?
Voluntary buyouts started in the 1970s, primarily in manufacturing.
Companies have been conducting involuntary layoffs over the same time span, and voluntary buyouts have become another important tool for workforce reductions.
text:
On October 26, Microsoft offered voluntary buyout packages to 60,000 employees—one quarter of its global workforce. It’s part of a growing trend of profitable companies taking dramatic steps to cut labor costs, but the tool—voluntary buyouts—is hardly new. Wayne Cascio, now a Distinguished University Professor Emeritus at the University of Colorado Denver, has been studying how companies downsize workers since the 1990s, when he wrote the book Responsible Restructuring: Creative and Profitable Alternatives to Layoffs.

He spoke with me to put the Microsoft news into perspective. Here are some edited excerpts.

HBR: Is Microsoft’s offer to 60,000 people one of the largest ever?

Wayne Cascio: It’s a big number, but it’s not the largest. In the early 2000s, as people shifted from landlines to mobile phones, Verizon offered buyouts to 152,000 employees. In 2006, Ford offered buyouts to 75,000. Both of those companies were losing money and trying to execute turnarounds. Microsoft’s offer to one-quarter of its workforce the same week it beat analysts’ earnings estimates is significant.

When did companies start using voluntary buyouts, and how have they changed over time?

Voluntary buyouts started in the 1970s, primarily in manufacturing. During the global financial crisis in 2008, they were widely used by all kinds of companies. Companies have been conducting involuntary layoffs over the same time span, and voluntary buyouts have become another important tool for workforce reductions.

What’s changing now is the types of people who are being offered buyouts. In the past, companies usually required employees to have reached a minimum age and minimum tenure—say, people over 55 with at least 10 years at the company. Effectively, that means most people were usually within a couple of years of qualifying for retirement. We called them buyouts, but they functioned as early retirement programs. Often, they included early vesting or other retirement sweeteners. Microsoft’s buyouts have no age limitation and almost no tenure requirement. They’re being offered to everyone in certain departments. That approach is becoming more common. Having so many people of all ages affected—that’s different from what we’ve seen before.

Are buyouts always driven by over-hiring or soft economic conditions?

No. Recently, they’re often driven by the need to preserve profit margins. Four tech companies—Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google—are projected to spend $700 billion this year on AI infrastructure and chips. If they want to do that and avoid destroying profit margins, they’ve got to find other ways to cut costs. And labor is a big cost. The goal with a voluntary buyout, instead of a layoff, is to preserve employee morale and brand equity, so that people still want to join or stay at the company.

Does that typically work?

To some extent, yes. People want to have a sense of control. When you’re involuntarily laid off, it feels like things are happening to you and are out of your control. Psychologists talk about a need for self-determination. By giving employees a choice and a set period of time—often 45 days or more—to consider their options, companies allow employees to feel they control their fate. The impact on morale also depends partly on the structure and terms of the buyouts—how generous the packages are perceived to be.

What are the drawbacks?

The big one is that companies lose high-performers—the people who are in demand no matter what the economy is doing. Companies try to manage that by excluding certain teams or departments from the offer. (At Microsoft, many employees in sales, marketing, quantum computing, and other units didn’t receive the offer.)

And there are other ways to manage that risk. During the 1990s, Procter & Gamble had worked to determine why high-potential women frequently left the company. The most common answer was “Nobody told me I had a future here.” In response, P&G became really proactive about having managers communicate with employees about their career growth and opportunities. When P&G conducted a voluntary buyout in the early 2000s, managers met with high performers to sell them on their future if they stayed and to let them know they were highly valued.

I’ve worked at companies that have done buyouts. I thought it was illegal for managers to try to sway people one way or the other.

No, that’s a misconception. Many companies assume they can’t do this, but they should. It’s important to hold onto your best people.

Imagine a CHRO calls you and says, “I need to reduce headcount. I can use attrition. I can do a layoff. Or I can do a buyout. What do you recommend?” How would you guide them to the right choice?

I tell them that it often depends on the mindset of the CEO and other leaders. I’ve studied these issues for decades, and I’ve found there are two types of leaders: those who view employees as a cost, and those who view them as an asset to develop. When leaders see people as a cost, it leads to a predictable set of decisions to lay off people. Managers who view employees as assets tend to favor buyouts. If you look at MBA curricula, we spend very little time teaching students how to manage when times get tough at a company. That can lead to the employee-as-a-cost mentality.

What’s an example of a company with the employees-as-an-asset mentality?

Look at Johnson & Johnson. It lists its responsibility to employees near the top of its famous credo. That’s playing out as part of the shift to AI. Like all companies, J&J has employees who want to take advantage of upskilling and reskilling, and others who feel they just can’t handle this new technology. For people who don’t want to work with AI, J&J helps people voluntarily design an exit from the company or find jobs within the company that don’t require AI. J&J does this because it’s consistent with its credo and it’s aligned with the mental model of the leaders and how they see the people in the organization.

Here’s a hypothetical: You have two companies that are identical. One offers a buyout to 20,000 people, and 5,000 take it. The other does a layoff of 5,000. Which will perform better going forward?

I don’t know of any research that can answer that question directly. I’ve worked with finance professors to study the financial effects of layoffs, and we’ve consistently found that if a company conducts a layoff and doesn’t change how the work gets done, reduce assets, or make other changes, it never outperforms its competitors during the two years after the layoff. But there haven’t been studies on the long-term effects of buyouts. Right now, I’m working with colleagues to study companies that are profitable while doing layoffs. We’re using matched samples to compare similar companies. Again, if all they do is cut people and don’t change anything else, it looks like even these profitable downsizers don’t outperform after layoffs, but it will be a few months before we have final results and can say that definitively.

Imagine you have a friend who received the Microsoft buyout offer. They’re agonizing over whether to take it. What advice do you give them?

One story I tell is about IBM’s first layoffs. For most of its history, it had never downsized, and its leaders felt bad about it. So, they gave people two years of pay as severance plus a $25,000 bonus. In subsequent years, IBM conducted many rounds of layoffs and buyouts, and it was never that generous again. Research shows that companies tend to become less generous with these offers over time, so it can be smart for employees to take the first one.

But mostly when I have these conversations, I try to pretend I’m a doctor listening to a patient. I really try to hear what they’re saying. Are they looking to retire, or are they ready to move on to something completely different? Are they looking to transfer to another company that can make use of their existing skill set? Or are they high performers who might stay right where they are? I’ll share my opinions, but mostly I want to ask questions to help them make their own decisions. Remember, buyouts are all about personal control, so anything I can do to promote that sense of autonomy is all to the good.
