title: Microsoft's Voluntary Exit Is Not a Layoff. It's a New Model of Management - Josh Bersin
description:
When Microsoft announced its Voluntary Exit Offer last week, the headlines were immediate.
What Microsoft has done is not a layoff, rather a thoughtful workforce innovation, one which many companies will want to copy.
Microsoft introduced a voluntary exit offer available to 60,000 eligible employees across four markets: U.S., Canada, India, and the UK.
Based on industry precedent for voluntary programs of this breadth, the HR team expects an uptake rate of 3-1%.
Josh Bersin is a global industry analyst, author of Superpowered*, and founder of The Josh Bersin Company.
text:
When Microsoft announced its Voluntary Exit Offer last week, the headlines were immediate. “Microsoft Lays Off 60,000.” “Tech Giant Cuts Workforce.” “AI Takes Another Victim.” Quickly Instagram and TikTok were filled with angry videos: “another big company eliminates workers with AI.”

Well I hate to tell you, this is not what happened.

I spoke with Microsoft’s HR leadership team this week, and the story is much more positive than it seems.

What Microsoft has done is not a layoff, rather a thoughtful workforce innovation, one which many companies will want to copy.

What Microsoft Really Did

Let’s start with the facts. Microsoft introduced a voluntary exit offer available to 60,000 eligible employees across four markets: U.S., Canada, India, and the UK. Eligibility is determined by organizational unit, not performance. Employees from vice president level and below are eligible, with no tenure requirement, so you could have been at Microsoft for a week or for twenty-five years.

The goal of the program is not to force people out, rather to encourage people to move on with their careers. In other words, Microsoft is saying “if you aren’t 100% on board with our new strategy, we want to help you move on with your career.”

Microsoft CFO Amy Hood stated that they expect few employees to take the offer. Based on industry precedent for voluntary programs of this breadth, the HR team expects an uptake rate of 3-1%. The means only 1,800 to 3,000 people out of 60,000.

The offer itself is a standard severance package. It is not sweetened to encourage departure. It includes pay based on tenure, stock vesting, healthcare, and career transition services. There is no quota, no forced selection, and no predetermined headcount target.

Microsoft has been clear: they are not announcing layoffs. And critically, Microsoft just delivered a very strong financial quarter, so this is not the behavior of a company in distress: it’s the behavior of a company thinking ahead.

A New Model of Workforce Dynamism

So what is this, if not a layoff?

Well earlier this year, Microsoft introduced a Voluntary Retirement Program for tenured employees approaching the end of their careers: age and tenure at Microsoft had to add up to 70 or more. And what happened is that many non-eligible people said “I wish I had a deal like this!”

Amy Coleman, the CHRO, hear this message so they decided to broaden the program. She realized realized that others were ready to leave.

The result is a program focused a simple idea: not everyone who works at a company wants to be there. So let’s make it easy for disengaged people to move on.

If someone has been mentally preparing for their next chapter, starting a business, joining a startup, or simply changing industries, this new program gives them a supported path to do so.

I’ve thought about this in my own career. Years ago I worked for Sybase and was there during its decline. My job was important but I wasn’t very busy. I would show up, work 5-6 hours a day, and then often leave early to coach my kids’ soccer teams. Eventually I left for a new opportunity but if they had offered me a voluntary exit I would have taken it and we both would have been better off.

That is exactly what Microsoft is building: a release valve for mutual misalignment, rather than a forced program to reduce headcount.

This is all about quality of hire and talent density.

Amazon and Netflix famously offer new hires a financial incentive to leave within the first 90 days if the fit is not right. The philosophy is the same: a smaller, more committed team outperforms a larger, partially disengaged one every time.

The Talent Density Imperative

The concept at the heart of what Microsoft is doing has a name: we call it talent density.

It’s a simple idea: scale does not come from “more people,” it comes from “better capabilties, automation, redesign, and internal redeployment.” Every manager who asks for headcount should hear “let’s talk about how we can redesign what you’re doing to deliver more.”

The traditional talent management model, developed before skills shortages, was a supply chain: hire when growing, contract when slowing. That model no longer works because almost every role is being reinvented for AI. (Our new book Superpowered explains this in detail, with more than 100 case studies.)

This means new jobs, internal redeployment, and lots of learning and development. Our Dynamic Organization research details how companies who redeploy people well are 31 times more likely to lead their markets.

Google’s 2025 AI turnaround is a good example: rather than hiring hundreds of new engineers to compete in the AI race they redeployed talent from scattered product teams into Gemini, producing a game-changing product and a new business for the company.

Microsoft is playing the same game, just at a more sophisticated level. By creating space for self-selection out of the organization, they make room to redeploy talent into AI-critical roles, continuing to hire selectively in high-growth areas, and maintain the engagement of those who stay.

The Engagement Crisis We Face: How To Create More Energy

There’s another angle to consider: if misaligned people leave, the remaining teams are even more excited.

Gallup’s new engagement data shows that U.S. employee engagement has dropped below 30% for the first time in a decade, its lowest point in fifteen years. Only 21% of workers are fully engaged, down 10% from the prior year, and 66% of employees report “suffering.”

Two forces are driving this problem: constant messaging about AI job cuts and a slowdown in hiring driven by massive investments in tech. (Gartner estimates that AI and IT spending is up 15% to $7.35 Trillion next year.)

I see the fear in clients eyes each day. How do we energize people as they learn to reinvent their jobs and work around AI?

Well Microsoft’s answer is simple. Rather than keep a large, fearful workforce in place, Microsoft invests in the engagement and commitment of those who choose to remain.

CHRO Amy Coleman states publicly that Microsoft wants energized, ambitious, aligned employees. If you don’t feel excited, Microsoft makes it easy for you to leave.

That is not a process of “demanding engagemnt.” It’s a sober recognition that having the right people doing the right jobs in the right seats is a competitive advantage an AI-powered economy.

Transforming Into AI Without Forcing People Out

AI is not really a tool for reducing headcount: rather it’s a tool to drive growth, scale, efficiency, and customer intimacy.

Leaders (like Microsoft) understand the rise of the Superworker and embrace a growth mindset. Engaged employees will reinvent their jobs around AI.

I believe the companies that lead the next decade are not those who shrink: it’s companies that leverage AI for growth, efficiency, and scale. Microsoft is setting this example.

That is the real story. I hope the headlines catch up.

Josh Bersin is a global industry analyst, author of Superpowered*, and founder of The Josh Bersin Company.*

text:
Walmart said this week it will invest about $6 billion during the next several years to expand automated technologies with technology partner Symbotic across 25 U.S. distribution centers.

The expanded agreement also supports ongoing investment in Walmart’s global supply chain capabilities, the two companies said.

“Our work with Symbotic over the years, including this expanded agreement, helps us improve service, grow capacity, simplify work for our associates and lower costs,” said Rob Montgomery, executive VP for Walmart U.S. supply chain operations.

Walmart said it plans to bring additional automation capabilities to its regional distribution center network, which will support ecommerce inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve how products move through the supply chain. The retailer said the investments will help it offer a broader assortment, improve speed and provide more reliable replenishment.

Challenges in implementing automation

The expanded agreement follows a recent Wall Street Journal report that Walmart has struggled to update its distribution centers with automated technologies. The report cited issues such as cardboard boxes that are too big for some automated machines and wheeled robots that break down too often.

“New technology is never perfect on day one,” Walmart told Supermarket News following the WSJ report. “If we had waited for perfection, our associates and customers wouldn’t be getting access to the benefits they experience today. We’re constantly learning and adjusting—that’s what innovation in practice looks like.”

Meanwhile Symbotic said in an August conference call with investors that it had begun installation of its first SymMicro system for automated ecommerce fulfillment at the back of a Walmart store in Dallas. Symbotic said it could have the system running in about six months, after which it could be expanded to additional locations.

“We have a second site that will follow shortly after [the first site comes online],” said Richard Cohen, chairman, president and CEO of Symbotic, during the call. “And then that should trigger a bunch more sites once Walmart actually sees the system working.”

Symbotic, which had acquired Walmart’s previous automated ecommerce fulfillment partner, currently operates the older system at 19 other Walmart locations.

In addition, Symbotic said in the call that it has rolled out its BreakPack system to about half of Walmart’s regional distribution centers. The system allows the retailer to incorporate picking of individual items alongside full case picking within the same automated solution.

text:
The artificial intelligence (AI) story has been the focus of investors in recent times, but in a different way than in earlier stages of this tech boom. In those initial quarters, investors piled into AI stocks, recognizing the potential of AI to transform businesses and drive earnings growth and share price performance. In many cases, they made the right bet, with hardware and services companies generating explosive growth. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has been one of the biggest winners as it dominates the AI chip market.

But over the past year, investors have started to worry about the AI story, with the idea that tech giants building out infrastructure may be overspending. This has weighed on the performance of some of these stocks and prompted investors to pay particularly close attention to tech companies' spending plans.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia has continued to report double- and triple-digit growth, but its stock performance hasn't been as eye-popping as in the past. For example, Nvidia stock climbed more than 1,100% over the past three calendar years, but the stock is only up 15% this year.

This week, however, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) said something that may be seen as quite positive for Nvidia. In fact, the tech powerhouse just announced incredible news for Nvidia shareholders. Let's check it out.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia's GPU leadership

We'll start with a quick summary of the Nvidia story so far. As mentioned, Nvidia leads in the AI chip market, selling the fastest graphics processing units (GPUs) around. The GPU fuels key AI tasks, such as training models and inference -- that's the process of actually "thinking" to address a problem. Nvidia entered the market ahead of rivals and has maintained its position through strong customer relationships, its vast ecosystem of products, and constant innovation.

All of this has helped power earnings higher, with revenue and profit climbing in the triple digits in the latest quarter. But investors have worried that any potential slowdown in tech spending could significantly hurt Nvidia. After all, data center sales make up 92% of Nvidia's total sales.

Now this brings us to Microsoft, one of Nvidia's biggest customers. You may know this tech company best for its popular software like Word and Excel, but Microsoft is also a massive player in the AI world. Microsoft's cloud business serves a vast array of AI products and services to customers, and the company has been investing heavily in the infrastructure build-out to address growing demand.

Monitoring the pace of AI growth

This week, Microsoft reported fiscal 2027 first-quarter earnings, and as part of the report, it spoke of capital expenditures. Capex has been a major focus for investors, allowing us to monitor the pace of AI growth and better understand levels of demand.

Now, here's the good news for Nvidia shareholders. Microsoft said that in the first quarter, about 75% of its capex went toward "short-lived assets," mainly central processing units (CPUs) and GPUs. This suggests significant growth for Nvidia, as a provider of these products. (Central processing units are the main chips found in computers, and Nvidia recently launched its first stand-alone CPU. Prior to this, Nvidia wasn't largely present in the CPU market, but shifted into this area as the CPU emerged as a critical tool powering AI agents.)

The news for Nvidia gets even brighter if we look at Microsoft's capex forecasts: The company says that in the second half it expects capex to accelerate, again driven by spending on CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft forecasts $170 billion in capex for the calendar year. And all of this is based on ongoing high demand -- so Microsoft isn't building to serve what might unfold but instead to serve a trend that is already in place.

Microsoft, one of Nvidia's main customers, clearly sees high demand for the chip designer's key products and plans to continue spending heavily on them. And that means, even as some market participants worry about the AI spending environment, the actual situation continues to show strength. Nvidia's earnings could continue to roar higher throughout the coming year, and that's fantastic news for shareholders.

Dive Brief:

Meta has signed a multi-year deal with low-carbon cement manufacturer Fortera that will give the tech and social media conglomerate access to lower-carbon cement for constructing its projects, as well as environmental attribute credits associated with its production.

Under the agreement, Meta will get access to the environmental attribute credits associated with the production of 200,000 tons, according to a Thursday press release.

Fortera co-founder and CEO Ryan Gilliam called the deal “an important first step in Fortera and Meta’s relationship” in the release. Last year, the low-carbon cement startup secured an investment from Microsoft that will help fund a full-scale production facility in exchange for a board observer seat, EACs and cement for its data centers.

Dive Insight:

Meta’s investment will help fund a Fortera cement plant in Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, along the Mississippi River, according to the release. Fortera uses captured carbon dioxide in its cements, which leads to a product with 70% less emissions than traditional cement, according to the release.

Meta said that the agreement will connect “its demand for low carbon cement with the development of domestic supply in markets where it is building.” Meta Head of Net Zero Strategy Devon Lake said the tech giant signed a multi-year deal because that “is what gets a cement plant financed.”

“Our agreement helps Fortera move the Ste. Genevieve plant from plan to production, which means construction jobs and long-term manufacturing jobs in Missouri, and low-carbon cement available to builders well beyond Meta,” Lake said in the release.

Meta, which owns social media platforms Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, said in its 2025 sustainability report that its data center emissions increased 22% in 2024, despite a 3.5% decrease in its scope 1 and scope 2 emissions. The company has yet to release a report documenting its 2025 emissions.

“Agreements of this scale and duration are what unlock financing and move projects from plans to production,” Fortera’s CEO said. “They also show the market that low-carbon cement is a product that buyers are serious about and planning around for years to come.”

The deal will also give Meta the option to extend or expand the deal by volume or duration, the release said.

text:
London: Eli Lilly raised its full-year revenue forecast and beat third-quarter earnings expectations on Thursday, propelled by surging demand for injectable weight-loss drugs that could allay investor concerns about price erosion in US government health plans.

The Indianapolis-based drugmaker now expects full-year revenue of $91 billion to $92 billion, underscoring its expanding lead in the multibillion-dollar GLP-1 market over Danish rival Novo Nordisk that has propelled Lilly to a $1.2 trillion market valuation.

Lilly trimmed its adjusted profit outlook, however, to $35.00 to $36.00 per share, as $4.57 per share of acquired research charges from recent deals more than offset a $4.07 improvement in underlying profit guidance at the midpoint. The charges, taken in the third quarter, are primarily related to the acquisitions of AtaiBeckley and Curevo, Lilly said.

Advt

Lilly previously forecast revenue of $85.0 billion to $87.0 billion and earnings of $35.50 to $36.50 per share.

Lilly posted third-quarter revenue of $24.4 billion, topping analyst expectations of $22.61 billion, while adjusted profit of $7.48 per share beat estimates of $6.26, according to LSEG data.

Revenue included about $900 million of benefits, primarily $410 million of milestone payments tied to diabetes drug Jardiance, which Lilly said are the last it expects to receive, and favorable adjustments to rebate and discount estimates.

Third-quarter sales of diabetes drug Mounjaro reached $10.72 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $10.16 billion, according to LSEG data, while its related obesity injection Zepbound brought in $5.35 billion versus estimates of $5.09 billion.

The robust sales will help ease market worries that severe price erosion from the $50-a-month price tag for Medicare recipients would outweigh explosive volume gains. Analysts at Bernstein said data showed that Lilly had captured about 70% of the 700,000 Medicare patients who recently initiated treatment with a GLP-1 medication.

While the new US pilot unlocked coverage for potentially millions who use the government's Medicare program for people aged 65 and over, the bulk of Lilly's non-reimbursed volume has historically moved through its $449-a-month cash-pay platform, raising stakes over how the discounts will impact long-term margins.

Advt

Lilly's newer obesity pill Foundayo brought in $184 million, compared with analyst estimates of $216.86 million.

Investors are closely tracking the Foundayo rollout as a key test of whether Lilly can blunt Novo Nordisk's first-mover edge with its oral Wegovy.

While initial US Foundayo prescriptions have trailed its Danish rival, some investors have downplayed the early lag, expecting the Lilly pill to emerge as a significant growth driver as it launches in more international markets.

Oral Wegovy led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, and Foundayo about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, in separate studies.

Foundayo was launched in the US and Britain earlier this year and could potentially begin selling in other European countries by year-end.

Lilly's realized prices fell 15% in the third quarter, offsetting part of a 53% rise in volume. US prices fell 7%, a decline Lilly attributed primarily to Zepbound and said was partly offset by adjustments to rebate and discount estimates. Outside the US, prices fell 29%, driven mainly by Mounjaro's inclusion on China's national reimbursement drug list.

Even as Lilly's obesity injections maintain commercial momentum, Wall Street's attention is shifting toward retatrutide, the company's next-generation weight-loss candidate slated for regulatory submission next year.

Retatrutide has been shown to drive average weight loss of 24% in midstage trials, topping results from drugs already on the market.

(Reporting by Patrick Wingrove in London. Editing by Bill Berkrot and Mark Potter)

text:
Stryker is facing a slowdown in joint replacement procedures, which CEO Kevin Lobo attributed to a broader market deceleration.

The company reported fewer hip and knee procedures in the third quarter than expected, with knee sales growing 1.1% in the quarter compared with the year-ago period and hip sales decreasing by 1%.

“Beginning with hips and knees, it is now clear that there is a market slowdown,” Lobo said in a Thursday earnings call. “In the U.S., we are seeing slower procedural growth amid affordability concerns from higher insurance premiums and deductibles.”

CFO Preston Wells first flagged the slower sales at an event last month. While Stryker has grappled with a cyberattack this year and a new software implementation within its orthopedics business, Lobo attributed the numbers to a slow market and economic challenges.

The company hasn’t lost business in hips and knees to the competition, Lobo said, but patients are delaying the procedures due to insurance costs and pre-authorization denials.

“There are patients that today are having trouble being able to make their deductible because their deductibles are higher,” Lobo said. “They’re actually living with pain a little bit longer than they would like to.”

He added that the market for joint replacement procedures has historically been tied to economic cycles.

Stryker lowered its sales guidance for 2026 to a range of 6.5% to 7.0%. The company previously forecast a range of 8.3% to 9.3%.

Lobo, who plans to step down as CEO at the end of the year, said he would “have preferred to deliver better news” in his last earnings call. Lobo has led Stryker for 15 years and will hand over the reins to Chief Operating Officer Spencer Stiles in January.

CMR Surgical partnership

Earlier this month, Stryker announced a $400 million investment into soft tissue robotics firm CMR Surgical. As part of the agreement, Stryker will become the exclusive U.S. distributor of CMR’s robot.

“Our hope and our plan is that we will eventually purchase this,” Lobo said, but he did not share a timeline.

When CMR came along with the upgraded version of its robot, called Versius Plus, “we got a chance to see something that we felt very excited about,” Lobo said. “We feel it is the best robot on the market to be able to succeed in multiple sites of care; the modular nature makes it great for the ambulatory surgery center as well as working well in hospitals.”

Lobo said Stryker decided to partner with CMR first rather than acquire the company outright, because an outright purchase carries a lot of risk and development costs. Stryker also wanted to ensure CMR’s robot is a commercial success in the U.S., a critical market.

Comparing CMR with Mako Surgical, which Stryker bought back in 2013 for its orthopedic surgical robots, Lobo said CMR is further along than when the company acquired Mako. However, Mako had implants attached to it, Lobo said, while CMR is a “pure adjacency, and it’s not something we wanted to rush into necessarily.”

title: Amazon Slides 7% as Earnings Miss and AI Spending Turn Free Cash Flow Negative
description:
A cash-hungry AI build-out is dominating a still-accelerating cloud business at Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction).
With the slide, Amazon stock is down 2% year to date (YTD).
Citizens made a steep cut to $275 from $315, and MoffettNathanson raised its Amazon target to $357 from $315.
Amazon’s Cash Burn Faces Its Next Test Amazon’s next challenge is whether AWS growth speeds up as new capacity comes online.
A cautious approach could make sense until the debate over Amazon’s cash burn resolves.
text:
A cash-hungry AI build-out is dominating a still-accelerating cloud business at Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction). Amazon stock is at $226.26 in premarket trading, down 7%. Checking on tech stocks in general, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is at $697.49, down 2%. As a broad-market gauge, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is at $761.91, down 0.97%.

The e-commerce and cloud giant closed at $243.79 on October 29, before releasing its Q3 2026 results. With the slide, Amazon stock is down 2% year to date (YTD).

Amazon’s Earnings Miss Exposes a Deepening Cash Squeeze

Amazon posted third-quarter earnings per share (EPS) of $1.89, missing the $1.97 Bloomberg analyst consensus. Its $201.9 billion in revenue also trailed the $202.25 billion Bloomberg analyst consensus. Management at Amazon said Prime Day’s shift into Q2 2026 cost approximately 400 basis points of growth.

Q4 2026 net sales guidance from Amazon of $240 billion to $247 billion straddled the $244.5 billion Wall Street analysts expected, but its center fell short. Operating income guidance from Amazon of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion trailed the $32.99 billion Wall Street analysts expected at the center.

For the 12 months ended September 30, Amazon’s free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier. Put simply, negative free cash flow means Amazon spent more on AI infrastructure than its operations generated. For retirement-minded investors, this signals a smaller buffer.

Still, Amazon repeated its expectation of $220 billion in 2026 cash capital expenditures, and management expects to spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. CEO Andy Jassy granted, “On the CapEx involved to grow the way we’re talking about, it’s meaningful.”

AWS Growth Hands Amazon Bulls a Strong Counterpoint

Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue grew 39% year over year (YoY). Jassy put the AWS annualized revenue run rate at $184 billion and projected growth above 40% in both 2027 and 2028. A $578 billion AWS backlog, cited by Jassy, supports that outlook.

Bank of America said investor expectations for AWS growth had run as high as 42%, which helps explain Amazon’s cool reception. Advertising at Amazon grew 12% YoY, down sharply from 26% in the prior quarter, a possible concern as AI shopping agents emerge.

Wall Street Splits Over Amazon’s Selloff

TD Cowen called the Amazon selloff excessive and kept its Buy rating, though it trimmed its price target to $340 from $350. Mizuho lifted its target to $335 from $330, while UBS raised its target to $352 from $348. Meanwhile, BofA lowered its target to $317 from $320.

Citizens made a steep cut to $275 from $315, and MoffettNathanson raised its Amazon target to $357 from $315. Koyfin’s average 12-month analyst price target is $332.41.

Meta and Alphabet Extend Their Slides as Walmart Rallies

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stock is at $613.10, down 2%. That leaves Meta Platforms stock down 17% over the past month. The company’s October 21 report included a $9.89 billion settlement charge that dragged its EPS to $3.83, versus $7.40 without it.

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock is at $280.62, down 1%. The move follows Alphabet’s October 28 report, which disclosed an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities that cut its EPS by $0.55. At the same time, Microsoft stock is at $528.48, down 0.3%.

Amazon’s main retail rival is moving the other way. Walmart stock is at $123.80, up 2%. Over the past month, Walmart stock has climbed 16% as a defensive counterweight to the AI-spending selloff.

The NASDAQ Composite closed more than 1% lower on October 29 as Alphabet’s slide weighed on the AI trade. Gartner raised a concern on October 14. It estimated that $3.5 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could face impairment by the end of 2030, a worry that helps explain why Amazon’s AWS strength wasn’t enough to offset its cash burn. We featured seven suppliers powering the AI expansion. For investors looking past the hyperscalers, they range from power to cooling in a free report you can grab here.

Amazon pairs a thin-margin retail network with a cloud arm that rents computing power to other companies. Meta Platforms relies heavily on advertising. Alphabet pairs ads with a fast-growing cloud unit, and Walmart runs a store-based model with far lower tech spending.

Amazon’s Cash Burn Faces Its Next Test

Amazon’s next challenge is whether AWS growth speeds up as new capacity comes online. Bulls see the backlog as proof the spending works, while the bears fear heavier 2027 outlays could keep free cash flow negative for longer.

Shareholders can watch for Amazon’s free cash flow trend in coming quarters. A cautious approach could make sense until the debate over Amazon’s cash burn resolves.

title: Microsoft Is Borrowing $25 Billion for AI, Its First Bond Sale Since 2017 - 24/7 Wall St.
description:
On October 29, 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) priced $25 billion of senior unsecured bonds.
It was the company’s first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017, the year it raised $17 billion.
Capital spending, including finance leases, was $45.2 billion, and cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion.
Microsoft now expects about $175 billion of capex for calendar 2026, compared with $190 billion in April.
What Could Move MSFT Stock After Its First Bond Sale Since 2017 Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion.
text:
On October 29, 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) priced $25 billion of senior unsecured bonds. It was the company’s first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017, the year it raised $17 billion. Orders topped out at $115 billion, or 4.6 times the deal size.

The stock hardly moved. Shares closed that day at $530.14, down 0.16%, for a market value of $3.94 trillion. That came after a 4.1% after-hours jump to $552.55 on October 28, which faded.

Bond buyers accepted a premium for rare AAA debt from the strongest borrower in corporate America, while stock buyers were looking at a company whose spending is growing faster than its cash. Microsoft holds more cash than long-term debt, so the real question is why it chose to borrow.

What Microsoft Committed To and What It Only Intends

Once the bonds were priced, the debt was committed. The deal has 10 tranches, meaning separate bonds that mature at different dates, running from two years to 40 years. The bond due 2066 priced at 1.05 percentage points over Treasuries. That was as much as 0.3 points tighter than initial guidance, so investors accepted a smaller premium than first offered.

How the money gets spent is only stated intent. Microsoft listed general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures and share buybacks. So the bonds help pay for an AI-driven build, but none of the money is specifically set aside for AI. The size and coupon of each tranche had not been widely reported as of October 30, 2026.

On the October 28 earnings call, CFO Amy Hood spoke. She said Microsoft has “lots of options to be able to tap the financing markets when they make sense and they’re attractive.”

Why a Cash-Rich Company Borrowed

Before the deal, Microsoft had $64.5 billion of cash and short-term investments and $31.1 billion of long-term debt. The reason it borrowed anyway shows up in the fiscal first quarter. Capital spending, including finance leases, was $45.2 billion, and cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion.

A finance lease gets recorded like a purchase. It is a long-term rental of data center capacity, which is why those two numbers differ. Microsoft now expects about $175 billion of capex for calendar 2026, compared with $190 billion in April. Most of that difference comes from an accounting change that shifts more leases to operating leases, and those sit outside capex.

Borrowing at AAA rates lets Microsoft keep its cash for buybacks and construction while spending runs ahead of what the business brings in. It also locks in 40-year money while lenders are eager to supply it.

AI Spenders Pay Very Different Prices for Credit

The 2066 bond priced tighter than Alphabet’s (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) 40-year bond, which trades near 1.33 points over Treasuries. Alphabet sold $25 billion of bonds on August 6.

Five-year credit default swaps measure the yearly cost of insuring a company’s debt against default. Microsoft’s sit at about 54 basis points, compared with 116 for Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and 275 for Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). Lenders therefore see paying for Oracle’s expansion as much riskier than paying for Microsoft’s.

Microsoft was a latecomer to the borrowing wave. Hyperscalers and data center developers have issued more than $313 billion of investment-grade bonds globally in 2026, and the proceeds flow well beyond the chipmakers to the power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind each facility (we profiled seven of those winners in a free report you can grab here). Brett Kozlowski of GW&K called the timing “opportunistic”. Still, the fact that Microsoft borrowed at all shows that even the strongest balance sheet now wants outside money for this cycle.

What Could Move MSFT Stock After Its First Bond Sale Since 2017

Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion. Azure grew 48% in constant currency, ahead of Microsoft’s own 44% to 45% forecast, and management said customer demand continued to exceed available supply.

The falling stock reflects a fair worry about spending, since Microsoft expects second-quarter capex of over $50 billion. That risk grows. It grows further if AI demand slows while borrowed money funds buybacks, or if repeated bond sales put pressure on the AAA rating.

The test is the fiscal second-quarter earnings report. Microsoft guided for Azure growth of 49 to 50% in constant currency. The case for the stock weakens. If Azure falls short of that range while capex tops $50 billion, a close below the October 29 low of $519.56 would signal market agreement.

name: Instacart
title: DoorDash to Buy Instacart for $17 Billion, Raising Antitrust Concerns | Law Commentary
description:
DoorDash has agreed to acquire grocery delivery rival Instacart for approximately $17 billion, a deal that would combine two of the country’s largest delivery platforms and face federal antitrust review over its potential effects on grocery prices, competition, and gig workers.
The purchase would give DoorDash control of Instacart’s grocery delivery business, retailer partnerships, and technology used by grocery chains to manage online orders.
DoorDash has expanded rapidly beyond restaurant deliveries, competing directly with Instacart in the growing online grocery market.
Instacart would retain its name, app, and technology products, while DoorDash would connect its delivery network with Instacart’s grocery operations.
DoorDash and Instacart will continue operating independently while the acquisition moves through the approval process.
text:
DoorDash has agreed to acquire grocery delivery rival Instacart for approximately $17 billion, a deal that would combine two of the country’s largest delivery platforms and face federal antitrust review over its potential effects on grocery prices, competition, and gig workers.

The companies announced the agreement Thursday, October 29, 2026, offering Instacart shareholders $65 per share in cash, DoorDash stock or a combination of both. The purchase would give DoorDash control of Instacart’s grocery delivery business, retailer partnerships, and technology used by grocery chains to manage online orders.

DoorDash has expanded rapidly beyond restaurant deliveries, competing directly with Instacart in the growing online grocery market. Its share of U.S. grocery delivery orders has climbed from 44% to 59% over five years, while Instacart’s share has fallen from 26% to 18%, according to market data reported by The Associated Press.

Combining the businesses would give DoorDash a larger share of grocery deliveries and greater influence over the technology retailers use to sell products online. The acquisition could also affect delivery fees, consumer choices, and the terms grocery stores negotiate with competing platforms.

Federal regulators will review whether the transaction could substantially reduce competition, the standard applied to mergers under the Clayton Act. The Federal Trade Commission could focus on whether the combined company would make it harder for rival delivery services to compete or give DoorDash greater leverage over participating retailers.

DoorDash has defended the acquisition as a way to help smaller grocery stores compete with Walmart and Amazon, which operate extensive shopping and delivery networks. The company says retailers will remain free to use competing delivery services after the merger and continue controlling their relationships with customers.

Instacart would retain its name, app, and technology products, while DoorDash would connect its delivery network with Instacart’s grocery operations.

For customers, the companies are promising access to more than 50,000 additional stores and a combined subscription offering extending benefits across DashPass and Instacart+. DoorDash estimates the arrangement could save subscribers approximately $100 million annually.

The larger network would also bring together substantial information about consumers’ shopping habits and purchasing preferences. How the companies use that data could receive added scrutiny as regulators examine the role personal information plays in online pricing.

Approximately 600,000 independent contractors who shop and deliver orders through Instacart would continue to choose their assignments and could gain access to additional work through DoorDash. The company has also pledged to preserve shoppers’ flexibility to accept orders through either service.

Bringing the two platforms under common ownership, though, would leave gig workers with one fewer major company competing for their labor. Merger reviews can consider effects on workers as well as consumers, including whether consolidation reduces competition for jobs, assignments or earnings.

The proposed acquisition comes one day after the FTC launched a separate inquiry into how DoorDash, Instacart and seven other major companies use personal information to set consumer prices and worker compensation.

The agency ordered the businesses to disclose whether they rely on browsing histories, loyalty programs, purchasing behavior or other personal data to charge customers different prices for comparable goods and services. Investigators are also examining whether gig workers receive different compensation offers based on factors such as their previous acceptance of assignments or information collected through their phones.

FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said the agency wants to determine whether companies use personal information to calculate the highest prices consumers may be willing to pay and whether similar practices affect workers’ earnings.

The orders, issued under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act, require the nine companies to provide information within 45 days of receiving the requests. The inquiry is separate from the proposed merger review but adds another layer of regulatory scrutiny around the same companies as they seek approval for the $17 billion deal.

DoorDash and Instacart will continue operating independently while the acquisition moves through the approval process. Instacart’s board has unanimously approved the agreement, and shareholders controlling approximately 19% of its outstanding shares have committed to supporting the transaction.

text:
DoorDash’s $17 billion bid for Instacart could give CPG brands a bigger advertising platform and broader delivery reach, but antitrust critics warn it would also create a food delivery monopoly.

The deal would unite two of the largest US food delivery companies for a cash-and-stock transaction that values Instacart at approximately $17 billion, or $65 per share.

“The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash’s delivery network and Instacart’s grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores’ own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built,” the two companies said in a joint announcement.

Delivering a big deal

The deal, which is projected to close in 2027 or 2028 if approved by federal regulators, would give market leader DoorDash an even bigger presence in the food delivery business.

According to a statement released Oct. 29 by market intelligence service Consumer Edge, 59% of spending across major US delivery apps in the third quarter went to DoorDash, up from 44% in Q2 2021. Meanwhile, roughly 18% each went to Instacart and Uber Eats, with Instacart dropping from 26% in 2021 and Uber Eats increasing from 16%.

The statistics include both grocery and restaurant deliveries. “These trends partly reflect the expansion of DoorDash and Uber Eats into grocery, convenience and other retail categories, increasingly competing in areas historically associated with Instacart, and highlight how the boundaries between restaurant, grocery and broader retail delivery have become increasingly blurred,” Consumer Edge noted in an email.

The merger is a bet that “the next phase of US delivery will be won on the weekly grocery order rather than the takeout order,” said Alex Frederick, senior foodtech analyst at PitchBook, a financial data and research firm.

“DoorDash already handles about two-thirds of US food delivery volume, and Instacart adds the grocery software, retailer relationships and advertising tools it has been slower to build,” he said. “Few venture-backed challengers are left to contest it: global VC investment in online grocers fell from $20.3 billion in 2021 to $566 million through Q3 2026, according to PitchBook data, which leaves consolidation as the main path to scale.”

DoorDash and Instacart already appear to be building their argument against charges that the deal constitutes a monopoly, noting in their announcement that “the biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs and AI shopping assistants.”

They argued that smaller grocery retailers “running on thin margins” will find it harder to compete with these larger companies and that a combined DoorDash-Instacart helps level the playing field.

“DoorDash and Instacart believe that communities benefit when Main Street competes, and they build the tools that empower local businesses,” the two companies said. “Together, they could help local stores grow online. More grocers could deploy Instacart’s technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, bringing them more sales and advertising revenue.”

Frederick said the move is a play against mega-retailers.

“The real competition is Walmart and Amazon, which have been taking share in same-day grocery delivery with their own networks, and a combined DoorDash-Instacart gives independent grocers a partner with comparable reach,” he said.

What could the deal mean for CPG brands?

DoorDash and Instacart make the case that the deal will be a boon for CPG brands, giving them a “scaled alternative for reaching customers online.”

Those products also could make it to consumers faster due to DoorDash’s own fulfillment services, the delivery companies said. “Grocers could add capacity for online orders through DoorDash’s DashMart Fulfillment Services and offer faster, more accurate and more affordable delivery,” the companies said.

Instacart CEO Chris Rogers also said the deal would benefit CPG brands through DoorDash’s expanded network of retailers.

“When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers and deliver compelling value for our shareholders,” he said.

CPG value could be the primary motivation for the deal, according to Frederick.

“If the deal clears, advertising may matter more to the investment case than delivery fees, because selling shelf space to CPG brands earns far better margins than moving a bag of avocados across town,” he said.

Antitrust concerns

The proposed acquisition is already drawing scrutiny from antitrust advocates.

Lee Hepner, Senior Legal Counsel at the American Economic Liberties Project, called out the two companies for what he described as “ongoing harms” the two delivery companies have made against grocers, delivery drivers, consumers and restaurateurs.

For example, FTC reached a $60 million settlement with Instacart in December 2025 over allegations of deceptive advertising, failure to provide refunds and unlawful subscription enrollments. The company denied wrongdoing.

On Wednesday, FTC launched an inquiry into personalized pricing and ordered the two would-be partners, along with Uber, retailers Target and Walmart and several US airlines, to turn over information about their use of personal data to set prices.

“We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service,” said FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson. “Consumers deserve to know whether companies use their web surfing habits or other personal data to estimate the highest price they can charge each consumer. Workers also deserve to know if their compensation is affected by how companies use their personal data.”

Hepner accused both companies of “bullying mainstreet businesses” and exploiting workers.

“No one with a clear conscience believes a food delivery monopoly is in the best interests of the public,” Hepner said.

Hepner cited a Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative investigation released in December 2025, showing that Instacart had used AI by Eversight to charge different prices.

description:

text:
This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Sustainability in hospitality is moving beyond a standalone set of environmental commitments. Skift Research found that accommodations are the trip category where U.S. travelers are most likely to pay more for a sustainable option, while hotel websites are where they most often encounter sustainability messaging.

For Accor, sustainability is not a new priority. Building on a 40-year track record of environmental and social commitments, the Group’s refreshed 2026-2030 sustainability roadmap, Hosting Change, connects sustainability more directly with hotel performance across four areas: future-proof operations, guest experience, talent, and the broader ecosystem. The goal is to create shared value while giving individual regions, brands, owners, and hotels room to adapt the strategy to their local needs.

The roadmap also reflects sustainability’s growing role in Accor’s corporate leadership. Coline Pont, who returned to Accor in 2025 as chief sustainability officer and joined the Group Management Board, brings sustainability into the Group’s highest-level management discussions, reinforcing its relevance to business strategy, hotel owners, and investors.

“The roadmap was designed to make it easy to answer very practical questions,” Pont said. “What does this mean for my hotel, for my team, for my day-to-day decisions?” Skift Studio spoke with her about how Hosting Change was developed, the business case behind it, and how Accor is trying to turn four decades of sustainability commitments into action across more than 5,800 hotels.

Skift Studio: What’s new about Hosting Change?

Coline Pont: It’s not a “start from scratch” program. It’s about building on what already exists and taking it several steps further. The logic is simple: Hosting is what we do every day. Change is what we have to manage. Hosting Change is designed to make them work hand in hand to create shared value.

A hotel performs better when it uses resources wisely, keeps great people, delivers a memorable stay, and stays connected to its community. Our business objectives and sustainability objectives are not competing priorities. They reinforce each other.

The program focuses on carbon, food waste, diversity and inclusion, and eco-certification, alongside four “Extra Miles”: reducing energy, water, and waste; making plant-forward food desirable; opening employment pathways; and supporting people affected by violence.

How do you create a common framework that works across such a diverse network?

Operating more than 5,800 hotels across 110 countries and with a portfolio of more than 45 brands, the challenge is making the strategy work on the ground for very different owners, brands, and markets. A thing that works in one hotel is interesting. A thing that works in five thousand changes the business.

Each region and brand has autonomy to go further on the issues that matter most in its context. In water-stressed regions, that autonomy translates into practical solutions. Mövenpick Petra converted 90% of its rooms from bathtubs to walk-in showers, while Raffles Bali built a dual-source water system that returns 97% of the water it draws back to the land. We also created a Sustainability Owners Advisory Board, bringing together owners who represent around 50% of our network.

What is the strongest business case for owners to invest in sustainability?

Owners face real pressure: rising energy costs, corporate clients with their own ESG targets, and investors who price sustainability into asset valuations. The business case now sits in their P&L every quarter.

The first lever is resource efficiency. Energy and water represent about 7% of a hotel’s annual operating costs. In 2025, we cut water intensity by 5.2%. The second is commercial performance. More than 73% of our largest corporate clients require ESG criteria when selecting hotel partners. The third is long-term asset value. Owners who invest today aren’t just cutting costs. They’re protecting what they own.

How are guest expectations shaping the strategy?

Guests care, but sustainability rarely wins on its own against comfort, price, and location. So we focus on embedding sustainability into the quality of the experience.

Single-use plastics are a good example. We began phasing them out in 2019, formalized a groupwide commitment in 2020, and have since removed more than 50 types across the network.

We found that the replacements often became more thoughtful and more local. What could have looked like a downgrade turned out to be an improvement, and the backlash we braced for never came.

Food is another opportunity. It represents 17% of our carbon footprint. Our commitment to 35% plant-forward dishes by 2030 keeps meat on the menu, but makes more sustainable choices part of an offer guests choose because the food tastes good.

Hosting Change puts a strong focus on talent. In an industry that runs on people, what does it really mean to “empower” a workforce as vast and diverse as Accor’s?

Hospitality is fundamentally a human industry. You can have the most beautiful hotel in the world, but if the people inside it don’t feel valued, the experience falls flat. Empowering talent is probably one of the most complex and exciting challenges we face. It has three dimensions for us.

The first is making sure every single Heartist [Accor’s term for its employees] works in a safe, fair, and dignified environment. Human rights are the non-negotiable foundation on which everything else is built.

The second is making sure everyone has the knowledge and tools to contribute to our sustainability transition in their daily work. That’s why we’ve rolled out our School for Change program to Heartists across the network since 2022, training them to integrate sustainability into their daily on-the-job decisions.

The third dimension is creating real pathways for growth and belonging. Diverse teams perform better: 41% of our roles above the vice president level are held by women, and we intend to keep pushing that further.

And then there is what we call our Extra Mile on talent, which I am personally passionate about. We are reaching beyond our own walls to open pathways to employment for people facing barriers. Through partnerships with NGOs, we offer training, mentorship, and experiences to discover hotels.

By 2030, we are committed to certifying 20,000 people through this Social Mobility program. It does two things at once: creates real social impact and builds a more diverse, motivated workforce for our industry.

Beyond its own operations, Hosting Change extends to suppliers, local communities, and people at risk. Why is it important for a hotel group to look beyond its own walls, and where can hospitality have the greatest positive impact?

Our hotels don’t stand alone. They depend on suppliers, they’re rooted in neighborhoods, and they’re part of communities. We work alongside our suppliers, providing tools, frameworks, and guidance to strengthen their own sustainability performance.

Today, 98% of our nominated suppliers are certified through EcoVadis, and in 2025, we won the World Sustainable Travel and Hospitality Award for our supply chain decarbonization program.

On communities, every property we operate is part of a local ecosystem. Our presence creates lasting value through local partnerships, employment, cultural heritage, and support for local businesses. Last year, 25,000 people benefited from solidarity projects, and through our ALL loyalty program, our members donated 9 million points to social and environmental causes.

Then there’s our Extra Mile initiative: 1,000 hotels opening their doors to people fleeing gender-based violence by 2030. Thirty percent of women aged 15 and older have experienced violence at least once in their lifetime. With thousands of hotels embedded in communities across the globe, we have the infrastructure, the reach, and the responsibility to provide safe shelter when it’s needed most. That’s what responsible hospitality means to us.

We’ve talked a lot about Accor’s own initiatives. How important is it for the wider hospitality industry to work together on sustainability?

The problems are too systemic for any one company to solve alone. I see it every time sustainability leaders from competing hotel groups sit down and openly discuss what’s working and what isn’t.

In December 2026, we’re hosting the World Sustainable Hospitality Alliance Summit, bringing together an organization that represents more than 66,000 hotels and 8 million rooms.

Being first in the race for sustainability isn’t the point. What matters is whether the rest of the industry follows. That’s why our Sustainability Innovation Program is designed to share what works. By 2030, our goal is to pilot and scale 100 resource-saving solutions across our network, then make successful solutions available to the wider hospitality industry.

This year’s focus is water, and we’ll share what we’ve learned at the UN Water Conference. We’ll also participate in COP31, with senior leadership representing Accor.

By 2030, what would success look like?

By 2030, I want all of our brands to be recognized for their sustainability efforts and increasingly chosen because of them.

A traveler who books an Ibis, a Novotel, a Sofitel, or a Raffles should know that responsible choices come with the stay, from the water saved to the food enjoyed. Corporate clients are already moving in that direction, and leisure travelers are starting to follow.

When guests choose our hotels because of these efforts, our hotel owners see it in their bookings, and talented people have one more reason to join us. That is the success and virtuous circle we are building toward.

Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

President of Lilly Neuroscience - Dr. Carole Ho

President of Lilly Oncology and Head of Business Development - Jacob S. Van Naarden

President of Lilly International - Patrik Jonsson

President of Lilly Cardiometabolic Health - Kenneth Custer

TAKEAWAYS

Revenue -- $24.4 billion, growing 39% year over year driven by volume expansion in the Mounjaro and Zepbound franchises.

Non-GAAP EPS -- $7.48, which included $4.57 of acquired in-process research and development charges related to business development activity.

Mounjaro Revenue -- $10.7 billion, representing 65% growth due to strong demand and volume increases in the U.S. and international markets.

Zepbound Revenue -- $5.3 billion, an increase of 48% versus last year primarily driven by domestic volume growth and consumer demand.

FY 2026 Revenue Guidance -- $91 billion to $92 billion, raised from previous expectations based on strong performance across the incretin portfolio.

U.S. Pricing -- Declined 10% when excluding a favorable adjustment to rebate and discount estimates, reflecting competitive dynamics in the weight management market.

Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Program -- Over 500,000 people filled prescriptions since July 1, with 7 out of 10 new bridge patients choosing a Lilly medicine.

China Mounjaro Performance -- Surpassed $1 billion in revenue during its first full year following its inclusion on the National Reimbursement Drug List.

Kisunla Revenue -- $193 million, a 175% increase versus last year, maintaining leadership in the U.S. amyloid targeting therapy market.

Non-GAAP Gross Margin -- 84.4%, an 80 basis point increase driven by favorable product mix and improved manufacturing efficiency.

Performance Margin -- 54.2% on a non-GAAP basis, up 5.9 percentage points from the prior year due to operating leverage from significant revenue growth.

Retatrutide Phase 3 Results -- Delivered a 2.2% HbA1c reduction and 20% to 21% weight loss, more than doubling the weight loss achieved by 2 milligrams of semaglutide.

EloraTZP Phase 2 Results -- Delivered 23.3% weight loss at 48 weeks, representing a 57% improvement over tirzepatide alone in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Orforglipron Safety Profile -- Demonstrated a 57% lower risk of all-cause death versus insulin glargine in the ACHIEVE-4 cardiovascular outcomes trial.

Manufacturing Investment -- Broke ground on $11.5 billion in new U.S. facilities, including a $6.5 billion site in Houston and a $5 billion site in Richmond.

Foundayo Uptake -- Captured a 40% share of patients starting an oral obesity medicine, with quarterly new patient counts doubling since the prior period.

R&D Investment -- Increased 23% to $4.2 billion, reflecting continued spending on early and late-stage clinical programs.

SG&A Expense -- Rose 14% to $3.1 billion, driven by investments in promotional activities for ongoing and planned product launches.

Specialty Portfolio Revenue -- Combined revenue from oncology, immunology, and neuroscience doubled versus the third quarter of 2025.

Shareholder Capital Returns -- Distributed $1.5 billion in dividends and conducted $400 million in share repurchases during the quarter.

Incretin Obesity Market Growth -- Total prescriptions in the U.S. incretin market for obesity grew 82%, with Lilly medicine accounting for 6 out of 10 total prescriptions.

International Incretin Market Share -- Gained nearly 4 percentage points of share since the second quarter to reach 58% of the international market.

Type 2 Diabetes Incretin Growth -- Total prescriptions for type 2 diabetes incretins rose 8% year over year, with Lilly maintaining a market share of more than 60%.

Milestone Revenue -- Revenue included a $410 million milestone payment related to Jardiance, representing the final payment under the existing agreement with Boehringer Ingelheim.

RISKS

CFO Montarce stated, "Consistent with previous years, we expect net realized price to be a headwind more than offset by volume growth," indicating persistent pricing pressure across the portfolio despite volume expansion.

SUMMARY

Eli Lilly and Company (LLY +3.50%) reported significant revenue growth driven by global demand for its incretin franchise and growth in its newest products across multiple therapeutic areas. Management stated that performance was bolstered by the rapid adoption of the Medicare GLP-1 bridge program and strong volume growth in international markets, particularly China. The company raised its full-year guidance to reflect these trends while continuing to invest in large-scale manufacturing expansions to support long-term supply needs. Strategic focus remains on advancing a broad clinical pipeline, including next-generation oral and injectable treatments for obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Management reported that the Medicare bridge program has the potential to generate over $20 billion in cumulative savings over 10 years based on independent policy research.

The launch of Foundayo in four international markets is tracking in line with expectations, with the medicine expanding the overall oral incretin market.

CFO Montarce indicated that the 2027 revenue outlook will be impacted by approximately $2 billion in one-time milestone and rebate benefits from 2026 that are not expected to recur.

CEO Ricks noted that three-fourths of the clinical pipeline is focused on diseases outside of obesity, aiming for diversified and durable growth.

Diagnostics for Alzheimer's disease showed momentum as the number of P-tau217 blood tests more than doubled year over year, aiding Kisunla adoption.

The company completed the acquisitions of AtaiBeckley and Merida Biosciences to enhance research capabilities in neuroplasticity and precision immunology.

Lilly announced the retirement of Patrik Jonsson and the appointment of Ilya Yuffa to the new role of President of Lilly Global Markets.

INDUSTRY GLOSSARY

Incretin: A group of metabolic hormones that stimulate a decrease in blood glucose levels.

HbA1c: A blood test that measures average blood sugar levels over the past three months.

IPR&D: In-process research and development, representing the value of research projects acquired through business combinations.

P-tau217: A blood-based biomarker used for the diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer's disease.

BTK inhibitor: A type of drug that blocks the enzyme Bruton's tyrosine kinase, used to treat certain B-cell cancers.

Oral SERD: Selective estrogen receptor degrader, a type of oral medication used to treat certain types of breast cancer.

MACE-4: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events, a composite endpoint typically including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and hospitalization for unstable angina.

NRDL: National Reimbursement Drug List, a list of medicines covered by China's basic medical insurance system.

Amyloid targeting therapy: A class of treatments designed to remove amyloid plaques from the brain in patients with Alzheimer's disease.

CDK4/6 inhibitor: A class of drugs that interrupt the growth of cancer cells by blocking specific proteins.

PI3 kinase alpha inhibitor: A targeted therapy that inhibits the PI3K pathway, which is often mutated in breast cancer.
