Lucas E. Montarce: And I think the starting point, if you go back when we set up the guide at the beginning of the year, you may remember that we have that slide with again, the opportunities and still events we had in front of us for 2026. We talked about the launch of Foundayo in Q2. We talked about starting the Medicare bridge program. And then, of course, we talk about the variable of the growth OUS, in particular, on the increasing out of pocket business and the runway of that growth. Again, what you see now in the latest guidance that we just shared today is actually a confirmation that we are tracking well across all of them.

Even better than what we anticipated. So that is, I think, a positive confirmation of the trends and the solid performance that we continue to see. Back to your second part of the question about the runway of that, is that pulling forward or not, The way that we think about it is you look at just the Inkredgen business, we are still scratching the surface on the number of patients that we can reach. You look at The US, and we are talking about 1 out of 10 patients that we are reaching nowadays, And in all US, we are talking about 2 patients out of 100 patients.

So it is actually a really low base, though the number seems really big, $16 billion this quarter of incretin business. The runway of opportunity for growth is still years to come from my perspective. And on top of that, we continue to expand the breadth across all the therapeutic areas. Super also happy to report the 100% growth on the rest of the key products across oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. So that is just to give you some color about the short term and how we think about also long term.

Michael Czapar: Great. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Geoffrey Meacham with Citi. Your line is live.

Geoffrey Meacham: I want to ask about what data you have on tirzepatide persistency in obesity just over the course of the past year or so. And importantly, when you look to next year, would you expect Foundayo and retatrutide to be different than that in terms of real world experience? Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Jeff. To talk about tirzepatide persistency and obesity and thoughts on the pipeline looking in the future, we will go to Ilya.

Ilya Yuffa: Jeff, thanks for the question. What we have seen in persistency, and actually before we even launched Zepbound and we have had success with Trulicity in the past. And that was kind of the standard for chronic medicine for adherence, which ended up becoming around 16 to 18 months of adherence. What we are seeing with Zepbound is that in the covered space, we continue to see the trajectory of being just as beneficial in terms of adherence as we have seen in Trulicity. And even in the self pay, we are seeing that close to the covered market. So the persistency actually for chronic medication, Zepbound is doing extraordinarily well. Now expectations for oral, it is still early.

But as typical chronic medications has as well as if you take a look at orals, they typically are lower adherence overall relative to weekly injectable therapies. And that is what we expect to see. 1 additional data point I think will be important we look at even the success of Bridge, early days in Bridge, having a low out of pocket helps with that friction point, and we are seeing improved adherence in Bridge. So that will all play out as part of the different friction points, both in terms of out of pocket as well as the benefit that gain from these therapies.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thanks, Ilya. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Seamus Fernandez with Guggenheim. Your line is live.

Seamus Fernandez: Oh, thanks so much. So I am gonna do the nonobesity question. is actually starting to show the prospect of becoming a blockbuster product and, you know, starting to grow faster, maybe a little bit faster overseas. But you know, I was hoping, Daniel, you might weigh in on the prospects for Trailblazer-3, the prospects for success, and how you see that program really evolving the treatment paradigm should it succeed. Particularly in the context of some of the novel tau biomarkers that we are starting to see. I think there are a lot of questions from investors that we get on what really is the market opportunity here.

Given the Kisunla uptake, but it does seem like some of those behaviors are changing. Thanks.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thanks, Seamus. Always welcome neuroscience questions. So we will go to Carol. Talk about prospects for Kisunla and maybe even kind of the neuroscience space more broadly? Yes. We are very excited to see the growth of Kisunla over the last year, and this growth is both driven by our confidence in this product with its convenient 30 minute infusion time, once monthly dosing, and the opportunity for treat to clear in the patient population. We have also seen a tremendous growth in the for diagnosis with blood based biomarkers with P-tau217 becoming available. And we see this becoming a diagnostic that enables access to early diagnosis, potentially even in primary care office in the future.

As we look at Trailblazer-3, which is our study looking at prevention in cognitively unimpaired people, looking at prevention of early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, these biomarkers will certainly also enable early diagnosis for people that have risk concerns about their cognition before loss of their cognition. So we are excited both about the growth and early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease, but also if Trailblazer 3 reads out positively, really expanding this market to earlier stages of disease where we already have preliminary evidence from our early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease space that treating earlier will have a more significant impact on cognition. Thanks, Carol. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Evan Seigerman with BMO Capital Markets. Your line is live.

Evan Seigerman: Hi, guys. Thank you so much for taking my question. Bigger picture 1 here So clearly, the incretin franchise is becoming an enormous earnings driver, but also raises the question of what comes next. When you look beyond the cardio. cardiometabolic disease, where do you see the best opportunity to build Lilly's next multibillion dollar growth pillar? And does recent BD activity suggests that neuroscience and immunology are emerging as higher strategic priorities? Thank you so much.

Michael Czapar: Great. Evan, for the question about the next big opportunity after incretin. So go to Daniel to talk about some of the pipeline opportunities he is excited about.

Daniel Skovronsky: Yeah. Thanks, Evan. I would say that we are excited about all 3 of our other therapeutic areas, which are immunology, neuroscience, and oncology. And the BD activity reflects just our strategic intent to grow those areas. But the intersection of that strategic intent with assets that are actually out there and that are attractive to us. Oncology is probably the space where we have made the most progress, we highlighted 8 really important late stage programs. Several of which could be quite large in size. For example, the recent Kelonia acquisition, which targets myeloma, is a huge opportunity if the data continue to hold out the way we expect them to.

Neuroscience, of course, is the area that has the largest unmet medical need and really the least progress in the pharmaceutical industry towards addressing that. We are firmly committed to making a difference for patients in this space, and you can see our acquisitions in sleep and psychiatry combined with our in house expertise in neurodegeneration are aimed to really grow that market on behalf of patients. And then finally, immunology. I think there is been a lot of crowding in immunology on a few probably important targets, but we also see great opportunity actually to raise expectations in immunology with breakthrough therapies that I think can deliver efficacy that is never been seen before.

And that is what we are trying to do with programs like the Merida acquisition, or the Orna acquisition, which is aimed at immune reset. So lots of growth opportunities across those areas.

Michael Czapar: Thank you, Daniel. Next caller, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Kerry Holford with Berenberg. Your line is live.

Analyst: Thank you for taking my question. I wonder if you can speak a little more about Medicare Bridge. How does the split between injectable and pill and how does that mix look different from others? It seems by the majority of Medicare demand is injectable. I wonder if that surprised you with regard to your products in that space. And also, could you talk to what proportion of patients in that Medicare channel for the bridge program specifically are naive versus existing patients transferring from other channel.

Michael Czapar: Thank you, Kerry. I will go to Ilya to talk a bit about Bridge, the injectable versus pill split, as well as naive versus switches.

Ilya Yuffa: Yep. Thanks for the question. For Bridge, it performed extraordinarily well. I think we knew that it was going to be a significant benefit for seniors. The program itself is simple in understanding the criteria. And a low out of pocket. And so all of those things combined, we have seen about 3 quarters, 75% of people coming into Bridge going into injectable therapy. 7 out of 10 in total choosing a Lilly medicine. And so we have performed really well across Bridge. That is higher than maybe some of the self-pay segment.

1 of the components of that is these same low out of pocket and getting the greatest efficacy and the standard care that is been established in obesity, has favored Zepbound in particular, But we are seeing good growth and uptake of orals and Foundayo as well. In terms of expanding number of people actually being treated, after the first bolus of people coming into Medicare. We are seeing now that about 80% of the people getting treatment under bridge are naive or have not been on therapy in the past.

And so we see this as a significant driver of access long term, and it is still early days And while it is performing above our expectations, we see continued opportunity here to expand access and utilization and not only improve care of seniors, but, as we shared earlier, on independent study, also a potential of saving significant amount for Medicare overall.

Michael Czapar: Thank you, Ilya. Next caller, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Asad Haider with Goldman Sachs.

Asad Haider: Great. Thanks for taking the question, and congrats on all the progress. Maybe just back to Foundayo. Thanks for the comments earlier. And I know that is still very early in the trajectory. But just curious to hear any updated framing on how the launch is playing out both in The U. S. As well as internationally in the context of both competitive dynamics versus oral Wegovy and then your own internal expectations. And then on the titration schedule, for Foundayo, the 2 lower doses still represent about 75% to 75% to 80% of TRx in recent weeks. So where do you see that going at steady state? Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thanks, Assad. I think we will start maybe with Patrik to talk a bit about some of the ex U. S. Launches and then Ilya will add maybe a couple of nuggets on The US as well.

Patrik Jonsson: Thank you very much. We have now launched in 4 markets outside The US. We started with UAE, very late in Q2, and the second half of Q3, launched in UK, Saudi, and Mexico. I would say that so far, the launch is very much in line with our expectations. A lot of similarities with the learnings from The US in terms of orals are truly expanding the market, and we see a huge amount of patients actually being new to incretins. In Middle East, I think we have a geopolitical situation to take into account, but we are a market leader in UAE with competition from Wegovy.

In Saudi, we have launched in both type 2 and chronic weight management, and we have a good uptake there. UK, we have been subject to the pre vetting requirements by the MHRA. We have actually not been able to fully promote until now in October. But the signs here are also that the orals are expanding the market. Mexico, week 6, a very good uptake and slightly above our expectations. But most importantly, I think we see that there is a lot of work to be done here. We need to do all of the work that has been done in The US as well.

We also recently got a CHMP positive opinion that should hopefully result in a regulatory approval by year end. And we are ready to launch a cross chronic weight management in type 2 diabetes in more than 40 markets next year. But the initial focus is going to be on cash pay and chronic weight management since type 2 reimbursement will take some time.

Ilya Yuffa: Yeah. And in The US, we have made significant progress since last quarter. You have seen over half a million TRx in the quarter, but fundamentals and some of the key indicators that we have been talking about as part of our initial launch have been moving in a really positive direction. Consumer awareness and interest has improved with our investment and campaign with Martha Stewart. You are seeing also a number of trialists have more than doubled since last quarter. And so we are seeing good progression of adoption from providers. And that is showing up in our shared markets. So our NBRx share of market is approaching around 4 out of 10.

And so good progress overall for the growth of Foundayo in the oral segment and even in the sequential growth of orals within from Q2 to Q3, we are taking 45% of that growth with Foundayo. In terms of the titration, it is expected that it takes time to titrate to the maintenance doses, but we have actually seen good progress on our maintenance doses. We have multiple maintenance doses, so about 25 percent of people are at 1 of our maintenance doses. that is actually higher than what you see on the Wegovy. And so we are encouraged by that.

Of course, that is something to continue to monitor, but the experience overall that we are seeing both from provider and consumer has been positive.

David A. Ricks: I would just add we are under review for type 2 diabetes and we see that as an extraordinary opportunity for Foundayo as well. Remembering today in The US, roughly half the volume of GLP-1s is in diabetes. So that is a big market expansion. Of course, needs access and reimbursement when we get that. But that is very promising sort of another leg to the stool here for the Foundayo performance.

Michael Czapar: Okay. Thank you all. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Steve Scala with TD Cowen.

Steve Scala: Oh, thank you so much. This is a follow-up to Christopher's earlier question. And with all due respect, Lily's financial guidance has not been a good predictor on ultimate results. And I am curious, what is the most frequent source of the surprise? So, specifically, has it tended to be positive unit developments, or has it been lack of negatives on price, or is it some desire to just lean incredibly cautiously on guidance? And if it is the latter, why is that? A key for investors, I think, is to determine when the surprise factor runs its course. So any color would be appreciated. Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thanks, Steve, for the direct question. We will go to Lucas to maybe provide a little extra color on guidance. And David, if you want to add anything, feel free as well.

Lucas E. Montarce: Yeah. Steve, thank you for the question. I think in terms of the variables that I described on the first question are still. Again, the variables that we had when we started the year that of course, again, now with yesterday's newspaper, you think about that again, are performing way much better than again, what we had initially guided to. But if you look at the runway of that growth across The US and OUS, has been all the events we were public about again that the unknowns associated with that. Starting with the bridge program, when that bridge program will start, the uptake of that as well. The progression of all US markets both ensure and also penetration.

And those all played out better than what we anticipated. So still the drivers are those ones, Again, we continue to guide to what we forecast in our internal bottom up approach that we have on our forecasting model. and try to be as public as possible about how we see the projections, and now we provided some perspective into 2027 as well. So I think from my perspective, we continue to drive again a very thorough every single quarter and be public about, again, the variables that could affect positively or negatively as well our guidance projections.

David A. Ricks: Yes, Steve. I appreciate the question. You have followed the company a long time. You know, our goal is to give as accurate a projection as we can. But, of course, you know, there is asymmetry with missing on the downside. that is, like, everyone's impulse. But let's remember, like, we are in the middle of the largest new category expansion in the history of the pharmaceutical industry. And Lilly's leading that. So there is a number of things that have never actually happened before. That we are trying to project And you know, we prefer to, you know, give a posture that investors can rely on versus 1 that is more speculative.

And at the JPMorgan Conference at the beginning of the year, I said there is, like, 2 big variables this year. If I knew the answer to, we would have had a tighter range. 1 was the uptake in Bridge, which we did not really know. We were not even sure about the start time of Bridge at that point. And the other was the depth of the consumer purchasing internationally and whether we were really just skimming very high net worth individuals in these out of pocket markets or if more middle income households would be interested improving their health and losing weight at scale.

And I think both of those this year turned out to be positive for us. Thus the roughly $10 billion improvement over first time guide You know, as time goes on, I suspect we will have fewer and fewer of those never before done things. And the guidance can become more predictable. So appreciate the question. But, you know, that is sort of how I have seen it over the last 3 years. And you know, we are we are beating on the up, and that is better than missing on the down.

And I think that is good news mostly not because of the earnings beats, but because we are actually executing against a really scaled opportunity and performing well.

Michael Czapar: Thanks. Thank you, David and Lucas. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Terence Flynn with Morgan Stanley.

Terence Flynn: Great. Thanks for taking the question. Maybe on the pipeline for Daniel. there is been a growing focus on longer-acting incretins. You guys recently said you have 3 different programs in the clinic. So just wondering if we can expect any clinical data at the R and D Day on these programs or if you can tell us what the stage is of development because I think that is the probably, the only hole you have in your, incretin pipeline. Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Terrence. We will actually go to Ken to talk about the long acting approach and if there is anything to share beyond what is been public.

Kenneth Custer: Thanks for the question, Terrence. As we discussed previously, we do see an opportunity for longer acting incretins, particularly in a category that is big with such a consumer emphasis, we are taking the same approach usually do when we see an important square on the board that we want to fill, is we are baking off several competing platforms to see which 1 provides the best product possible. This is a space where we think the molecule properties are really going to matter, so that is why we have not signaled anything yet. but it is true we have multiple efforts in the clinic.

Those are a range of different technological approaches including existing time extension technologies as well as ones that could be part of the future and we have other efforts that we have disclosed in business development around formulation Again, we will look at all these data and make an informed decision on which effort or efforts to advance to Phase 3.

Michael Czapar: Thank you, Kenneth. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Shyam with RBC.

Analyst: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. So as you look to 2027, what are you seeing in terms of in trends for GLP-1 coverage amongst the larger employers in The US? And with those dynamics in mind and bridge continuing to ramp, could your US channel mix meaningfully evolve next year? So it potentially creates additional pricing pressure amongst the mid teens decline that you have absorbed in 2026. Or could we see pricing headwinds in the same range for 2027? Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Shyam. We will go to Ilya to talk about 2027 early opt in trends and maybe the broader access environment as well as we look into the next year?

Ilya Yuffa: Yeah. Overall, obviously, there is been noise around a number of employers opting out of coverage. At the same time, we are having positive discussions for our Connect, and other channels on improving access there as well. Our expectation is that overall, access on the commercial side will maintain relatively stable, through 2027. Obviously, we will continue to have conversations to improve on that. The main access improvements overall for 2027 will most likely be predominantly growth of Medicare. And Medicaid as opportunities for expanded coverage. That will have a segment mix more towards a lower price, a lower net price, not decreasing the price overall, but more just a segment mix.

That as well as some level of self pay in the lower net price per TRx. And in terms of commercial overall pricing, I would expect modest and disciplined approach around pricing and access to maintain. But overall stable on the commercial and increased coverage in Medicare and Medicaid.

Michael Czapar: Okay. Thank you, Ilya. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Akash Tewari with Jefferies. Your line is live.

Akash Tewari: Hey. Thanks so much. So your team's talked about generally predictable and consistent GLP-1 pricing declines in The U. S. Out to the end of the decade. How does that look ex U. S? Could we see more stability there than maybe investors expect? And how do you think about the net price per patient in The U. S. Versus international markets ex China evolving over time? Currently seems quite similar. And, David, you mentioned something interesting. Can you talk a bit more about the size of this emerging middle income cash pay international market opportunity. Relative to what we have seen in The US so far. Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Akash. Some questions for Patrik. So we will talk a bit about pricing expectations kind of on the cadence from here, thinking about net price US versus ex US, and anything about the emergence of a middle income cash pay market.

Patrik Jonsson: Yep. Thank you very much. You know what? We have taken a very deep disciplined approach to pricing OUS. And I think we have seen that both providers, consumers and payers willing to pay for a differentiated product. And we have seen that even the launch of generics in India, Brazil, and Canada, holding our shares and continue to grow. And that is a discipline that we will continue to apply. In terms of the out of pocket willingness, we are actually see quite a big willingness to pay out of pocket OUS as well.

Of course, when market are getting further penetrated and like The UK, where we long more than 2 years ago, and where we have a penetration very much along the lines of The US. We see a lower growth as we expected. But I think overall, taking into account where we are penetration wise, low single digit, Long term, we see a tremendous opportunity, OUS, for the incretins, and we will continue our efforts as well to gain type 2 reimbursement, which is very important And we made some progress in Q3 here now having 9 European markets covered, but we will continue those efforts and continue to take a disciplined approach in terms of pricing.

David A. Ricks: Maybe just a comment on the ex US versus US. I mean, our goal because of the consumer nature of this, is to much tighter band of pricing on obesity medicines than maybe you have seen historically in other medicine categories.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, David and Patrik. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Umer Faff with Evercore.

Umer Raffat: Morning, guys. I wanted to spend a quick second on a potentially sizable in the early breast cancer for Imlanestrant. I understand there is a planned interim for you guys. A competitor trial stopped on interim. A, how should we think about early stoppage odds for your trial? And perhaps more importantly, if you could put the effect size comparisons versus Lidera in perspective knowing that the treatment setting for you is a little more real world with meaningful post CDK 4 penetration. Thank you very much.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thank you, Umer. We will go to James to talk a bit about EMBER 4.

Jacob S. Van Naarden: Yeah. Thanks, Umer. Super excited about Inluriyo both in its current actual commercial performance where it is doing great and helping lots of people with, monotherapy and new combination with Verzenio. And as you mentioned, the real big opportunities in the adjuvant setting with the EMBER-4 study. We have not talked about interim analyses on this study. We have been pretty consistent that we expect the study to read out in 2027 next year. So we are sticking with that. That is what we expect. I think you are raising a good point. The treatment setting that we are exploring is much more real world, I think, than what was examined in Lidera.

Both in the context of the prevalent population that exists may want to switch from existing endocrine therapy to new oral SERD, and a study run-in the context of modern standard of care of CDK4/6 inhibitor, Verzenio,, which our study had and theirs did not. So a bunch of differences, I think if our study does read out successfully, I hope it will be much more relevant to clinical practice and easy to understand how to slot it in. I do not want to comment on anticipated effect sizes because we just need the study to read out and see what it shows us, but excited to get to that point.

Michael Czapar: Thank you, James. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Carter Gould with Cantor. Your line is live.

Analyst: Great. Congrats on the quarter. Maybe just to go back to the Bridge program. Have you had conversations with the admin or the various Plan D sponsors that give you confidence this program will either be extended or balance will be revisited in a different iteration. I guess the point just your confidence that there will not be a disruption at the end of 20 Yeah.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Carter. Well, I will go to David to talk a bit about discussions with administration.

David A. Ricks: Yeah. Well, I think we are pretty optimistic about expansion, I think, for 3 reasons, Carter. 1 is the early uptake is strong, and I think you see both demand and appropriate on label use of the medications The administration did a fantastic job implementing the PA criteria in a way that was not kind of over indexed or under indexed. And I think if we look at the people using the medicines, relatively high BMI, comorbid people. And that leads to the second point, which is cost effectiveness. And I think we highlight today the independent study from USC that estimates not just breakeven, but, like, massive cost savings for Medicare due to this program.

CMS will, because it is being done as a pilot program, will do their own analysis But I think all signals now point to a pretty successful cost effectiveness which could yield either a legislative or a regulatory shift in the coverage permanently. In the meantime, I think there is a lot of energy with the people running CMS at current point to continue this, and the right way to do that is put this into the Part D benefit. So I would expect. And it is probably a good conversation to have, on our Q1 call, that this to then shift to working with the carriers for the 28 calendar year.

And, you know, we will certainly work with the administration and all our partners who supply Part D coverage to have good access across our portfolio. And, you know, continue the success of the program so far.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, David. We will try to squeeze in 2 more if we could, please. Next question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is coming from Michael Yee with UBS Securities. Your line is live.

Michael Yee: Great. Thank you. Maybe just a long term portfolio question around obesity and how you view a consumerism driven market where people will gravitate towards differentiated or different options within your portfolio. So I am thinking about retatrutide and amylin. Can you maybe just put on your prediction hat about what that portfolio would look like and how consumers would choose between these different products, given various competition price declines. Thank you.

Michael Czapar: Thanks, Mike. We will go to Ken to talk about the breadth of the obesity portfolio and how to think about what patients each are for.

Kenneth Custer: Thanks Mike for the question. Let's start with the size of the problem we are confronting here. 1 hundred and 10 million or so people living in The US with obesity or overweight. Internationally. That number has a B at the start of it. that is why we are pursuing a portfolio approach knowing that many individuals will seek out and find over time what works best for them. Each of the molecules in our growing portfolio have unique features and probably each of them can fill multiple roles. We talked about how Foundayo is a great on ramp for earlier in the weight loss journey but can be a great maintenance option as well.

Tirzepatide we see as sort of a cornerstone with a growing body of evidence to support it, including surmount MMO very soon. And then as we focus on retatrutide, this is a molecule that looks like it could do a lot of jobs on the high end delivering tremendous power. Lower end delivering a lot of simplicity and really differentiated responses in some important subpopulations, including men and type 2 diabetics, where it is the first agent that is ever shown greater than 2% or excuse me, 20 percent weight lowering. Beyond that, we have our selective amylin portfolio, which opens up a new pharmacological axis that can offer incretin like weight lowering with really more placebo like GI tolerability.

And then last but not least, the Olora-TZP, we see this as sort of the most physiological approach yet. To weight loss that could also again play a lot of roles in this including providing really differentiated HbA1c lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes. So again, of these agents we think they can play a lot of roles We probably cannot a priority stipulate any individual patient what is going to work best for them. But what is important to us is that we offer all of them We offer choice. We put them on a really a platform with a consistent appearance.

Experience that allows patients to start switch, and step up to any Lilly medicine that works best for them And overall, no matter which 1 they choose, they will still be on a Lilly medicine.

Michael Czapar: Great. Thanks, Kenneth. We will go to the last question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Our final question is coming from Kerry Holford with Berenberg.

Courtney Breen: Hello, team. Thanks for the question today. I know we have spoken a little bit about the pipeline, but I instead wanted to think about other sources of innovation and namely the M&A that you have been doing and licensing that you have been doing, externally to support your pipeline. Obviously, there is been a rapid pace for the first part of this year. Can you just help us understand where you believe you are at in terms of the risk reward balance across your portfolio, the types of areas that might be of interest to continue adding, and how you are kind of ensuring that you are keeping the bar high.

As you continue to take on and broaden this pipeline. Kind of beyond what we see in Phase 2 right now. Thank you so much.

Michael Czapar: Yeah. Thanks, Courtney. We will go to James to talk a bit about the kind of BD strategy the process to assess different transactions and kind of the interest across the board.

Jacob S. Van Naarden: Yeah, thanks for the question. it is funny, mentioned risk reward. Risk is really our friend here. Risk allows us to actually create value. And 1 of the ways we can deploy that for the reasons we can is because we do not need revenue tomorrow. You know, I think, you know, we have this opportunity while the incretin business and the rest of the commercial businesses are doing so well to plan for the next decade or 2 ahead, which allows us to take more risk in a calculated way. And some of that is very early stage deal making, which, you know, oftentimes are not really even press released by us.

So some of them, you do not maybe know as much about. And, you know, we have done a bunch of I would say, clinical stage, but not super late stage clinical deals this year where we see enough risk still within the program for us to create value, but enough derisking for us to feel confident that there is a real medicine or maybe more than 1 medicine there. And, you know, we can point to a handful of deals even on the year. This year, that fit that paradigm. So, you know, you are. I think you will see more of both of those categories from us across all the therapeutic areas.

We are not solving for any 1 given therapeutic area. We are just solving for great products, great science, and great people that we can bring into the company and fuel growth into the decades to come. I think that gives us a competitive advantage, frankly, in how we look for what we wanna take inside relative, to our peers. So we have a pretty rigorous process to stay disciplined on a deal by deal basis, and excited about what we have done so far and what is to come.

Michael Czapar: Thanks. Thank you. Day.

David A. Ricks: Closing comments? Okay. Excellent. Thanks for joining us for today's call. Obviously, a strong quarter for the company. I want to take a moment, though, to promote an upcoming event, our December 7 Investor Day. This will really be an R&D and pipeline focused day. We will have other sections in that as well. And I hope all of you can join us live or if not, remotely for that event. Also wanna take a minute just to again congratulate Patrik on a great career, and I think this will be your last earnings call with us.

You played a big part in our success over the last well, 30 years of your career, but certainly the most recent 6 or 7. So thank you, Patrik, for everything. Please follow-up with the IR team if you have additional questions we did not get to, and look forward to seeing everyone in early December. Thank you.

name: HP Inc
title: It is reported that HP Inc, ASUS, and Acer intend to move their production lines back to China.
description:
Gelonghui, October 30 | Surging demand for artificial intelligence has tightened the supply of storage chips, driving up costs significantly for PC manufacturers.
According to a report by Nikkei Asia on October 28, global PC makers—including HP Inc., ASUS, and Acer—are relocating some production lines from Thailand and Vietnam back to China, reviving Chinese contract manufacturers to cope with rapidly rising component costs and boost production efficiency.
Multiple sources familiar with the matter say that China boasts a mature pool of manufacturing talent, lower production costs, and a complete electronics industry chain, giving it a distinct advantage in component supply and making it one of the best options for PC manufacturing today.
The sources added that Dell, the world's third-largest PC maker after Lenovo and HP Inc., is also evaluating the possibility of shifting part of its production back to China.

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft killed Windows 10 to push Windows 11, but Windows sales crashed 27% as ...
description:
Windows OEM revenue fell 27% as Windows 10’s upgrade boom faded During the FY27 Q1 earnings call on October 28, CFO Amy Hood said Windows OEM revenue “was below expectations” and fell 27%, or 28% in constant currency.
Windows OEM revenue is what Microsoft earns from PC makers like HP, Dell and Lenovo for preinstalling Windows.
It’s part of a larger category, Windows OEM and Devices, which also includes Surface.
Microsoft doesn’t share revenue from only Windows 11, which I feel is odd.
It’s not a secret anymore now that all major industry analysts confirmed the effect of Windows 10’s end of service on Windows 11 PC sales.
text:
Microsoft’s Windows OEM revenue fell 27% in the July to September 2026 quarter, and Microsoft says it was “driven by the Windows 10 end of support demand in the prior year, inventory drawdowns by OEM and channel partners, and weaker PC market demand.” As it turns out, the people who rushed to buy PCs before Windows 10 support ended last year don’t have a reason anymore to upgrade…

Meanwhile, a big chunk of PC users still hasn’t moved on. In September 2026, nearly a year after Windows 10 support ended, Steam’s hardware survey shows Windows 11 at 71.34% with 0.37% growth, while Windows 10 had 0.71% growth and 23.61% market share.

Windows OEM revenue fell 27% as Windows 10’s upgrade boom faded

During the FY27 Q1 earnings call on October 28, CFO Amy Hood said Windows OEM revenue “was below expectations” and fell 27%, or 28% in constant currency. “Inventory levels remain elevated,” she added.

Windows OEM revenue is what Microsoft earns from PC makers like HP, Dell and Lenovo for preinstalling Windows. It’s part of a larger category, Windows OEM and Devices, which also includes Surface. Revenue in that category fell 22% from $4.55 billion to $3.55 billion, according to Microsoft’s earnings release. Microsoft doesn’t share revenue from only Windows 11, which I feel is odd.

Anyway, what I find interesting is how the inventory story flipped so quickly. Back in July, Hood said Windows results were “ahead of expectations as OEM and channel partners continue to build inventory.” Three months later, these partners are selling through that stock and buying fewer Windows licenses.

Ironically, Bing and Edge did just fine. Search advertising revenue grew 12%, helped by “higher volume and rate across LinkedIn, Edge, and Bing.” This comes as Microsoft is reducing Bing’s presence in Windows!

Windows 10’s end of support sold a lot of Windows 11 PCs in 2025

If you look at it from another angle, the 27% drop looks so bad because the comparison is with a quarter when businesses and consumers were rushing to replace Windows 10 PCs.

In the third quarter of 2025, global PC shipments grew 8.2% to nearly 70 million units. “Worldwide PC shipments were driven by the Windows 10 end-of-support (EOS) refresh cycle in most regions,” Gartner’s Rishi Padhi said at the time. By the end of 2025, shipments grew 9.1% for the year, with fourth-quarter demand “fueled by the Windows 11 upgrade cycle,” according to Gartner.

PC makers weren’t hiding the facts. In August 2025, Dell COO Jeff Clarke said he expected growth “driven by an aging installed base and the Windows 10 end of life.” Microsoft admitted in July that it was up against “a high prior-year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support,” which is why we said Windows 10’s end of support was the real Windows 11 sales driver.

Unfortunately for Microsoft and its partners, a deadline only works once. Many people who needed a new PC bought one before October 2025, and they’re not buying another one a year later.

Windows 10 holdouts still aren’t switching

The rest are holding on (I personally know a few). Lansweeper found that Windows 10 still ran on 16.9% of Windows PCs it tracked in July 2026, and 21.4% in small and mid-sized businesses. I understand the conflicting numbers can be confusing, but tracking OS market share can only go so far. However, the interesting bit is that, from the numbers Lansweeper found, only about 2.8% of those PCs can’t run Windows 11, so most of them could upgrade if their owners wanted to.

HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill said in May that “roughly 30% of the installed base” is still on Windows 10. Microsoft didn’t help its case either, when the company extended free consumer security updates for Windows 10 to October 12, 2027. “We understand that moving to a new PC can take time,” Microsoft said.

Then there’s the giant elephant in the room: buying a new PC is now insanely expensive thanks to the memory shortage. Counterpoint says global PC shipments fell 21% in Q3 2026, blaming higher prices for RAM, SSDs and processors, along with a Q3 2025 that was boosted by Windows 10’s deadline. It’s not a secret anymore now that all major industry analysts confirmed the effect of Windows 10’s end of service on Windows 11 PC sales.

To be clear, Microsoft didn’t say that Windows 10 holdouts caused the 27% drop. But as long as they stay put, the software giant can’t count on another wave of Windows 11 upgrades, especially as Copilot+ PC branding didn’t do much to drive sales.

Microsoft expects Windows revenue to fall even further

For the October to December quarter, Microsoft expects Windows OEM and Devices revenue to “decline in the mid-thirties.” Hood said, “Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand, and a prior-year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support,” adding, “We expect these trends to continue through the rest of this fiscal year.”

Three months ago, Microsoft expected a decline “in the high teens” for the full fiscal year. Now, it’s guiding for a drop roughly twice as steep in a single quarter.

The seemingly stoic Satya Nadella talked about “making every PC a secure agent box” that runs AI models locally on new chips from AMD, Intel, Qualcomm and NVIDIA. On the call, he also said, “We think of Copilot as the new OS for work.” I’m not sure Windows fans will love hearing that from the company that makes Windows.

Meanwhile, IDC believes Apple’s $599 MacBook Neo is “putting real pressure on the entire PC ecosystem,” and is continuing to do so. Apple also launched the new Touch enabled MacBook Pro, giving another reason for Windows 10 holdouts to switch to the other side. Not a good sign for the Windows PC ecosystem!

Windows 11 needs a reason to upgrade that isn’t a deadline

Windows 11 has to sell itself on being fast and reliable, which is why fixes like the faster right-click menu in KB5127936 do more for Windows than any AI or agentic capabilities in the OS.

If Microsoft wants the remaining Windows 10 users to upgrade, it has to give them a reason to want Windows 11, and my top picks would be better privacy, no ads and recommendations, faster and cleaner.

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft Insiders Explain Why 60000 Employees Got Buyout Offers - Business Insider
description:
Microsoft doubled down later and told Business Insider it anticipates 3,000 or fewer employees will take the buyout.
Layoff concerns Earlier this year, the company offered a retirement buyout to employees based on age and tenure.
That's led to speculation that more layoffs may come in the wake of this week's bigger buyout offer.
Misconceptions and differences Business Insider spoke to Microsoft executives who said there are misconceptions about the current buyout offer.
This person thinks Microsoft made latest buyout offer because some employees complained that they weren't eligible for the retirement buyout earlier this year.
text:
Microsoft's huge employee buyout stunned the industry this week, raising urgent questions about why the software giant might want so many people to leave.

Inside the company, concerned staff debated the meaning of the move. Why might Microsoft want to shed 60,000 workers? Will roles be replaced by AI? Are more layoffs ahead?

Business Insider spent recent days speaking with Microsoft insiders to find out what's really happening. The people asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters.

The main takeaway so far is that Microsoft seems to have unnecessarily spooked employees with the sheer size of its buyout offer, leaving leaders scrambling to calm the troops.

Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood in an internal memo explained the offer was intended to "offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms" and said the company expected "very few people" to accept.

Microsoft doubled down later and told Business Insider it anticipates 3,000 or fewer employees will take the buyout. That's only about 5%, or less, of those eligible.

Layoff concerns

Earlier this year, the company offered a retirement buyout to employees based on age and tenure. About one-third accepted.

Soon after, Microsoft did another round of layoffs. Some employees who didn't accept the retirement offer ended up losing their jobs.

That's led to speculation that more layoffs may come in the wake of this week's bigger buyout offer.

"Future workforce needs will continue to be based on business needs and priorities," Microsoft said in a statement.

Misconceptions and differences

Business Insider spoke to Microsoft executives who said there are misconceptions about the current buyout offer.

These executives could only speak about their own teams, and they were hesitant to definitively say layoffs aren't coming. However, they pointed out a few differences between the current buyouts and the retirement offer.

"Microsoft doesn't want to shrink by 60,000 people," one executive said, while asking not to be identified. "We are not replacing everyone with AI."

This person thinks Microsoft made latest buyout offer because some employees complained that they weren't eligible for the retirement buyout earlier this year.

And in the case of the retirement buyout, when employees left, Microsoft didn't fill those roles — the headcount went away.

This week's buyout works differently. In some cases, when staff leave this time their roles will be backfilled with new hires.

Why the latest buyout looks so big

One reason the latest buyout looks so huge: Some leaders decided it would be simpler to offer it to their entire organization, rather than try to pick which specific teams or individuals should be included.

"It's easier to opt-in giant organizations," one Microsoft executive told Business Insider.

Charles Lamanna, the executive in charge of the Copilot Platform, AI agents, Office and Word, decided to offer it to everyone in his organization, one of the people said. That includes many people in critical positions. The organization is prepared to backfill roles if any of those critical employees accept the buyout, this person said.

The Cloud + AI group took a different approach

Microsoft's key Cloud + AI division took a slightly different approach, according to another executive from the company.

Two teams — Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure and Cloud Operations + Innovation teams — decided not to offer the latest buyout to staff.

Most other groups within the Cloud + AI division did offer the buyout to employees. And this division can backfill some roles, this executive told Business Insider.

Cutting costs and avoiding layoffs

Backfilling roles could still help Microsoft cut labor costs. One executive at the company said if a senior person were to leave, they would likely backfill the role with someone more junior who would potentially be paid less. A Microsoft spokesperson said that's not an official company position.

If all this seems overly complex, compared to layoffs, there may be a reason: Microsoft has been under fire for cutting American staff while employing foreign workers.

The Trump administration recently suspended Microsoft from a federal program that sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency, accusing the company of laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft has denied those claims.

"Never say never, but there's a lot of desire not to do big layoffs, especially as an American company," one of the Microsoft executives told Business Insider.

title: Walmart and Symbotic Expand Commercial Agreement to Support Supply Chain Transformation
description:
Under the expanded agreement, Symbotic will bring additional capabilities to Walmart's U.S. distribution network.
This agreement also supports the continued growth of Walmart’s supply chain capabilities globally, helping deliver greater value for customers in markets around the world.
ABOUT SYMBOTIC Symbotic is an automation technology leader reimagining the supply chain with its end-to-end, A.I.-powered robotic and software platform.
As the backbone of commerce, Symbotic transforms the flow of goods and the economics of the supply chain for its customers.
CONTACTS For Symbotic: Matt Buckley Vice President, Communications mediainquiry@symbotic.com Charlie Anderson Vice President, Investor Relations & Corporate Development ir@symbotic.com For Walmart: Walmart.com/Reporter
text:
WILMINGTON, Mass., Oct. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Symbotic Inc. (Nasdaq: SYM), a leader in A.I.-enabled robotics technology for the supply chain, and Walmart Inc. (Nasdaq: WMT) today announced an expanded commercial agreement to bring further automation capabilities to 25 U.S. regional distribution centers, while supporting additional opportunities across Walmart’s global supply chain network.

Symbotic continues to invest in innovations that use AI to improve supply chain performance. Under the expanded agreement, Symbotic will bring additional capabilities to Walmart's U.S. distribution network. This agreement also supports the continued growth of Walmart’s supply chain capabilities globally, helping deliver greater value for customers in markets around the world. The agreement includes an initial commitment of approximately $6 billion in spend, covering work over several years across multiple locations.

"Our partnership with Walmart started with a single product over a decade ago, and now we offer a full end-to-end solution to help power Walmart's growth across its supply chain for years to come," said Rick Cohen, Chairman and CEO of Symbotic. "This expanded agreement reflects the strength of that collaboration – a partnership defined by trust and shared ambition."

Symbotic’s integrated solution has been developed through relentless innovation, and today includes a BreakPack each-picking solution and the SymMicro micro-fulfillment solution for e-commerce. All Symbotic solutions are underpinned by its proprietary software, which harnesses AI to orchestrate and optimize the movement of millions of cases, every day.

“At Walmart, we're focused on bringing more items to more customers and members, faster than ever. Our investments in the physical and digital supply chain help us serve them however they choose to shop, whether in stores, at the curbside or at home,” said Rob Montgomery, Executive Vice President for Walmart U.S. Supply Chain Operations. “Our work with Symbotic over the years, including this expanded agreement, helps us improve service, grow capacity, simplify work for our associates and lower costs.”

Through its expanded work with Symbotic, Walmart plans to bring additional automation capabilities to its regional distribution center network, supporting e-commerce upstream inventory management, increasing storage capacity and improving how products move through the supply chain. These capabilities will help Walmart offer customers a broader assortment, improve speed and provide more reliable replenishment across its network.

ABOUT SYMBOTIC

text:
“This medicine could be one of our largest medicines in history,” Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC on Tuesday, as the Swiss drugmaker backed remibrutinib, its experimental MS medicine, to generate more than $4 billion in peak annual sales.

Days before, Barclays cut its forecast for the drug’s peak sales after detailed results from two late-stage trials showed the drug had reduced relapses in MS patients by less than analysts expected.

It highlights a challenge for Novartis as it prepares to outline its long-term growth strategy in mid-November.

The drugmaker reported sales growth this week despite losing key patent protection for blockbuster heart drug Entresto. But Barclays analysts said that the market is already looking to the next patent cliff, with bestsellers Kisqali and Kesimpta facing patent expirations around 2032.

watch now

That’s “the market’s bigger question,” Barclays analysts said on Wednesday, noting Kisqali and Kesimpta expiries alone represent $18 billion in peak sales.

Against that backdrop, Novartis has guided for $8 billion-plus in total sales of remibrutinib, including indications other than relapsing MS.

Amit Bar-Or, a multiple sclerosis specialist at the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC that remibrutinib appeared to offer a promising safety profile but was unlikely to control relapsing MS as effectively as high-efficacy antibodies like Novartis’ own Kesimpta.

He added that the drug’s biggest opportunity to expand the market could emerge if ongoing trials demonstrate a benefit in progressive multiple sclerosis, where treatment options remain limited.

How remibrutinib works

Remibrutinib belongs to a class of medicines known as BTK inhibitors, which aim to reduce the immune system activity that damages nerves in MS patients.

Kesimpta works differently. It is a monoclonal antibody that binds to the CD20 protein, depleting B cells involved in the autoimmune response in MS.

Unlike Kesimpta, remibrutinib aims to regulate the cells’ activity without eliminating them.

Bar-Or distinguished the biology of relapsing MS — in which patients experience flare-ups — from progressive MS, which worsens gradually over time.

Clinical results for remibrutinib in relapsing MS appear to be similar to Roche’s rival BTK inhibitor fenebrutinib, but less effective at preventing relapses than anti-CD20 treatments such as Kesimpta, according to Bar-Or.

No head-to-head trials have yet compared remibrutinib with fenebrutinib or anti-CD20 treatments, making direct comparisons difficult.

It could still be an attractive switch for patients who are experiencing progressive MS while on an anti-CD20, he added. An ongoing clinical trial testing whether remibrutinib can effectively treat progressive MS is expected to read out in 2031.

One potential advantage of BTK inhibitors is that they regulate immune cells rather than eliminate them, which could make them safer over the long term than some existing MS treatments, Bar-Or said. However, there is not yet enough long-term safety data to confirm this, he added.

A Novartis spokesperson told CNBC that it views remibrutinib primarily as an opportunity to expand its MS portfolio, rather than replace sales of Kesimpta.

The company is targeting newly diagnosed patients, those currently taking oral treatments, and patients receiving anti-CD20 therapies who may be eligible to switch.

Novartis sees a $6 billion-plus peak annual sales opportunity for Kesimpta alongside $4 billion-plus for remibrutinib in relapsing MS.

Remibrutinib sales outlook

Morningstar analyst Jay Lee told CNBC that Novartis’ $4 billion-plus peak sales forecast for remibrutinib in MS was “within the realm of possibility” but wasn’t “de-risked.”

Lee added that this would depend on how remibrutinib compares with Roche’s rival fenebrutinib, drug pricing negotiations, whether its potential tolerability advantages translate into patients staying on treatment longer, and whether clinical trials support switching patients from existing MS treatments.

“In the near term, I expect the largest market for remibrutinib will be the oral switch market, i.e. patients taking a generic oral treatment who need to switch, particularly due to tolerability reasons.”

For now, investors are focusing on the RESHAPE trial, which enrolled patients aged 40 to 70 taking Roche’s anti-CD20 antibody Ocrevus, and is expected to read out in 2028.

While that could allow remibrutinib to take some market share from CD20 drugs like Ocrevus and Kesimpta, it “may still work in Novartis’ favor if it means they gain overall RMS patient share from Roche, which currently leads the market,” Lee said, adding that Novartis estimates about 75% of switch-eligible patients on CD20 drugs are not on Kesimpta.

Additionally, remibrutinib is already approved to treat certain forms of chronic hives, and a late-stage clinical trial testing it for the chronic inflammatory skin disease hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is expected to read out before Nov. 19.

Barclays estimates a $2 billion peak annual sales opportunity in HS but assigns the drug only a 50% probability of success, citing an unusual dose-response pattern in mid-stage trials and a history of late-stage trial failures in HS.

title: DoorDash Acquires Instacart As Consolidation Comes For Mobility Media - AdExchanger
description:
DoorDash on Thursday confirmed the rumors and announced its intention to acquire Instacart at a $17 billion valuation.
While DoorDash doesn’t regularly break out ad revenue, it disclosed a year ago that it had surpassed $1 billion in such revenue in 2024.
Instacart does discloses advertising revenue, and announced it earned it more than $300 million in Q3 this year.
And Instacart and DoorDash are neatly incremental to each other.
Instacart converts a tenth as many checkouts, but its gross marketplace sales are a third the size of DoorDash.
text:
DoorDash on Thursday confirmed the rumors and announced its intention to acquire Instacart at a $17 billion valuation.

The deal is a logical one for a variety of reasons.

The two fit into the same category of mobile app-based, last-mile-fulfillment specialists that have shoehorned their way into the brick-and-mortar shopping habits.

These companies fall into a sort of “mobility” sub-category of retail media, too. While DoorDash doesn’t regularly break out ad revenue, it disclosed a year ago that it had surpassed $1 billion in such revenue in 2024. Instacart does discloses advertising revenue, and announced it earned it more than $300 million in Q3 this year. So these are billion-dollar ad businesses.

And Instacart and DoorDash are neatly incremental to each other. At least that’s the framing from the companies’ joint press release on the deal.

“Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour,” per the release.

In other words, the two may seem to have competitive friction, since they work with many of the same convenience, pharmacy, grocery, clothing and apparel chains. But they exist as part of different types of shopping habits and convert different types of purchases, even if it’s the same product from the same store. Imagine an impulse-buy snack and soda order and the same items in a grocery cart.

And this somewhat anecdotal hypothesis is borne out by their respective data. DoorDash reported in its quarterly earnings today (busy day!) that it processed 993 million total orders in Q3. It earned $33.9 billion on those orders.

Instacart had only 91.4 million total sales, per its quarterly earnings report (also today, can you imagine?). And it earned $10.5 billion.

Instacart converts a tenth as many checkouts, but its gross marketplace sales are a third the size of DoorDash. Thus proving, at least, that its average order size is much larger.

When considering the timing of this proposed acquisition, one cannot ignore the politics of antitrust and acquisition, and of this moment.

DoorDash has expanded its lobbying presence in recent years and has ingratiated itself with the Trump administration. Perhaps you caught this DoorDash-White House photo op. The delivery firm was a Trump inauguration donor, too, but it has been opposed by some prominent Democrats with stances on labor policy and litigation.

The Biden administration would perhaps have taken a sharp look at this merger as a potential antitrust violation. Especially considering the spree of mobile marketplaces DoorDash has acquired, including Wolt (in Finland), Deliveroo (the UK) and SevenRooms (a marketing platform for restaurants, hotels and venues).

Compare what I predict will be the breezy way this DoorDash-Instacart deal goes through to the nightmarish undoing of the proposed merger between Kroger and Albertsons, which was opposed by the Biden-era DOJ. The two grocery chains are now embroiled in a massive lawsuit themselves over who caused the deal to crash and burn.

If Kroger and Albertsons had waited – and, frankly, paid some millions of dollars in lobbying funds to a President Trump-approved recipient – that deal might have skated by without a fuss.

Which is all to say, don’t expect the deal-making to stop. There are still valuable independent mobility-and-advertising businesses like Lyft, Gopuff (which white labels its own ad sales through DoorDash, by the way) or even GSTV (it sells ads on gas pump screens).

Nowadays, who knows what could happen?

Megaspeed buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell compute to Chinese AI labs, including Qwen AI maker Alibaba.

text:
The companies behind powerful AI technology are high-stakes territory for international espionage. A new investigation from The New York Times published Thursday found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of Chinese spying activity, with the US government identifying a data center executive with whom he had developed a “close relationship” as a possible operative for the Chinese government.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Megaspeed buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell compute to Chinese AI labs, including Qwen AI maker Alibaba. But while US intelligence agencies had her under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law, officials discovered she was also allegedly funneling information to the Chinese government in Beijing.

There are no details about what information Alice Huang may have shared with China, or how valuable it might be, though the Times reports that an investigation and surveillance of her are ongoing. Jensen Huang was not given a heads-up by the US government because it could have risked the US’ investigation into the Megaspeed exec, the Times said, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

More from CNET

An Nvidia spokesperson told CNET that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang are “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” Nvidia added that customers like Megaspeed are “no different than many other regional cloud customers” that don’t receive sensitive trade secrets, and the company is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

This report is the latest incident highlighting how AI technology and infrastructure are a key part of international trade and conflict, underscoring concerns about AI’s capabilities and its outsized share of the global economy. It isn’t even the first time this month that a major AI company has dealt with alleged espionage: The FBI arrested a Saudi Arabian national for planting a recording device in one of OpenAI’s executive conference rooms.

AI and international law

You can’t do AI without cutting-edge computer chips. That’s what has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company by market cap — $5 trillion this year — because it makes and sells the most advanced computer chips, the kind that AI data centers use. Big Tech companies are hustling to build data centers, in spite of significant environmental concerns and public backlash. It has created a firestorm in the computing industry. With advanced chips in such high demand, the costs of RAM and storage have risen across the board. Many hardware manufacturers are passing the additional cost on to consumers.

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025. Now the US government gets 15% of revenue from Nvidia and fellow chipmaker AMD from certain chip sales to China. But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

Trump has a friendly relationship with many Big Tech leaders, including Jensen Huang, which has resulted in millions in personal donations for the president and relaxed regulations for tech companies. The Times reports that Trump was briefed on the investigation into Alice Huang a year ago and chose not to take any action.

The White House, the US Department of Justice and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

text:
Eli Lilly’s revenue is growing so fast that analysts are continually being caught off guard on earnings day. It’s a good surprise, with billions of dollars earned over expectations, but a surprise nonetheless, and analysts don’t like surprises.

As analysts try to read the crystal ball and provide investors with as clear a view as possible on potential investment risks, anything that throws off their calculations could be seen as a bad thing. So CEO David Ricks and his executive team were asked on a Thursday morning earnings call why guidance has been so unreliable, consistently underestimating the revenue that Lilly will actually bring in.

“A key for investors, I think, is to determine when the surprise factor runs its course,” Steve Scala, a long-time analyst with TD Cowen, said on the call.

Providing accurate guidance is always the goal for Lilly, Ricks said, but the rapid expansion of the incretin market has simply been too unprecedented to predict.

“We’re in the middle of the largest new category expansion in the history of the pharmaceutical industry, and Lilly’s leading that,” Ricks said. “There’s a number of things that have never actually happened before that we’re trying to project, and we prefer to give a posture that investors can rely on versus one that is more speculative.”

He admitted that Lilly’s guidance has missed on the low side, with actual earnings arriving much above consensus. But Ricks said the alternative—underperforming expectations—is worse. “We’re beating on the up; that’s better than missing on the down.”

Following third quarter earnings, where revenue rose 39% to $24.4 billion, Lilly again raised full-year guidance after the third quarter to a range of $91–92 billion. At the end of 2025, Lilly had expected a range of $80–83 billion for 2026.

Major factors behind that $10 billion guidance increase include the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, an access program launched by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in July that has spurred more uptake than expected. Lilly reported that 500,000 patients are now using the program to access Lilly’s obesity medications, with 80% being those new to incretins.

Growth in all regions defied expectations, explained CFO Lucas Montarce.

Ricks recalled back to the J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference in January when he pointed to the Bridge program and consumer uptake as major variables. “If I knew the answer [then] we would have had a tighter range,” he said on Thursday.

Lilly also wasn’t sure how many patients it would reach as GLP-1s went to a more consumer market. Were they going to reach beyond high-net-worth individuals into the middle class?

“As time goes on, I suspect we’ll have fewer and fewer of those never-before-done things, and the guidance can become more predictable,” Ricks assured analysts on the call.

How to spend it

The staggering revenue growth has left Lilly with plenty of cash to play with for deals. Already, the company has executed 11 new pacts this year with chief dealmaker Jacob Van Naarden promising more during the earnings call.

“Risk is really our friend here. Risk allows us to actually create value,” said Van Naarden, who serves as executive VP and president, Lilly Oncology and head of Corporate Business Development.

But Lilly’s strategy is evolving. After completing the acquisitions of psychedelics biotech AtaiBeckley and Merida Biosciences, the pharma has now shifted its dealmaking to preparing for the next decade and beyond with early bets, Van Naarden said, as the incretin portfolio carries the rest of the business. He even cryptically hinted at some deals that have been done without much fanfare beyond known acquisitions.

“Some of that is very early-stage deal making, which oftentimes are not really even press released by us, so some of them maybe you don’t know as much about,” he said.

Van Naarden promised deals across all of Lilly’s therapeutic categories, including cardiometabolic, immunology, oncology and neuroscience.

“We’re just solving for great products, great science and great people that we can bring into the company and fuel growth into the decades to come,” he said on the call. “I think that gives us a competitive advantage, frankly, in how we look for what we want to take inside relative to our peers.”

text:
Strong Quarter Signals Strategic Pivots

Board a runaway train, folks, 'cause Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY) is steaming ahead with third-quarter results that'll make any investor sit up and take notice. Revenue's up 39% to a hearty $24.4 billion, with Mounjaro and Zepbound doing some serious lifting. This ain't just small potatoes; it's full-on farm territory.

Financial Peaks and Valleys

Lilly's crew didn't just stop at a hefty revenue jump. Earnings per share (EPS) on a reported basis ticked up 16% to $7.22. Sure, there's more than meets the eye here with IPR&D charges gobbling up $4.57 per share, driving EPS higher on the non-GAAP ledger to $7.48. Smart moves or savvy positioning? Maybe a bit of both.

"The gains we've seen underscore our commitment to innovation," CEO David Ricks mentions, but it's the numbers doing the real talking.

Guidance: Turned Up to Eleven

When a company re-evaluates its annual guidance from $85-87 billion to jaw-dropping $91-92 billion, it's time to sit up and take stock, literally. The mid-year revenue springboarded $5.5 billion, making the rest of 2026 look sunny indeed. Yet, don't let the rosy spectacle blindside you: key product strategies might have curbed short-term risks, but hefty IPR&D charges muddy the waters somewhat.

Regulatory Ball Game

The regulatory turf ain't without its fair share of lemons, but Lilly's making lemonade by scoring new FDA nods. Mounjaro’s cardiovascular chops, Inluriyo's breast cancer combo, and insulin Onswik's weekly dosing against type 2 diabetes. Each approval sits pretty in Lilly's basket, affirming their knack for navigating the regulatory maze.

Pipeline Plunge: What's Brewing Beneath

Beyond the immediate, Lilly’s future stands bolstered by a pipeline prepped for a positive jolt. The latest phase trials of some eye-catching candidates—retatrutide, EloraTZP, and new blips from Omvoh and Ebglyss—signal the upswing could be more robust than ever. It’s not just the deals in Q3 sweetening the scene but the whole expected cadence of moving the needle.

Retatrutide's Phase 3 outcomes against Ozempic could reshape diabetes care.

EloraTZP: Phase 2 positive hits, gearing for Phase 3.

Expanding territories in immunology and oncology—it's the kind of play that screams long-term value-proposition.

Ah, the Acquisitions Angle

With AtaiBeckley adding muscle to Lilly's treatment-resistant depression arsenal, and Merida Biosciences beefing up the immune and allergic disease roster, Lilly is snapping up pieces like a player on the chessboard looking three moves ahead. These strategic buys aren't mere whimsy, they pivot Lilly toward sustainable growth arenas.

Conclusion: Navigating New Heights

Investors better buckle in, as this pharmaceutical stalwart shows no signs of throwing the brakes on anytime soon. From shaking loose vast sums in revenue to smoothing out R&D investments, Lilly is brushing off the dust of quarterly charges with an agile twist of maneuverable strategy. Anyone wagering on the healthcare titans should keep Eli Lilly on the radar—a loaded pipeline and aggressive portfolio playbook are both cause and catalyst. So, in the tale of revenue races and FDA dances, here it seems, the patient hand may very well catch the lion's share.
