text:
"I believe risk management is not about avoiding every risk, but about appropriately managing risks the company can bear and supporting sustainable growth."

In a recent interview with The Asia Business Daily, Cho Eunhee, Chief Risk Officer (CRO) of AXA General Insurance, said, "The capabilities that will become increasingly important in insurers' risk management are the ability to link risk analysis results to business strategies and to maintain a balance between profitability and stability."

Cho is a finance and risk management expert with more than 20 years of experience in the financial industry. After working in various fields, including business planning, accounting, and investment, she took on the role of CRO at AXA General Insurance in 2017. She currently supports management decision-making by developing strategies to address major risks facing the company, including insurance, financial, and operational risks, and by reviewing risks associated with new product development and new investments.

"A CRO must do more than review and control individual risks; the role also involves offering objective opinions on the direction of business initiatives while taking the company's risk appetite into account," she said, explaining the role of a CRO. She added, "In particular, a CRO should help executives balance short-term performance with medium- and long-term financial soundness." She also said, "When launching new products or adjusting the business portfolio, companies should consider not only expected returns but also potential losses."

In the "2026 Future Risks Report," recently published by global insurance group AXA, "artificial intelligence (AI) and big data" ranked first among the future risks that experts are most concerned about, overtaking climate change for the first time. AXA has analyzed major future risks around the world in an annual report since 2014. "In the global survey, AI and big data surged to first place from fourth last year. This can be seen as reflecting concerns that social responses and risk management systems have not kept pace with the speed of AI development," Cho said. "AI is a focus of interest for everyone, but the reality is that fears about it are also growing."

"AI and big data" were also identified as the greatest future risk in Korea. "Korean experts, like those in the global survey, identified AI and big data as the greatest future risk," Cho said. She also noted that "'cybersecurity,' which ranked fourth in the global survey, came in second in Korea, indicating relatively high concern about security threats in the digital environment." She added, "Rather than replacing existing risks, new risks are becoming closely interconnected, allowing individual risks to spread to other areas and potentially trigger cascading effects across the economy and society."

A series of hacking incidents in Korea in recent months has heightened awareness of security threats and personal information protection. In this regard, Cho emphasized that the domestic insurance industry should pay close attention to cyber and information security risks. "Cyber and information security risks are directly linked to 'trust,' so they must be managed as a priority," she said. "When a security incident occurs, companies must quickly identify the scope and cause of the damage and prevent further harm through cooperation among relevant departments. They must also take timely measures to protect customer information and restore normal services." She added, "Companies should establish measures to prevent a recurrence, address vulnerabilities in existing security systems, and strengthen their ability to respond to similar incidents."

AI is prompting changes in how insurers manage risk. The scope of risk management, which once focused on areas such as insurance claims and market fluctuations, is expanding to include new risks arising from the spread of digital technologies. "Until now, insurers' risk management has centered on traditional risks, such as claims-related risks that affect the solvency ratio, but the development of AI is making the nature of risks more complex," Cho said.

One prominent example is insurance fraud involving the misuse of generative AI and deepfake technology. In June, the Financial Services Commission launched a task force (TF) to establish an "AI-based insurance fraud prevention system," with participation from the Financial Supervisory Service, the insurance industry, and the National Health Insurance Service. The task force is discussing measures such as comparing insurance claim documents against original information to determine whether they have been forged or altered.

"Insurers' risk management is expanding beyond individual company responses toward the early identification and prevention of risks through AI-based detection technologies and data sharing between institutions," Cho said. "Going forward, greater efforts will be needed to strengthen customer protection and the reliability of the insurance system through cooperation with relevant institutions."

As climate change alters the patterns and scale of damage caused by natural disasters, concerns have been raised that relying on historical data to predict future risks has its limitations. "When assessing natural disaster risks, companies should consider not only claims history but also the likelihood of each type of disaster and the regional distribution of insurance policies," Cho said. "If extensive damage is concentrated in a particular region, the burden of insurance claims could surge, so it is necessary to assess both the concentration of risk and the potential maximum loss."

AXA Group is strengthening its capabilities to analyze and manage a range of risks, including climate change, geopolitical risks, and risks related to assets and buildings, using AI and data technologies. "For insurers to manage natural disaster risks, it is also important to properly distinguish between risks the company will bear itself and those it will transfer to external parties," Cho said. "Reinsurance, in particular, is a key tool for distributing losses caused by natural disasters and maintaining stable claims-paying capacity." She added, "We plan to examine risk management measures involving reinsurance, taking into account patterns of natural disasters and their impact on financial soundness."

She emphasized that, in managing insurers' capital adequacy, companies should comprehensively assess the impact of major risks, including market risks, on available capital and required capital, and manage capital and risk in a balanced manner. "An insurer's capital adequacy provides the foundation for reliably meeting its insurance payment obligations and keeping its promises to customers, even when unexpected losses occur," Cho said. "We aim to manage capital adequacy by advancing profitability-focused businesses such as health and accident insurance and expanding the share of long-term insurance, while considering both the capital requirements and risk levels associated with changes in our business portfolio."

name: Instacart
title: DoorDash offers $17 billion for Instacart in what would be big grocery delivery consolidation
description:
DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad.
The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery.
The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform.
DoorDash has been growing its grocery business DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products.
Groceries and restaurant delivery each solve part of that problem.
text:
DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad.

The companies say the tie-up would combine DoorDash's global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart's purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals like Amazon.

READ MORE: Instacart ends program where users see different prices for the same item at same store

But it could also lead to less competition in the delivery space, which could raise prices for consumers and give grocers fewer partners to negotiate with.

"They were competing for a share of consumers' wallet," said Randall Sargent, a partner specializing in grocery and retail at the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. "As a general economic principle, less competition and more consolidation tends to be worse for consumers."

The deal is expected to be finalized by the end of 2027 or in early 2028 if it's approved by Instacart shareholders and government regulators.

Instacart's name and app will remain

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app would remain, and Instacart's 600,000 shoppers — who are independent contractors — would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before.

Consumers who are currently paying $9.99 per month for separate DashPass and Instacart+ memberships, which give them free delivery on most orders and other perks, would be able to pay one fee instead of two, DoorDash said. Instacart customers would also have access to 50,000 additional stores that are on DoorDash's platform.

Grocers would also be able to choose either delivery platform. Tony Xu, DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, said the deal could help local grocers compete with larger players. Walmart is the largest U.S. grocer, with 21% share of spending, followed by Costco and Amazon, which each have 8% share, according to Numerator, a market research company.

"Over the past decade or even two decades, what you see is the largest companies are only eating more and more of the pie. Why is that? It's because they've invested aggressively into capabilities like a modern technology stack, like fast delivery, like new fulfillment models," Xu said Thursday during a conference call with investors. "That's what this combination is really about, where DoorDash and Instacart can give every retailer a fighting chance at competing in the modern-day era."

The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery. Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer and has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin' and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform.

DoorDash has been growing its grocery business

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. That dwarfs Instacart, which fulfilled 338 million orders last year. DoorDash has a market value of $73 billion.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.

DoorDash's move into grocery has hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash's share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats' share held steady at just under 20%.

Combined company could attract more ads, but also scrutiny

Sargent said a combined DoorDash and Instacart could potentially attract more ad revenue from food companies. Right now, Instacart can only share what consumers put in their baskets, for example, but a combined company could also show them what customers ordered for takeout lunch.

"Food companies want to spread their ad dollars around and reach customers efficiently," Sargent said. "The more you can hand them an audience that you know all about, the more formidable a challenger this new company is."

But the tie-up will also be subject to scrutiny from antitrust regulators in the U.S. and elsewhere, particularly at a time when consumers are agitated about food price inflation. Ethan Litwin, an antitrust attorney and partner with New York-based Shinder Cantor Lerner, said it could be problematic if DoorDash controls Instacart's technology, since many grocers use that technology to power their online storefronts.

"DoorDash could therefore cut rivals off, outmatch them on targeting and logistics, or monitor competitors' pricing and discounting in real time, which could facilitate coordination on pricing," Litwin said. "I expect that the parties will call these efficiencies, but an advantage big enough to build a monopoly will not stay consumer-friendly for long."

Acquisition was discussed for a while

Apoorva Mehta, who founded Instacart but left the company after its initial public offering in 2023, said Thursday that he and Xu had explored the idea of combining Instacart and DoorDash for years.

"We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear. Customers have 21 meals a week to figure out. Groceries and restaurant delivery each solve part of that problem. Serving customers well means bringing together the best of both," he said.

Mehta said the combination would also benefit shoppers, who would have more opportunities to earn money.

It wasn't immediately clear how delivery drivers would be impacted by a combined company. The Associated Press left a message seeking comment from the Service Employees International Union, which has unionized gig workers in California.

Litwin said combining DoorDash and Instacart would potentially give drivers fewer options.

"In many markets, these two companies are two of the three major buyers of shopper labor," he said.

DoorDash shares were up 5% in Thursday afternoon trading. Instacart shares were down 1.6%.

AP Retail Writer Anne D'Innocenzio contributed from New York.

On Oct. 15, Medtronic reported it had a 5.4x oversubscription for its exchange offer for MiniMed. While all shareholders with 100 shares or less received a full exchange, a Medtronic spokesperson tells TCB that allocations were done “pro rata for holders who tendered more than 100 shares.” Medtronic said it returned the remaining shares that weren’t able to be exchanged back to its shareholders.

Following the split, MiniMed is officially an independent business and has moved its operational headquarters to California. Medtronic retained 0% equity ownership in the new entity. The move is part of a larger push to sharpen the company’s focus on higher-growth opportunities across cardiovascular care, neuroscience, surgical technologies, and robotics, a company spokesperson told Twin Cities Business in a July story about its acquisition activity in 2026.

Startup? Or scaling up? Bridgewater Bank breaks down what small business owners should know before approaching a lender, from what to bring to the table to where SBA financing may fit.

So, what does this all mean for Medtronic moving forward?

Medtronic’s Bet

For Medtronic, the split-off is primarily about concentrating resources on its other businesses.

But by separating MiniMed, Kevin Orth, a retired business development director for 3M and a guest lecturer at the University of St. Thomas Opus College of Business, says Medtronic “can also control operating expenses on its diabetes business.” And because “Medtronic has historically been a significant dividend payer, retiring the Medtronic shares accepted in the exchange reduces the number of outstanding shares on which it pays dividends,” he adds.

That does not mean Medtronic has eliminated every financial consequence. The company exchanged shares rather than receiving a cash payment for its remaining stake, and it gave up any future ownership-related upside from MiniMed. The potential benefit is a more focused business with fewer competing demands for capital.

The broader question is, will investors reward Medtronic for becoming a more streamlined company?

Matt Arens, founder and CEO of Edina-based First Light Asset Management, says, “sometimes it spins out for negative reasons, like if it’s not an attractive business segment or its growth is dragging. So, spinning it out is a way to capture value and to try to create a vehicle of a self-standing business that can garner a more significant multiple rather than be buried in the portfolio of the parent company.”

For Medtronic, the split-off means shareholders can now evaluate its remaining portfolio with a clearer view.

The deal is considered a split-off, rather than a spin-off, Orth explains, because Medtronic gave its investors an exchange offer to voluntarily choose whether to surrender—or exchange—all or part of their parent company stock in return for shares in MiniMed. In a spin-off—like what 3M did with Solventum—existing employees receive shares of the new subsidiary based on a fixed ratio without having to give up anything. So, they end up with stock in both entities, Orth adds.

Why are large med-device companies breaking themselves apart?

Medtronic is not the only major medical device company to break off one of its businesses this decade.

3M spun off its healthcare business as Solventum in 2024, while Johnson & Johnson spun off its consumer health business, Kenvue, in 2023. Those transactions presented similar questions: Does a collection of businesses create more value together, or would investors value them more highly as independent companies?

“There has for a long time [been] a trend to consolidate businesses [in this industry] together,” Arens says. “That was the flavor of the day for a significant period of time.”

Now, companies are taking another look at their portfolios and asking whether individual businesses could perform better independently.

RELATED: Why Is Medicare Advantage Exiting Dozens of Minnesota Counties in 2027?

One reason is that different investors have different priorities. Some want established companies with dependable cash flows and dividends. Others are looking for businesses with faster growth and greater upside potential, even if they carry more risk.

Orth also points to the growth of capital markets and the availability of investors willing to fund newly independent companies. “Right now, there is a lot more investor money available in capital markets that did not exist 10-20 years ago,” he says. “Part of this is investment banks wanting to create new, investible entities.”

Arens says anything that leads to a healthy Medtronic is a good thing for the Twin Cities market. “The fact they are making moves is a healthy thing because they are manually managing their portfolio,” he says.

The ball is now in MiniMed’s court. It has to prove to its new shareholders that it can sustainably grow, and that independence was worth the bet on future growth.

text:
The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) launched its Tokenization Service on October 28, 2026, a significant step for post-trade operations in the U.S. stock and bond markets. This service enables the creation of blockchain tokens that represent traditional securities, using the Canton Network, which relies on Canton Coin (CRYPTO: CC).

To date, 20 participants have signed up to use this service from DTC, the depository arm of the DTCC, including major banks and brokerages that hold securities at DTC. DTC holds over $114 trillion in assets under custody, and the participants include Barclays (NYSE: BCS), Citigroup (NYSE: C | C Price Prediction), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Morgan Stanley, and State Street (NYSE: STT).

The Tokenization Service operates on two networks: the Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network, with plans to add more networks in 2027.

Despite these advancements, Canton Coin’s value has continued to decline. CC traded at $0.1005, up 1.1% over the past 24 hours but still down 20.4% for the month. This dip is significant, as CC is 48.2% below its all-time high of $0.1942, reached on February 3, 2026.

Canton Strategic Holdings Is the Listed Company Closest to Canton Coin

LEE WA DA / Shutterstock.com

Canton Strategic Holdings (NASDAQ: CNTN) recently divested its legacy biotech division, Gravitas Life Sciences, to focus on Canton-related businesses. As a Super Validator on the Canton Network, the company earns CC rewards. It also offers a Locking-as-a-Service product that secures CC for participants who must maintain minimum balances according to governance rules.

In the second quarter of 2026, these operations generated about $1.5 million in revenue, primarily from the new Locking-as-a-Service, which contributed $1.3 million. However, the company reported a net loss of $19 million due to the declining value of its 3.71 billion CC holdings, resulting in a $24 million unrealized loss, which reflects the depreciation of assets still on the books.

Looking ahead, the company plans to list tokenized shares on TSV LLC, a blockchain trading platform, with trading expected to start as soon as November 2 under the SEC’s Innovation Exemption.

Fairmint’s tokens are designed to carry the same rights as the company’s Nasdaq shares. However, the announcement does not clarify whether buyers will use CC for these transactions, suggesting trades may involve cash tokens or stablecoins, with CC serving only as a fee currency.

Banks Have Yet to Commit to Buying Canton Coin

Kirill Aleksandrovich / Shutterstock.com

While DTCC has welcomed 20 banks and brokers to its network, it has not guaranteed they will purchase, hold, or transact in Canton Coin. Institutions can avoid public-token systems entirely by using the Besu network. Their participation signals support for DTCC’s initiatives rather than a direct endorsement of Canton Coin.

CC serves as the utility token for the Canton network, enabling applications to pay synchronizer fees—a system that organizes and confirms transactions. CC fees are burned, permanently removing those tokens from circulation.

The network mints new tokens as rewards for app providers and validators based on their activity, so the overall CC supply grows as usage increases. However, under governance proposal CIP-0129, traffic on dedicated synchronizers will not contribute to burning CC.

DTCC has not specified which type of synchronizer it will use for its Canton transactions, leaving CC holders uncertain. If transactions occur on a dedicated synchronizer, it may generate DTCC fees while saving banks time, but it could also burn less CC.

The participating banks are also developing their own systems. Citi’s CEO, Jane Fraser, highlighted on the October 13 earnings call that Citi Token Services and tokenized deposits are key areas of focus, and the bank operates its own competing network connecting 300 banks.

State Street CEO Ron O’Hanley said on October 14 that its tokenized fund platform will launch by year-end, with its cash fund operating on Stellar. Meanwhile, JPMorgan has its own tokenized fund offerings.

Canton Coin Gains Only When Burning Outpaces Minting

On October 23, Canton’s Super Validators approved CIP-0129, which introduces universal burning: every production synchronizer will burn CC at a specified list price, with volume discounts for high-frequency users. A subsequent proposal is needed to set prices, but for now, the network is minting more CC than it burns.

The discounts could mean large users, likely banks, burn less CC per transaction. Additionally, the Canton Development Fund has allocated 15.8 million CC (valued at about $1.6 million) to RedStone to develop CAPS, a privacy-focused pricing standard still in development. If grant recipients sell their CC, it could further exert downward pressure on the token’s price.

This ongoing situation is reflected in CC’s performance, which is trading below its 20-day, 50-day, and 200-day moving averages, indicating continued market struggles.

Lilly reported third-quarter (Q3) revenue of about $24.40 billion, up 39% from last year and above Wall Street estimates of about $22.62 billion, according to Fiscal.ai. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 7% to $7.48, comfortably beating consensus estimates of around $6.61.

text:
DoorDash (DASH) announced plans to acquire hyperlocal grocery delivery provider Instacart (CART) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion.

DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock's Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."

DoorDash stock popped over 5%, while Instacart stock fell 1.5%.

The acquisition comes as Walmart (WMT) and Amazon (AMZN) have been taking share of the grocery delivery market, especially for same-day and one-hour delivery.

Prior to the announcement, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian said the combination of Instacart and DoorDash could "potentially prove to be a competitive differentiation."

"A combination of strong restaurant delivery plus a marketplace including various grocers from Instacart can be a critical combination against Walmart and Amazon in particular, who continue to push in this market as well," Arounian said.

Walmart currently holds a roughly 30.9% share of the online grocery market, ahead of Amazon at roughly 23.6%, per Wedbush.

For customers worried about what the Instacart acquisition means for prices, the company said shoppers will now get two memberships for the price of one and more choices.

"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," the release said.

For local business owners, the company said this would allow them more ways to earn.

“By bringing Maybelline’s makeup expertise into ChatGPT, we’re creating an intuitive, engaging experience that empowers every consumer to experiment freely and dare to be exactly who they want to be,” said Yasmin Dastmalchi, president of Maybelline New York.

The launch follows a pilot L’Oréal unveiled at VivaTech 2026 and is part of the company’s broader effort to make its beauty expertise and services available through conversational AI environments.

Here are some details: • OpenAI reorganized the Model Spec around five values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care • The ‌company ​said faithfulness to human intent ⁠is the foundation of ⁠the framework, requiring models to understand what users, developers and OpenAI intend and value, rather than simply following instructions literally • OpenAI said the update is ​part of its AI alignment efforts to help models apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while ⁠remaining subject to human oversight • ⁠The revised framework says models should minimize ​harm, be transparent about what they know and do ​not know, and help users make their own ‌decisions and pursue their own goals • The company said current models do not yet fully reflect the updated Model Spec and that it is exploring new ⁠training methods to help models internalize the principles • The move echoes rival Anthropic’s Constitutional AI approach, which uses a ⁠written “constitution” of principles ‌to guide model behavior and make ⁠the values shaping AI systems more ​transparent • ‌The move follows growing scrutiny of AI ​alignment after ⁠OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous AI agent hacked Hugging Face during testing, a case that highlighted how advanced models can break rules or bypass safeguards while pursuing assigned goals (Reporting by Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Shailesh Kuber)
text:
Oct 29 (Reuters) – OpenAI on Thursday updated its Model Spec, a public roadmap for how it wants its AI models to behave, reorganizing ​the framework around five core values as ‌AI systems become more capable.

Here are some details:

• OpenAI reorganized the Model Spec around five values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care

• The ‌company ​said faithfulness to human intent ⁠is the foundation of ⁠the framework, requiring models to understand what users, developers and OpenAI intend and value, rather than simply following instructions literally

• OpenAI said the update is ​part of its AI alignment efforts to help models apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while ⁠remaining subject to human oversight

• ⁠The revised framework says models should minimize ​harm, be transparent about what they know and do ​not know, and help users make their own ‌decisions and pursue their own goals

text:
DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad.

The companies say the tie-up would combine DoorDash’s global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart’s purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals like Amazon.

But it could also lead to less competition in the delivery space, which could raise prices for consumers and give grocers fewer partners to negotiate with.

“They were competing for a share of consumers’ wallet,” said Randall Sargent, a partner specializing in grocery and retail at the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. “As a general economic principle, less competition and more consolidation tends to be worse for consumers.”

The deal is expected to be finalized by the end of 2027 or in early 2028 if it’s approved by Instacart shareholders and government regulators.

Instacart’s name and app will remain

Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app would remain, and Instacart’s 600,000 shoppers — who are independent contractors — would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before.

Consumers who are currently paying $9.99 per month for separate DashPass and Instacart+ memberships, which give them free delivery on most orders and other perks, would be able to pay one fee instead of two, DoorDash said. Instacart customers would also have access to 50,000 additional stores that are on DoorDash’s platform.

Grocers would also be able to choose either delivery platform. Tony Xu, DoorDash’s co-founder and CEO, said the deal could help local grocers compete with larger players. Walmart is the largest U.S. grocer, with 21% share of spending, followed by Costco and Amazon, which each have 8% share, according to Numerator, a market research company.

“Over the past decade or even two decades, what you see is the largest companies are only eating more and more of the pie. Why is that? It’s because they’ve invested aggressively into capabilities like a modern technology stack, like fast delivery, like new fulfillment models,” Xu said Thursday during a conference call with investors. “That’s what this combination is really about, where DoorDash and Instacart can give every retailer a fighting chance at competing in the modern-day era.”

The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery. Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer and has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin’ and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform.

DoorDash has been growing its grocery business

DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. That dwarfs Instacart, which fulfilled 338 million orders last year. DoorDash has a market value of $73 billion.

DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.

The partnership expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco.

DoorDash’s move into grocery has hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.

Combined company could attract more ads, but also scrutiny

Sargent said a combined DoorDash and Instacart could potentially attract more ad revenue from food companies. Right now, Instacart can only share what consumers put in their baskets, for example, but a combined company could also show them what customers ordered for takeout lunch.

“Food companies want to spread their ad dollars around and reach customers efficiently,” Sargent said. “The more you can hand them an audience that you know all about, the more formidable a challenger this new company is.”

But the tie-up will also be subject to scrutiny from antitrust regulators in the U.S. and elsewhere, particularly at a time when consumers are agitated about food price inflation. Ethan Litwin, an antitrust attorney and partner with New York-based Shinder Cantor Lerner, said it could be problematic if DoorDash controls Instacart’s technology, since many grocers use that technology to power their online storefronts.

“DoorDash could therefore cut rivals off, outmatch them on targeting and logistics, or monitor competitors’ pricing and discounting in real time, which could facilitate coordination on pricing,” Litwin said. “I expect that the parties will call these efficiencies, but an advantage big enough to build a monopoly will not stay consumer-friendly for long.”

Apoorva Mehta, who founded Instacart but left the company after its initial public offering in 2023, said Thursday that he and Xu had explored the idea of combining Instacart and DoorDash for years.

“We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear. Customers have 21 meals a week to figure out. Groceries and restaurant delivery each solve part of that problem. Serving customers well means bringing together the best of both,” he said.

Mehta said the combination would also benefit shoppers, who would have more opportunities to earn money.

It wasn’t immediately clear how delivery drivers would be impacted by a combined company. The Associated Press left a message seeking comment from the Service Employees International Union, which has unionized gig workers in California.

Litwin said combining DoorDash and Instacart would potentially give drivers fewer options.

“In many markets, these two companies are two of the three major buyers of shopper labor,” he said.

DoorDash shares were up 5% in Thursday afternoon trading. Instacart shares were down 1.6%.

text:
OpenAI has reorganised its Model Spec, the public rulebook for its AI, around five values led by faithfulness to human intent. It adds guidance on context and human agency, drops most style rules and renames the model GPT. OpenAI admits its models do not yet fully follow it.

OpenAI has rewritten its Model Spec, the public rulebook for how its AI should behave, around five core values, the company said on Thursday. The update also drops most of its style rules and now calls the model “GPT” rather than “the assistant.”

The five values are faithfulness to human intent, minimising harm, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. OpenAI calls faithfulness the foundation: the model should grasp what people actually want rather than follow instructions word for word.

“As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive,” OpenAI wrote.

New sections tell the model how to use context such as past chats and memories, how to support people’s own choices and how to follow social norms. Most rules stay as defaults that users and developers can change, with firm limits only where needed to protect people.

The model should also not tell people what it thinks they want to hear. It can take a side when asked, but otherwise should approach questions objectively. Chatbots’ habit of flattering their users has drawn growing criticism.

OpenAI admits its models “do not yet fully reflect” the Spec and says it is testing new training methods to teach the values. Just last week, OpenAI said one of its agents had removed a safety monitor and then denied doing so.

Moody’s has launched a casualty risk group with six leading insurers and brokers to close data gaps and improve the industry’s understanding of emerging liability exposures, including risks linked to artificial intelligence and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

The Moody’s Casualty Risk Intelligence Group (MCRIG), launched in New York, will focus on standardising exposure, loss and claims data, improving portfolio transparency and developing forward-looking intelligence on litigation trends.

Founding members include Axa XL, Convex, Marsh, RenaissanceRe, Tokio Marine, and Travelers.

The initiative comes as casualty insurers face questions about how emerging risks and litigation could affect future claims. Its founding members will work with Moody’s on data standards and analytics intended to give insurers a clearer view of their exposure.

Moody’s has also expanded its casualty analytics capabilities through investment in data and modelling, including its 2024 acquisition of Praedicat. Its wider data resources cover company profiles, financials, credit risk, mergers and acquisitions, directors’ and officers’ liability, litigation, cyber risk scores and satellite analytics.

Joe Melly, managing director and head of casualty and financial lines at Moody’s, said: “Casualty insurance is the next frontier for risk analytics, and Moody’s is committed to leading that transformation. The casualty industry carries enormous economic weight and growing complexity. It is ready to move toward new data standards, litigation intelligence, and decision-grade analytics to help firms understand and manage their exposure.

“The formation of MCRIG is Moody’s route to achieving this goal. By engaging with a range of participants, MCRIG aims to support the enhancement of independently developed analytical frameworks and insights intended to advance risk understanding.

“We are proud to launch the MCRIG in New York and to do so with such a strong and diverse group of founding participants.”

Noel Richardson, chief risk officer at Axa XL, said: “Casualty insurance faces significant complexity from emerging risks such as PFAS and AI liability, yet the industry relies largely on backward-looking analysis. Through MCRIG, we have an opportunity to develop the data standards, litigation intelligence, and forward-looking analytics that are currently missing. By working with peers and Moody’s, we can build the tools casualty underwriting genuinely needs—and create real value in how we assess, price, and manage risk.”

Christopher Ross, global casualty leader at Marsh Re, said: “Marsh believes strongly in the benefits of a collaborative approach to exploring emerging risk issues and welcomes the opportunity to work with our fellow MCRIG members to develop data-driven insights that empower our clients with new and cutting-edge views of risk. The casualty (re)insurance market has undergone significant changes over the past several years in response to the evolving nature of risk. The advent of AI and its downstream implications will only accelerate change, and we will lead the industry in evaluating and creating solutions that enable our clients to succeed in this market.”

Fiona Walden, senior vice-president and chief underwriting officer for casualty and specialty at RenaissanceRe, said: “We are proud to be a founding member of the MCRIG and look forward to contributing our expertise and partnering with Moody’s and our fellow members to advance casualty analytics and data standards across the industry. This group reinforces our efforts to bring greater transparency and forward-looking insight around emerging casualty trends, supporting our clients and the long-term health of the casualty market.”

Don Mahoney, vice-president of enterprise underwriting for casualty at Travelers, said: “We are pleased to join Moody’s and this exceptional group of partners. This initiative will provide better visibility into casualty exposures in an ever-changing environment and a stronger foundation for risk managers and underwriters across the industry.”

text:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.

DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.

Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.

"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.

For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.

He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".

The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.

Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.

"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.

The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."

"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

This summer both NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) reported record quarters, and each makes money from AI in a different way. NVIDIA sells the racks, chips and networking gear behind the data center expansion. Apple sells the devices where people actually use AI. Both are now racing for the title of world’s most valuable company, so it is worth asking which model holds up better.

Networking Surges at NVIDIA While iPhone Upgraders Flock to Apple

NVIDIA’s revenue reached $96.22B, up 105.8% YoY. Demand about doubled in a single year. Networking brought in $40.31B, up 138%, which shows customers are buying whole AI factories instead of just GPUs. Jensen Huang put it simply: “Now, compute is revenue.” NVIDIA’s limit is supply. Management said demand is growing about 100% while supply supports about 70%.

At Apple, iPhone revenue hit $54.3 billion, up 22%, which points to a strong upgrade cycle. Mac grew 29%, helped by MacBook Neo. Tim Cook called the shortages “a demand forecast issue, to be candid”. One note: tariff refunds added $0.11 to EPS of $2.02, so the earnings beat looks a little better than the core business.

One Builds AI Factories, One Keeps AI on Your Phone

NVIDIA makes more from every gigawatt of data center capacity with each new chip generation. That figure rose from roughly $18 billion on Hopper to $40 billion on Vera Rubin. The financing side makes me cautious. Payment terms extended to 60 days from 45, and guarantees are capped at $108.5 billion. Huang knows some critics call this circular financing, and he replied: “We see it differently.”

Apple wants AI to run privately on its devices. Cook called on-device AI “sort of a competitive weapon”. Services brought in $30.7 billion, up 12%, a steady subscription layer that grows as more people use Apple devices. Memory costs are the threat. Cook described “a 100-year flood on the memory pricing“.

Vera Rubin and Memory Costs Will Decide Who Pulls Ahead

NVIDIA guided Q3 revenue to $108.0B +/- 2%, with Vera Rubin making up about 20% of data center revenue. I will be watching margins as they ease toward the 71% to 72% range expected in Q4. For Apple, keep an eye on how incoming CEO John Ternus handles a Siri AI rollout that is still on hold in the EU and in China.

Why NVIDIA Looks Better to Me on Growth Per Dollar

Apple is up 26.82% this year, while NVIDIA is up 15.76%. CNBC has started calling Apple an anti-AI trade. Yet Apple trades at a P/E near 45, compared with about 43 for NVIDIA. Investors are paying more for slower growth.

For me, NVIDIA offers more growth for the price. Defensive investors who want steady cash returns will probably still prefer Apple. My view could change if NVIDIA’s payment terms keep getting longer or the Vera Rubin ramp slips.

text:
What Barclays is doing

Barclays Plc in London has been sounding out insurers in recent weeks about buying default protection on loans financing artificial intelligence infrastructure, covering north of $10 billion of debt. The idea is to create capacity for additional lending as the largest cloud players ask for bigger checks.

People familiar with the matter said the talks remain exploratory, with details such as how much and when still undecided. They requested anonymity because the conversations are private, and a Barclays spokesperson declined to comment. One of the people said Barclays is targeting insurance that would shoulder more than 50 percent of the credit risk on certain AI-related facilities.

Why insurers and banks matter here

Banks commonly use credit risk insurance to hedge loan portfolios, as well as employ derivatives, sell loans outright, and execute significant risk transfers. Shifting some loss risk to insurers or investors reduces regulatory capital needs, which lets banks bid for more business.

Credit risk insurers have already ramped up exposure to data center finance, per a Willis Towers Watson Plc survey published in May. But capacity looks tight, with several providers of non-trade credit risk insurance indicating they were near sector limits or already full on data center exposure. McKinsey & Co projects global data center spending to reach $6.7 trillion by 2030, and debt is expected to take on a bigger share of that bill.

Last week, an index tracking Meta Platforms Inc. credit risk reached its highest level on record after the company's plan to boost capital spending sparked renewed concerns about additional debt issuance. On Monday, Citadel co-chief investment officer Pablo Salame said the credit market is "getting jammed right now because it hasn't figured out a good way" to offload risks tied to the borrowing surge.

What this means for your portfolio

If insurers take larger portions of AI-related loan risk, banks could recycle capital faster into new facilities, keeping credit flowing as demand jumps. Eli Lilly said acquired in-process research and development charges of $4.57 per share tied to business development deals also weighed.

Eli Lilly therefore cut its adjusted EPS guidance to $35 to $36 from $35.50 to $36.50.

Eli Lilly Pulls Away While Its GLP-1 Rivals Stall

Year to date (YTD), Eli Lilly stock is up 30%. Novo Nordisk stock is down 20% YTD, a gap that shows Eli Lilly’s results pulling it further from its Danish rival while the strength isn’t spreading across the group. Where Eli Lilly has branched out, Novo Nordisk remains concentrated in diabetes and obesity drugs and faces U.S. pricing pressure, including Wegovy and Ozempic list price cuts it has announced for January 1, 2027.

Viking stock is down 29% YTD and is easing even after Eli Lilly reported surging demand. The company’s value rests on VK2735. The pre-revenue, clinical-stage developer’s dual agonist targets the GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptors in subcutaneous and oral Phase 3 trials, with VANQUISH results expected in 2027.

Viking Therapeutics reported a third-quarter net loss. On October 28, the loss of $1.55 per share was wider than Wall Street analysts expected, and the company ended September with $960 million in cash and investments after a capital raise. Every gain Eli Lilly makes in obesity care may raise the bar a late-stage challenger must clear on efficacy, convenience and price.

Further along the obesity-care chain, Hims & Hers Health (NYSE:HIMS) stock is at $28.80, down 2%. Hims & Hers stock is down 11% YTD, and the telehealth platform is switching its U.S. weight-loss offering toward branded GLP-1 medications.

Eli Lilly’s Next Chapter Hinges on Diversification and Obesity Share

Eli Lilly must now show whether its newer products can keep growing fast enough to branched out revenue beyond weight loss. Alzheimer’s treatment Kisunla generated $193 million for Eli Lilly, up 175%, and blood cancer drug Jaypirca brought in $228 million, up 59%. Growth at that pace could gradually ease the company’s reliance on tirzepatide.

Margins are one pressure point, with Eli Lilly’s adjusted operating margin falling to 35.3% from 41.8%. A second open question is whether Novo Nordisk or Viking Therapeutics can close the gap in obesity care, where Eli Lilly keeps adding volume.

Eli Lilly enters the next phase with momentum, while its rivals still face pivotal trial data and pricing changes in 2027. Investors may want to weigh both the growth and the margin risks carefully as the race for obesity-care share develops.

text:
Nvidia is reportedly facing questions from the United States Department of Justice over whether its purchase of Hugging Face will have an impact on competition in the growing AI space. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face in September, paying almost $13 billion. Hugging Face offers an open-source platform for the hosting and testing of new AI models, and that appears to be behind the DOJ's concerns. Reuters reports that the department has made inquiries about how the Hugging Face deal could change the landscape for Nvidia's competitors. The move could be seen as a way for Nvidia to lock in a key distribution channel for its own products. Hugging Face also sells AI infrastructure. Nvidia has declined to comment on the story.

This isn't the first time that Nvidia has found itself in the DOJ's crosshairs. As Nvidia becomes more vital to the tech industry as a whole and AI technologies specifically, the company has come under increasing scrutiny within the U.S. government, stretching back to the Biden administration. Things didn't improve when the Trump administration took over, with the U.S. president reportedly tempted to break the company up — despite being unfamiliar with what it was. More recently, Nvidia and other AI hardware makers found themselves under export controls. Nvidia's powerful AI-focused hardware can only be sold to approved entities, while it cannot ship to countries including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia.

At home, the DOJ has also looked into Nvidia's purchase of SchedMD, a company whose software is used to run supercomputers that have ties to national security. Nvidia promised to continue to support the software as part of a larger three-year investigation into its conduct. Officials have also considered whether Nvidia dangled a larger allocation of its AI chips in front of customers who also purchased its networking hardware as well as Groq chips — Nvidia bought Groq for $20 billion in December of 2025. The deal included the acquihires of key members of the AI chip startup's team, including its CEO.

As for Hugging Face, Nvidia has similarly confirmed that it will continue to support a range of chip and AI providers once the buyout completes. It's expected that Hugging Face will officially become part of Nvidia in the first half of 2027.

name: Albertsons
title: Albertsons argues executive greed at Kroger killed the deal - Food Navigator
description:
Kroger executives stood to collect millions of dollars if their proposed merger with Albertsons in 2024 had succeeded.
Kroger disputes Albertsons’ account, arguing that regulatory opposition would have defeated the merger regardless.
Two courts agreed, killing the deal, and now Albertsons is suing Kroger for more than $9 billion.
At the center of this colossal business deal flop, however, is the compensation structure for Kroger executives.
Albertsons is essentially arguing that corporate greed killed the deal.
text:
Kroger executives stood to collect millions of dollars if their proposed merger with Albertsons in 2024 had succeeded. Albertsons now argues that the conditions attached to those payouts helped ensure it never would.

In the trial over their failed $24.6 billion deal, Albertsons alleges that Kroger’s proposed $400 million executive incentive plan rewarded managers for protecting the merger’s financial benefits – even when winning regulatory approval required giving more of them up.

That is the conflict at the heart of Albertsons’ case: Did Kroger do enough to get the deal approved, or did executives’ financial incentives get in the way? Kroger disputes Albertsons’ account, arguing that regulatory opposition would have defeated the merger regardless.

Kroger and Albertsons: A brief history

As a refresher, Kroger, US’ largest pure-play grocery chain, attempted in 2024 to purchase its largest traditional grocery competitor, Albertsons, for $24.6 billion, in what would have been the largest grocery acquisition deal in US history.

Stakeholders in the grocery industry lined up to oppose the deal. The FTC, eight states and the District of Columbia challenged the proposal in federal court, while Washington and Colorado brought separate state-court cases.

That failed deal came in the wake of two decades of corporate consolidation in the US grocery industry, a point that was a central argument from opponents. They argued that although competition is widespread through online services like Amazon and mass merchandise stores like Walmart, the merger would create monopolies in some regions of the country where Kroger and Albertsons banner stores are the only pure-play grocers.

Two courts agreed, killing the deal, and now Albertsons is suing Kroger for more than $9 billion. Their key argument claims Kroger, and its ousted CEO, Rodney McMullen, did not do enough to work with federal regulators on the divestment of stores.

Ultimately, it was McMullen’s and Kroger’s plan to divest 579 stores to C&S Wholesale Grocers, a distribution company that had little experience running a grocery chain, that killed the deal.

Federal regulators and others argued that the proposed divestiture offered inadequate competition to the combined Kroger and Albertsons in several areas of the US, handing the proposed grocery giant local brick-and-mortar grocery monopolies across the country.

In a December 2024 ruling granting a preliminary injunction, US District Judge Adrienne Nelson wrote that supermarkets are distinct from other retailers, typically offering a larger selection of fresh and non-perishable items and other specialized departments like deli, meat and bakery.

“Both defendants gestured toward a future in which they would not be able to compete against ever-growing Walmart, Amazon or Costco. Without the scale afforded by the merger, defendants argue, it will be more difficult for traditional supermarkets to survive in the long term,” Nelson wrote in the decision. “The overarching goals of antitrust law are not met, however, by permitting an otherwise unlawful merger in order to permit firms to compete with an industry giant.”

In other words, you don’t get to break antitrust laws just because you’re losing market share to a bigger competitor.

Was the deal ‘doomed from the beginning’?

Since losing the case, Albertsons has argued that the deal with Kroger failed because of Kroger’s novel approach to divestment in essentially creating its own competitor and its unwillingness to budge with regulators.

So, some were surprised to see McMullen claim in court last week that the acquisition was “doomed from the beginning,” according to a BoiseDev article. That testimony contrasts sharply with McMullen’s public confidence while the merger was pending. But it also fits Kroger’s defense: that regulatory opposition, rather than a breach of its obligations, doomed the transaction.

A merger between the two grocery giants would certainly have helped both companies defend their slipping market share against retail giants like Walmart, Amazon and Costco, but make no mistake, millions in executive compensation was at the heart of the deal on both sides of the equation.

An Albertsons proxy statement filing in 2024 showed both Sharon McCollam, former president and CFO, who earned $6.6 million in 2023, and Susan Morris, executive vice president and COO, who earned $6.5 million that same year, would have received an additional $4 million as the result of a successful merger. Anuj Dhanda, executive vice president and chief technology officer, who earned $4.3 million, would have received $1 million.

At the center of this colossal business deal flop, however, is the compensation structure for Kroger executives. Kroger promised to do whatever it took to get the merger approved, but the company’s executive compensation package was not static like Albertsons’ – it was based on the merger’s profitability, which caused Kroger to position itself for a favorable divestiture plan. It’s all laid out in Albertsons’ lawsuit.

Kroger executives structured the deal so that executives would divvy up $400 million in compensation, receiving up to six times their base salaries if the deal achieved what Albertsons described as “upside or goal synergies in full.” If profits fell more than $200 million short of the base target, they got nothing.

That’s the conflict. When the merger blew up in court, Albertsons argued that Kroger failed to divest its more profitable stores and work with regulators to push the deal through. The court documents released in this new trial reveal a suspected reason why – not the success of the company, but instead multimillion-dollar payouts for executives.

Albertsons is essentially arguing that corporate greed killed the deal.

BoiseDev reports that McMullen blamed the Biden Administration’s Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan for the deal failing. We’ll see what a judge thinks. The Kroger Albertsons deal was a bad idea from the beginning, and maybe Khan would have sued irrespective of how many stores Kroger divested, but both companies would have been better served taking the billions they’ve paid on their grocery behemoth pipe dream and building better companies.

What Did The Cyberattack Cost Boston Scientific?

News reports indicated that a cybersecurity incident disrupted Boston Scientific's manufacturing and product shipments for eight business days. That outage reduced third-quarter sales by $150 million. During the same period, competitive and pricing pressures weighed on key cardiovascular franchises, according to the reports.

The quarter held up against analysts' estimates. Revenue reached $5.14 billion, coming in above the $5.09 billion estimate. Adjusted earnings per share were $0.73, in line with the $0.727 estimate. Revenue growth slowed sharply, however. Revenue rose 1.5% from a year earlier, compared to 7.5% growth in the second quarter of 2026.

The outlook provided a larger shift. Boston Scientific lowered its outlook and now expects full-year 2026 organic revenue growth of 4%, along with a fourth-quarter sales decline to end the year. Management also said it will be challenged to grow sales and adjusted earnings per share in 2027, excluding its pending acquisition of Penumbra. News reports linked the fall in the shares to the cut in fourth-quarter sales and full-year earnings guidance, alongside contracting margins and weaker segment sales.

Did Boston Scientific Fall On Its Own?

It did. The SPDR health care sector fund, XLV, gained 0.3% during the same session. Four of the five companies on the Trefis peer list for Boston Scientific rose, including Medtronic and Stryker, which were each up 0.9%. Abbott Laboratories was the only peer to fall, and its 0.4% drop was small compared to the decline at Boston Scientific.

Boston Scientific Stock More Than Halved In A Year

Over the past year Boston Scientific stock lost 58.6%, while the S&P 500 returned 14.0%. Declines like the one on October 28 have been part of that slide. Boston Scientific is expected to report its fourth-quarter results in February 2027. When it does, fourth-quarter sales against the year-earlier quarter will be the figure to watch.

text:
DoorDash announced on Thursday that it has agreed to acquire rival Instacart for $17 billion. The acquisition would bring two major players in on-demand delivery under one roof, combining DoorDash’s dominance in restaurant takeout with Instacart’s reach in grocery delivery.

DoorDash will buy Instacart for a total value of $65 for each Instacart share, the company said. The deal has been approved by the boards of both companies.

“Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Instacart CEO Chris Rogers in a press release.

“When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers, and deliver compelling value for our shareholders.”

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app. The company also notes that the two brands will continue to operate as separate and independent companies until the transaction closes.

DoorDash says the deal could help more grocers build out their own online ordering platforms and advertising businesses using Instacart’s technology, while grocers could also use DoorDash’s fulfillment services to handle more online orders and offer lower-cost delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the press release.

“Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts. Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery. It’s still early innings, but we know that when more people shop local, more dollars stay local,” said Xu.

Instacart currently has a market cap of more than $13 billion, and its stock price is up 25% for the year to date. The company likely viewed this as an opportune time to sell at a desirable price, ahead of intensifying competition in the grocery delivery market.

Bloomberg previously reported that Instacart was in talks with Uber, but that the company had walked away from discussions.

The deal is expected to close toward the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.

text:
NPR: What’s Gone Up Even Faster Than Gas Or Rent? The Cost Of Caregiving

As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average. The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index. (McGowan, 10/28)

On ACA, Medicare, surprise billing, and more —

Modern Healthcare: Centene, Elevance, Oscar Expand ACA Exchange Markets For 2027

Major health insurance companies, facing new regulatory requirements and other pressures, reevaluated their exchanges strategy for the 2027 plan year. Overall, there will be less competition as major insurers pull back from some markets, but several companies opted to expand. Open enrollment begins Sunday and ends Jan. 15 in most states. Not every state has finished negotiating with health insurers about premium increases for 2027. The Hill: Current And Former CMS Leaders Offer Advice On Medicare Changes Ahead

Current and former leaders at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on Wednesday advised Medicare beneficiaries to pay close attention to their options this year upon reenrolling in plans, as major changes in recent years have only made the landscape more complex. Speaking at The Hill’s “Bang for Your Buck: Get the Most from Your 2027 Medicare Benefits” event in partnership with the Alliance for Aging Research, CMS Deputy Administrator John Brooks and former CMS Chief Operating Officer Jonathan Blum both noted how provisions in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), such as the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, had changed how Medicare benefits are handled. Although most observers agree that the No Surprises Act did fix one problem -- nixing unexpected bills for out-of-network care -- lawmakers are still trying to fix other problems caused by the law. The act, passed at the end of 2020, was designed to protect patients who received bills for out-of-network care -- often emergency care -- even though the care was delivered at an in-network facility. This can happen, for example, if the in-network hospital contracts with out-of-network providers for emergency or specialty care. (Frieden, 10/27)

Rowell, 53, took Benadryl, and her father started driving her to the nearest emergency room, about 25 minutes away. title: Eli Lilly lifts revenue outlook on weight-loss drug sales, trims profit view on deal charges
description:
The charges, taken in the third quarter, are primarily related to the acquisitions of AtaiBeckley and Curevo, Lilly said.
Lilly previously forecast revenue of $85.0 billion to $87.0 billion and earnings of $35.50 to $36.50 per share.
Lilly posted third-quarter revenue of $24.4 billion, topping analyst expectations of $22.61 billion, while adjusted profit of $7.48 per share beat estimates of $6.26, according to LSEG data.

text:
By Patrick Wingrove

Oct 29 (Reuters) – Eli Lilly raised its full-year revenue forecast and beat third-quarter earnings expectations on Thursday, propelled by surging demand for injectable weight-loss drugs that could allay investor concerns about price erosion in US government health plans.

The Indianapolis-based drugmaker now expects full-year revenue of $91 billion to $92 billion, underscoring its expanding lead in the multibillion-dollar GLP-1 market over Danish rival Novo Nordisk that has propelled Lilly to a $1.2 trillion market valuation.

Lilly trimmed its adjusted profit outlook, however, to $35.00 to $36.00 per share, as $4.57 per share of acquired research charges from recent deals more than offset a $4.07 improvement in underlying profit guidance at the midpoint. The charges, taken in the third quarter, are primarily related to the acquisitions of AtaiBeckley and Curevo, Lilly said.

Lilly has been investing for growth beyond its GLP-1 drugs through internal research, tuck-in acquisitions and partnerships.

Shares of the company rose nearly 5% to $1,350 before the bell.

Lilly previously forecast revenue of $85.0 billion to $87.0 billion and earnings of $35.50 to $36.50 per share.

Lilly posted third-quarter revenue of $24.4 billion, topping analyst expectations of $22.61 billion, while adjusted profit of $7.48 per share beat estimates of $6.26, according to LSEG data.

Revenue included about $900 million of benefits, primarily $410 million of milestone payments tied to diabetes drug Jardiance, which Lilly said are the last it expects to receive, and favorable adjustments to rebate and discount estimates.

Third-quarter sales of diabetes drug Mounjaro reached $10.72 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $10.16 billion, according to LSEG data, while its related obesity injection Zepbound brought in $5.35 billion versus estimates of $5.09 billion.

The robust sales will help ease market worries that severe price erosion from the $50-a-month price tag for Medicare recipients would outweigh explosive volume gains. Analysts at Bernstein said data showed that Lilly had captured about 70% of the 700,000 Medicare patients who recently initiated treatment with a GLP-1 medication.

While the new US pilot unlocked coverage for potentially millions who use the government’s Medicare program for people aged 65 and over, the bulk of Lilly’s non-reimbursed volume has historically moved through its $449-a-month cash-pay platform, raising stakes over how the discounts will impact long-term margins.

Lilly’s newer obesity pill Foundayo brought in $184 million, compared with analyst estimates of $216.86 million.

Investors are closely tracking the Foundayo rollout as a key test of whether Lilly can blunt Novo Nordisk’s first-mover edge with its oral Wegovy.

While initial US Foundayo prescriptions have trailed its Danish rival, some investors have downplayed the early lag, expecting the Lilly pill to emerge as a significant growth driver as it launches in more international markets.

Oral Wegovy led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, and Foundayo about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, in separate studies.

Foundayo was launched in the US and Britain earlier this year and could potentially begin selling in other European countries by year-end.

Lilly’s realized prices fell 15% in the third quarter, offsetting part of a 53% rise in volume. US prices fell 7%, a decline Lilly attributed primarily to Zepbound and said was partly offset by adjustments to rebate and discount estimates. Outside the US, prices fell 29%, driven mainly by Mounjaro’s inclusion on China’s national reimbursement drug list.

Even as Lilly’s obesity injections maintain commercial momentum, Wall Street’s attention is shifting toward retatrutide, the company’s next-generation weight-loss candidate slated for regulatory submission next year.

Retatrutide has been shown to drive average weight loss of 24% in midstage trials, topping results from drugs already on the market.

(Reporting by Patrick Wingrove in London, Christy Santhosh and Sriparna Roy in Bengaluru. Editing by Bill Berkrot and Mark Potter)

description:

text:
Air Liquide expects its 200MW Normand'Hy electrolyser in northern France to produce its first hydrogen before the end of 2026, with the plant entering a phased commissioning programme.

The facility is designed to produce up to 28,000 tonnes of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen annually, with TotalEnergies' Gonfreville refinery among its principal customers and a quarter of capacity reserved for hydrogen mobility.

Air Liquide expects its 200MW Normand'Hy electrolyser in Normandy to produce its first hydrogen before the end of 2026, marking the start of commissioning at one of Europe's largest PEM electrolysis projects.

The more than €400 million [$445.9 million] plant, located in the Port-Jérôme industrial zone near Le Havre, is designed to produce up to 28,000 tonnes of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen a year for industrial and transport customers.

Air Liquide highlighted Normand'Hy at its October 5 Capital Markets Day. During its October 29 third-quarter earnings call, the company confirmed that the first hydrogen molecules were expected within weeks. Production will begin with one train, followed by the second and a gradual increase in output.

First hydrogen production will be a commissioning milestone and will not mean the full 200MW facility has reached commercial operation at design capacity.

Siemens Energy Supplies 12 PEM Electrolyser Modules

Normand'Hy uses proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis technology supplied through the manufacturing partnership between Air Liquide and Siemens Energy.

The facility incorporates 12 electrolyser modules manufactured through the companies' joint venture, which operates an electrolyser production plant in Berlin.

The new electrolyser will be connected to Air Liquide's existing hydrogen pipeline network serving the Normandy industrial basin.

That network already supplies hydrogen to refining and chemical facilities in the region. Normand'Hy will allow hydrogen produced by electrolysis to enter the established industrial supply system.

TotalEnergies will provide renewable electricity corresponding to the hydrogen supplied to its refinery, equivalent to 100MW of electrolysis capacity.

For the remaining electricity requirements, Air Liquide has outlined plans to secure renewable power purchase agreements, supplemented by low-carbon electricity from the French grid.

Air Liquide expects commissioning to proceed progressively as the two production trains enter operation.

TotalEnergies Refinery Among Main Hydrogen Customers

A substantial share of Normand'Hy's production is intended for industrial customers, particularly TotalEnergies' Gonfreville refining and petrochemical platform.

Under the agreement announced in September 2023, Air Liquide will supply the refinery with renewable and low-carbon hydrogen corresponding to 100MW of electrolysis capacity.

The wider Normandy hydrogen supply arrangement includes approximately 10,000 tonnes of green hydrogen and up to 5,000 tonnes of low-carbon hydrogen annually, according to TotalEnergies' regulatory disclosures.

Those figures cover the broader supply arrangement and should not all be treated as hydrogen produced exclusively by the new electrolyser.

The companies estimate that the arrangement could reduce emissions at the Gonfreville platform by up to 150,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually.

The reduction remains a projection and will depend on actual hydrogen deliveries and the displacement of existing production.

Air Liquide plans to allocate approximately three-quarters of Normand'Hy's production capacity to industrial customers in Normandy.

€50 Million Hydrogen Supply Chain Planned for Transport

The remaining quarter of the electrolyser's capacity is intended to support hydrogen mobility along the Seine corridor, stretching from Le Havre towards Paris.

In November 2024, Air Liquide announced an additional €50 million [$55.7 million] investment in hydrogen packaging and distribution infrastructure to supply refuelling stations.

The company has also signed a renewable hydrogen supply agreement with HysetCo, which operates hydrogen-powered vehicle fleets and refuelling infrastructure in France.

The new distribution facilities are intended to serve hydrogen taxis, buses, commercial vehicles and trucks along the Seine corridor.

Together with the electrolyser, Air Liquide's investment in the Normandy hydrogen production and distribution programme exceeds €450 million [$501.6 million].

French Government Provides €190 Million Support

Air Liquide committed more than €400 million [$445.9 million] to the construction of Normand'Hy.

The project received €190 million [$211.8 million] in French government support under the Important Projects of Common European Interest framework, through France's recovery programme.

At full planned capacity, Air Liquide estimates that Normand'Hy could avoid up to 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually by replacing conventional hydrogen production.

That figure is a projected emissions reduction rather than a measured result from the new plant.

Air Liquide is also developing the 200MW ELYgator electrolyser in Rotterdam, Netherlands, where commissioning is targeted for late 2027.

ELYgator is designed to produce approximately 23,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually, with TotalEnergies among its contracted customers.

For Normand'Hy, Air Liquide has confirmed that initial hydrogen production is approaching, but has not announced a date for the plant to reach its full 200MW operating capacity.

description:
