S&P Global Inc. SPGI outlined a potential reshaping of its business portfolio during its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, announcing a strategic review of Capital IQ and associated data businesses while raising its full-year outlook.

Adjusted earnings of $4.58 per share surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $4.43. Revenues of $3.68 billion topped the consensus mark of $3.63 billion. Management emphasized accelerating subscription growth, artificial intelligence adoption and stronger performance across its core franchises.

S&P Global Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

S&P Global Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | S&P Global Inc. Quote

SPGI Explores Separation of Capital IQ Businesses

President and CEO Martina Cheung announced a strategic review covering Capital IQ and associated data businesses within Market Intelligence, including a potential separation.

The review encompasses financial data businesses, including SNL and Visible Alpha, while S&P Global expects to retain Enterprise Solutions, RatingsDirect and RatingsXpress.

Responding to Morgan Stanley, CFO Eric Aboaf confirmed engagement with advisers and interest from potential counterparties. Cheung emphasized that separate ownership could accelerate innovation while allowing S&P Global to concentrate investment in credit, equities and commodities. Management expects greater clarity around February 2027.

S&P Global Raises Its Full-Year Outlook

Aboaf raised 2026 organic constant currency revenue growth guidance to 7.5%-8.5% compared with the previous 6%-8% range.

Adjusted operating margin expansion is now expected to be 75-100 basis points, up from the earlier 35-60 basis points. Adjusted earnings guidance increased to $17.70-$17.95 per share from $17.50-$17.75.

Management attributed the upgrades primarily to stronger Ratings and Indices performance, along with expense discipline. Fourth-quarter adjusted free cash flow is projected to be approximately $1.6 billion.

SPGI Sees Stronger Indices and Ratings Opportunities

Aboaf reported 20% revenue growth in Indices, supported by asset-linked fees and exchange-traded derivatives. ETF assets under management reached $6.5 trillion.

The extended Cboe licensing agreement is expected to contribute a couple of percentage points to Indices revenue growth in 2027.

Ratings revenue increased 2%, while billed issuance advanced 8%. Cheung expects $250 billion-$300 billion in full-year hyperscaler issuance. Responding to Deutsche Bank, she highlighted refinancing demand and private credit opportunities while reserving detailed 2027 expectations for February.

S&P Global Expands AI Monetization

Cheung emphasized growing adoption of AI-ready data and integrated solutions, with API call volumes increasing nearly 50% sequentially.

AI customers' annual contract value growth reached 1.8 times that of non-AI customers in Market Intelligence and approximately three times in Energy.

Responding to BofA Securities, Aboaf said discrete AI offerings contributed about 50 basis points to Energy revenue growth and a similar amount to Kensho Data & Platforms. Management also highlighted stronger pricing and normalized negotiations over AI usage rights.

SPGI Reports Improving Energy and Intelligence Trends

Energy revenues increased 6%, supported by Platts benchmarks and improving subscription activity. Adjusted operating margin expanded 190 basis points to 48.1%.

Market Intelligence revenue rose 7%, reflecting stronger Kensho Data performance and recovering customer renewals. Its adjusted operating margin reached 36.2%, expanding 110 basis points.

Aboaf expects Energy's organic constant currency revenue growth to normalize toward the previously outlined 6%-8% average range in 2027. Market Intelligence's full-year growth outlook remains 5.5%-7%, with management expecting performance slightly above the midpoint.

S&P Global Reinforces Capital Returns

Cheung emphasized continued shareholder distributions, with more than $4 billion in repurchases completed year to date.

Management expects total 2026 repurchases to exceed $7 billion. In response to BMO Capital Markets, Aboaf said it plans to issue about $2 billion in additional debt to support the expanded repurchase program.

The company also continued investing in productivity initiatives. Aboaf told Huber Research Partners that AI-driven efficiencies are integrated into broader workflow improvements, supporting reinvestment and margin expansion.

SPGI Maintains Focus on Core Market Leadership

Management's overarching message centered on sharpening S&P Global's portfolio while expanding its benchmark franchises, AI capabilities and recurring revenue streams.

Cheung emphasized that the strategic review does not change the company's broader priorities. The focus remains on market leadership, high-growth adjacent opportunities and operational efficiency.

text:
Delta Air Lines has shut down its text-message customer service channel, directing passengers to its AI-powered Delta Concierge instead. I have used the texting feature many times, and losing it is an absolute shame. Removing a convenient way to reach an agent strikes me as a questionable business decision, particularly for an airline that markets itself as a premium carrier.

Delta Ends Text-Message Customer Service, Directing Passengers To Its AI Concierge

Thrifty Traveler reports that Delta’s text-message support channel is no longer available. Its team encountered an automated response directing customers to Delta Concierge in the Fly Delta app or the airline’s online Help Center. Sure enough, I checked and found the same issue using iMessage:

The precise shutdown date is unclear.

No, Delta has not eliminated human customer service. Passengers can still reach an agent through the app’s “Concierge” section and can still call. What has disappeared is the ability to conduct that conversation through your phone’s regular messaging app.

The old service involved some automated questions too. Nevertheless, it provided a useful way to reach someone without making a telephone call and I found it not only practical, but much more effective and efficient than calling in.

It was great to be able to send a message, go about my business, and respond when an agent became available. While I mostly used it from home, for someone traveling, that convenience particularly matters. You may be walking through an airport, boarding another flight, onboard a flight, or somewhere else that makes a phone conversation impractical.

I would much rather send a message than spend that time listening to hold music, since Delta cannot seem to figure out its call-back feature either.

AI Has A Role, But Please Stop Making It A Gatekeeper

Delta expanded Concierge to all SkyMiles members in August. The assistant can use upcoming trip and account information to help with tasks including flight cancellations, disruption-related rebooking, and baggage tracking. Delta says it will retain its beta label as additional features are introduced.

I understand the attraction. If technology can resolve a straightforward request immediately, that is better for the passenger and frees an agent to handle something more complicated. AI is understandably part of the future of customer service, and has been for some time. But at this point, I too often find it an annoying gatekeeper that wastes valuable time before allowing me to reach someone who can actually help.

I realize I may sound like an old man cursing a horseless carriage while trying to cling on to my horse and buggy, but AI is simply not there yet and taking away this very convenient channel of communications strikes me as nothing more than being cheap.

If I can complete a transaction online, I generally will. By the time I am contacting customer service, there is usually a reason the website or app has not resolved it. Sending me back through a series of generic suggestions does not make the process more efficient. And when I ask for an agent, please connect me to one. I should not have to persuade a chatbot that my request deserves human attention.

I would welcome a genuinely better replacement, but I have trouble seeing the benefit to passengers of withdrawing a convenient channel while the replacement still carries a beta label.

Oh, and by the way…Untied Airlines still has text messaging support. As the epic battle continues between Delta and United, I’m not clear why Delta is eliminating such a convenient service…

Even The Empathy Is Being Outsourced

Meanwhile, JonNYC flagged another rather embarrassing Delta customer service example.

A Diamond Medallion member shared an apparent response to a complaint that began:

“Here’s a more polished and professional version with a warm, empathetic tone:”

That appears to be an AI editing instruction inadvertently left in the customer’s email. The complaint itself concerned problems with Delta’s chat service.

I do not expect an airline employee to compose every response from scratch, especially at the start of a conversation. Templates have existed for years, and using AI to improve the clarity of an email is a reasonable way to handle tremendous volumes of correspondence.

But someone still needs to read the complaint, understand what happened, and take responsibility for the response. An apology written in a warm tone is of little use if nobody fixes the underlying problem!

Nothing replaces the human touch when a situation requires judgment or someone willing to take ownership. A capable agent can recognize that the standard answer does not address the question. That is particularly important when a passenger is stranded and the available seats are disappearing while the conversation goes in circles. For an airline selling a premium experience, access to that help should be part of what passengers are paying for.

Delta may find it more efficient to consolidate support within its app. But I would want to know whether passengers are getting their problems resolved faster, rather than simply whether fewer of them are reaching an employee because they give up in anger.

CONCLUSION

Delta has ended its text-message customer service channel and is directing passengers toward its AI-powered Concierge, through which human agents remain available. I have used the texting service many times over the years and am sorry to see it go.

AI could eventually make airline customer service substantially better, and I welcome tools that actually save time. But removing a convenient option while putting more automation between passengers and help feels like a step backward.

Bottom line: give me an assistant that resolves my problem and I will gladly use it. When it cannot, give me a person without making me fight for one.

title: Boston Scientific (BSX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript | The Motley Fool
description:

Full Conference Call Transcript Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Boston Scientific Third Quarter 26 Earnings Call.

text:
Wed, Oct. 28, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Chairman and Chief Executive Officer - Michael F. Mahoney

Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Jonathan Monson

Executive Vice President and Group President, Cardiology - Joseph Fitzgerald

Chief Medical Officer - Dr. Ken Stein

Vice President, Investor Relations - Lauren Tengler

TAKEAWAYS

Net Sales -- $5.138 billion, representing 1.5% growth compared to the prior year period.

Adjusted EPS -- $0.73, declining 3% year over year and falling below the guidance range of $0.80 to $0.82.

Cybersecurity Impact -- 300 basis points of organic revenue growth reduction and a $0.07 impact to adjusted EPS, following an eight-day operational disruption in Aug. 2026.

Full-Year 2026 Organic Revenue Guidance -- 3.75% growth, revised downward from the previous 4% target due to segment-specific headwinds and cyber impacts.

Full-Year 2026 Adjusted EPS Guidance -- $3.16 to $3.18, reflecting anticipated headwinds from foreign exchange and lower operating margins.

Fourth Quarter 2026 Organic Revenue Guidance -- a decline of 1% to 3%, driven by the normalization of customer inventory following the third quarter cyber incident.

Fourth Quarter 2026 Adjusted EPS Guidance -- $0.77 to $0.79, incorporating an estimated $0.04 to $0.05 impact from residual inventory adjustments.

MedSurg Segment Revenue -- $1.733 billion, showing 0.7% organic growth as gains in Neuromodulation were offset by pressure in Urology.

Cardiovascular Segment Revenue -- $3.406 billion, growing 1.9% organically despite substantial sales declines in the Electrophysiology and WATCHMAN businesses.

Neuromodulation Organic Growth -- 13%, driven by performance in the pain franchise and Nalu technology adoption.

Urology Organic Growth -- a decline of 3.1%, reflecting commercial turnover and pricing pressures in the China market.

Endoscopy Organic Growth -- a decline of 0.6%, primarily due to Volume-Based Procurement (VBP) impacts in China and shipping delays.

U.S. Operational Revenue Growth -- 0.5%, constrained by an 8% decline in the Electrophysiology franchise and a 7% decline in WATCHMAN sales.

Asia-Pacific Operational Revenue -- a decline of 1.1%, impacted by price erosion from China's VBP initiatives and cybersecurity disruptions.

Restructuring Program Savings -- $500 million in expected cumulative savings over the next three years, with over half of the benefit anticipated by the end of 2027.

Adjusted Gross Margin -- 68.0%, a 300 basis-point decrease from the prior year driven by unfavorable manufacturing absorption during the cyber outage.

Adjusted Operating Margin -- 26.5%, contracting 150 basis points due to lower gross margins and cyber-related disruptions.

Free Cash Flow -- $867 million for the quarter, with full-year expectations set at approximately $3.6 billion.

Cash and Debt Leverage -- $690 million in cash on hand with a gross debt leverage ratio of 1.9x as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Future Market Opportunity -- $25 billion in potential new market value targeted by 2030 through ongoing R&D and strategic product launches.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email pr@fool.com

RISKS

Mahoney stated, "we believe we will be challenged to grow sales and adjusted EPS in 2027 excluding our pending acquisition of Penumbra," reflecting anticipated pressures in the EP and WATCHMAN franchises along with China pricing headwinds.

Mahoney noted, "We expect continued erosion of our PFA share position until we launch FARAWAVE Ultra, now expected in early 2028," citing intensified competition in the Electrophysiology market.

Mahoney warned that pricing dynamics in China continue to evolve and a number of our businesses have seen VBP and other pricing impacts as a result, which is expected to moderate regional growth to single digits.

SUMMARY

Boston Scientific Corporation (BSX -5.09%) reported third quarter results that were impacted by a cybersecurity incident and intensified competitive pressure in core business segments. Management characterized 2027 as a transition year with expected growth challenges due to pricing dynamics in China and share shifts in the U.S. Electrophysiology market. The company is responding with a restructuring program aimed at generating cost savings while continuing investments in high-growth platforms to support a return to performance targets by 2028.

Management expects 2027 to serve as a performance trough for the company before a targeted return to high growth in 2028. CEO Mahoney stated, "We believe that 2027 will be the trough in the cycle and we have several investments and new innovations coming over the course of the next 3 years."

The Electrophysiology segment faced significant share erosion in the U.S. market following the introduction of competing Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) technologies. Mahoney noted, "We have seen our strong market share position erode as new technologies are introduced and adoption of these different PFA form factors has been highly dynamic."

Management attributed a slowdown in the WATCHMAN Left Atrial Appendage Closure (LAC) market to shifts in patient identification as clinicians evaluate recent clinical evidence. Mahoney stated, "We continue to believe that the overall LAC market slowdown primarily reflects changes in patient identification and referral patterns."

Regulatory timelines have shifted the expected closing of the Penumbra acquisition to early 2027. Mahoney stated, "The regulatory process has taken a bit of time. We are still very confident in closing the transaction. But based on some of the discussions with the regulatory authorities, we anticipate an early first quarter close."

The company entered a strategic co-funding agreement with Blackstone Life Sciences to advance the Vitalist system for treating cardiogenic shock. CFO Monson stated, "Boston Scientific will receive funding from Blackstone which will be recognized as a reduction to R&D expense as the related costs are incurred."

The company is implementing an organizational restructuring aimed at streamlining operations and back-office functions. Monson indicated, "anticipate to achieve over $500 million of savings from the program over the next three years."

INDUSTRY GLOSSARY

VBP (Volume-Based Procurement): A Chinese government policy aimed at lowering medical device prices through high-volume, centralized purchasing.

EP (Electrophysiology): A specialty focused on diagnosing and treating heart rhythm disorders.

PFA (Pulsed Field Ablation): A non-thermal energy technology used to treat atrial fibrillation by selectively targeting heart cells.

IVL (Intravascular Lithotripsy): A technology that uses sonic pressure waves to break up calcified plaque in coronary or peripheral arteries.

LAC (Left Atrial Appendage Closure): A procedure to seal off the left atrial appendage to reduce stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation.

AMI (Acute Myocardial Infarction): A medical term for a heart attack, often involving sudden cardiogenic shock.

IDE (Investigational Device Exemption): A regulatory approval that allows a device to be used in a clinical study to collect safety and effectiveness data.

With me today are Mike Mahoney, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer John Monson, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. During the Q and A session, Mike and John will be joined by Joe Fitzgerald, Executive Vice President and Group President, Cardiology and our Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Ken Stein. So this is both an area of major need and an area where we know that mechanical circulatory support can improve outcomes. And we believe that with our vitalist platform we have differentiated advantages over the current incumbent in terms of dealing with shock. Where the catheter needs to play stay in place in the CCU for a longer period of time along with strategies aimed at just minimizing the complexity of managing these patients and minimizing vascular complications. And so that is why we are so excited about the potential for the Vitalist platform and why actually we like the move. Into AMI shock as the first trial. And then on TIVUS, on TIVUS, really, again, it is just a matter of continuing to execute on enrollment in clinical trial. Enrollment. I think frankly, it is been a little bit slower than we would have hoped as we navigated the transition and the integration of the Relievant team into the Boston Scientific ecosystem.

But again, you know, are confident that we can get that on track and that we will eventually finish enrollment in the trial. Believe in the technology. We do believe that ultrasound is the best of the energy sources that we can use for doing renal denervation. And we continue to believe that the TIVUS platform has differentiated advantages over the 2 current approved devices for renal denervation for hypertension. Thank you.

Likely it will be pushing into early 27. In terms of the some of the product delays, Joe is here. Joe can just add comments.

Joseph Fitzgerald: Yes, I will take I will take, Ultra first. As you know, Ultra is a PMA supplement that does not require a clinical study. So, most of the issues we have there are just on getting through what we call design verification and validation. And if you look at Ultra, that is a hardware, software, and a catheter project. So the let's call it 1-quarter delay that you see is just a summary of issues that we have to work through with V&V. It is related to our negotiations with FDA on getting the actual IDE approved. text:
By Padmanabhan Ananthan

Oct 28 (Reuters) – Boston Scientific lowered its full-year profit forecast on Wednesday and warned that revenue and earnings growth could be challenging in 2027, ​citing pricing pressure in China and weakness in ‌its key heart-device businesses.

Shares of the company were down 5.3% by afternoon.

“We anticipate continued top-line pressure into 2027, which we expect will make it challenging to grow revenue and adjusted earnings per share,” CFO ‌Jon ​Monson said in a conference call.

The ⁠medtech company now expects ⁠2026 adjusted profit in the range of $3.16 to $3.18, compared with a previous range of $3.28 to $3.32. Analysts on average expect earnings of $3.23 per share, according to data compiled by ​LSEG.

The company expects fourth-quarter sales to fall about 3% to 1% year over year and adjusted earnings of ⁠77 to 79 cents per share, ⁠below analysts’ estimate of 83 cents per ​share.

Chief Executive Mike Mahoney said, “there will be additional price headwinds ​in China in ’27, and the growth likely won’t be ‌enough to offset the pressure from electrophysiology and Watchman next year.”

Farapulse and Watchman are among Boston Scientific’s major growth drivers. The Watchman implant, which prevents blood clots and strokes ⁠has come under pressure in recent quarters due to softer uptake.

The company said China’s volume-based procurement program, which purchases medical devices ⁠in bulk at ‌sharply lower prices, is expected to pressure ⁠growth through 2027, particularly in its endoscopy business.

Boston ​Scientific ‌now expects to complete its $14.5 billion purchase ​of Penumbra ⁠in the first quarter of 2027, later than planned, citing longer regulatory reviews. The company said higher interest rates will increase the cost of financing the deal, making it a bigger drag on earnings.

(Reporting by Padmanabhan Ananthan in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Diti Pujara)

Navigating The 2027 Trough and Long-Term Growth Initiatives

During an earnings conference call, the CEO said, “In 2026, we’ve seen that cycle turn, and those two businesses (EP and WATCHMAN franchises) are now weighing on our total company growth as we navigate competition and market dynamics.”

“We believe that 2027 will be the trough in the cycle, and we have several investments and new innovations coming over the course of the next three years that we expect will support stabilization and growth for both the EP and WATCHMAN businesses.”

“While the remaining 75% of our business has grown consistently, we anticipate there will be additional price headwinds in China in ’27, and the growth likely won’t be enough to offset the pressure from EP and WATCHMAN next year. As a result, we believe we’ll be challenged to grow sales and adjusted EPS in ’27, excluding our pending acquisition of Penumbra.”

Boston Scientific plans strategic investments and restructuring to stabilize and drive growth, aiming to unlock $25 billion in new market opportunities by 2030.

“Importantly, we expect these actions to drive meaningful improvement in both our revenue and adjusted EPS performance as we aim to exit the cycle in ’27 and return to delivering high performance in ’28, with further improvement expected in ’29,” Mahoney commented.

As a result, Boston Scientific slashed its earnings and sales guidance for the third quarter in a row.
The new guidance, released along with third-quarter results, is a far cry from what was projected at the beginning of the year, when Boston Scientific outlined 2026 sales growth expectations of 10.5% to 11.5%.
Boston Scientific attributed previous sales guidance cuts to ongoing challenges in its Watchman and electrophysiology businesses, which have traditionally been key growth drivers for the company.
Amid these struggles, Boston Scientific pushed back its timing for closing its $14.5 billion purchase of Penumbra.

text:
By the numbers

Q3 revenue: $5.14 billion

1.5% growth year over year

Net income: $582 million

Compared with $755 million in the year-ago period

Boston Scientific had another challenging quarter as the fallout from a cyberattack and lingering struggles in two key businesses dragged on the company’s overall performance.

As a result, Boston Scientific slashed its earnings and sales guidance for the third quarter in a row. The company now forecasts full-year revenue growth of 4.25%, compared with a previous range of 5.5% to 6.5%.

The new guidance, released along with third-quarter results, is a far cry from what was projected at the beginning of the year, when Boston Scientific outlined 2026 sales growth expectations of 10.5% to 11.5%.

Boston Scientific also cut its adjusted earnings per share guidance, dropping it to a range of $3.16 to $3.18 from a range of $3.28 to $3.32. In February, the company forecast adjusted EPS growth in a range of $3.43 to $3.49.

The company’s stock price was down by nearly 7% to $42.02 when the market opened Wednesday.

Boston Scientific attributed previous sales guidance cuts to ongoing challenges in its Watchman and electrophysiology businesses, which have traditionally been key growth drivers for the company. Those challenges continued in the third quarter.

CEO Mike Mahoney, on a Wednesday earnings call, said that Watchman sales declined by 6% and electrophysiology by 5%. For comparison, Watchman sales grew by nearly 30% in 2025, and electrophysiology has seen as much as triple-digit growth in past years, fueled by sales of pulsed field ablation devices.

Mahoney told investors that the slowdown in the left atrial appendage closure market, which includes Watchman, is due to changes in patient identification and referral patterns, while electrophysiology was challenged by new technologies and competitive pressures in PFA.

The company also dealt with a cyberattack in the third quarter that temporarily shut down ordering, manufacturing and shipping capabilities. There was a roughly $150 million hit to revenue from the cyberattack in the third quarter, according to the company.

Overall, Boston Scientific brought in $5.14 billion in revenue in the third quarter, representing growth of 1.5%.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the MedTech Dive free daily newsletter

The medical device company’s challenges are likely to continue. Boston Scientific forecast a sales decline in the fourth quarter of 3% to 1%. Furthermore, Mahoney said that the company will be challenged to grow sales and adjusted EPS next year.

Amid these struggles, Boston Scientific pushed back its timing for closing its $14.5 billion purchase of Penumbra. The company now expects to close the deal in early 2027. When the deal was announced in January, Boston Scientific said it would close the acquisition this year.

title: UK Jewish leaders launch updated workplace guide to tackle antisemitism
description:
Produced through the Board's BoD@Work program after two years of stakeholder consultation, the comprehensive guide is for employers, HR professionals, managers, and Jewish employees navigating the workplace.
The manual explains that Jewish identity encompasses both religious and ethnic dimensions, noting that Jewish people are protected from discrimination on both racial and religious grounds under the Equality Act 2010.
The guide emphasizes that Jewish identity carries strong ethnic, historical, and cultural dimensions that exist independently of religious practice, meaning that individuals who are not strictly observant can still strongly identify as Jewish.
Practical guidance on Jewish identity, observance and the realities of antisemitism at work is a step forward; however, a guide is simply a start, not a finished solution.
Through the work of JewishERGs, I see every day how a network can also strengthen Jewish identity, feelings of safety and pride among colleagues.
text:
The Board of Deputies of British Jews launched a newly expanded edition of its Employer's Guide to Jews and Judaism at the Strengthening the Jewish Way of Life and Combating Antisemitism Conference, hosted by Lord Mann at Lancaster House on Monday.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds convened a roundtable of community and business leaders during the conference to discuss workplace antisemitism and welcomed the revised publication, stating, "I commend the expertise and commitment behind this important resource, which strengthens our shared determination across Government and in society generally to tackle antisemitism and ensure Jewish life thrives across the UK."

'One of the most significant initiatives of recent years'

Lord Mann, HM Government’s Independent Adviser on Antisemitism, praised the manual, stating, "It is one of the most significant initiatives of recent years. Every employer needs to get a copy and use it."

Produced through the Board's BoD@Work program after two years of stakeholder consultation, the comprehensive guide is for employers, HR professionals, managers, and Jewish employees navigating the workplace. The manual explains that Jewish identity encompasses both religious and ethnic dimensions, noting that Jewish people are protected from discrimination on both racial and religious grounds under the Equality Act 2010. It highlights that Jewish communities comprise approximately 300,000 individuals across the UK with diverse practices, identities, and denominations ranging from strictly Orthodox to progressive and secular.

To help organizations accommodate religious observance, the handbook walks employers through Jewish practices such as the Sabbath and festivals, which begin at sunset and involve strict work restrictions. It advises flexible work patterns and advance calendar planning to help employees adjust Friday hours or request time off without professional disadvantage. The manual also addresses life-cycle events, bereavement protocols, including the seven-day shiva mourning period, dietary laws regarding kashrut, and daily prayer requirements, which typically take about 15 minutes.

Regarding dress codes and modesty requirements, such as headcoverings or modest clothing, the text cautions that inflexible workplace rules can amount to indirect discrimination unless objectively justified by legitimate aims like health and safety.

The guide emphasizes that Jewish identity carries strong ethnic, historical, and cultural dimensions that exist independently of religious practice, meaning that individuals who are not strictly observant can still strongly identify as Jewish. To reflect this, the manual encourages workplaces to integrate Jewish heritage into equality, diversity, and inclusion initiatives by adding Jewish Culture Month, a project launched by the Board of Deputies, to corporate calendars alongside other commemorative months. Employers are advised that celebrating diversity in this way creates opportunities for staff to share aspects of their heritage, food, or holidays, such as incorporating a Hannukiah display during December.

Additionally, the guide recommends establishing inclusive, colleague-led Jewish staff networks. These forums offer peer support, build relationships, promote cultural exchange, and provide a direct line of communication to management. The manual notes that endorsing such a network clearly signals an employer's solidarity, showing that the employer takes faith and ethnicity issues seriously and will properly address any instances of antisemitism.

Addressing the sharp rise in antisemitism recorded by the Community Security Trust since October 2023, the manual outlines how international conflicts can trigger workplace tensions and reiterates that holding Jewish employees collectively responsible for actions of the Israeli state is a form of antisemitism. To counter this, the guide advises employers to offer adequate training to staff in understanding Jewish identity and antisemitism within wider equality, diversity, and inclusion training programs, recommending specialized training partners such as the Community Security Trust, the Antisemitism Policy Trust, JHive, and the Union of Jewish Students alongside cultural competency providers to ensure workplaces effectively address and prevent discrimination. It explains that the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism can serve as an interpretive tool alongside UK equality law, which prohibits direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, and victimization.

Daniel Levy, Executive Director of Jhive, a UK charity providing antisemitism awareness training and Jewish inclusion support to employers in the UK and internationally, which was listed in the guide as a training partner for both antisemitism awareness and Jewish cultural competence, told The Jerusalem Post, “Much of Jhive’s work has grown since 7 October 2023, as employers realized they did not fully understand what their Jewish staff was experiencing or how best to respond. The new edition of the Board of Deputies’ guide responds to a real need among employers, and it is right to say that organizations should not rely on Jewish employees alone to educate their colleagues about antisemitism.”

“A guide is an important starting point, but it needs to be backed up by training, clear policies and confident management. What matters is whether organizations are equipped to recognize and respond appropriately to antisemitism, and whether Jewish staff feel confident raising concerns. Jhive is already working with employers in the UK and internationally to help turn this guidance into practical action,” Levy told the Post.

'Network can strengthen Jewish identity, feelings of safety and pride among colleagues'

Steven Phillips, the Executive Director of JewishERGs, a global network connecting Jewish employee resource groups across over 250 workplaces in 9 countries worldwide, told The Jerusalem Post, “I am pleased to see the launch of the Board of Deputies’ updated Employer’s Guide to Jews and Judaism. For many HR or Inclusion teams this guide may be the first such document they have seen. Practical guidance on Jewish identity, observance and the realities of antisemitism at work is a step forward; however, a guide is simply a start, not a finished solution. A lot of work remains to educate those leading HR and diversity functions on the real issues facing Jews in the workplace and beyond.”

“I believe that Jewish Employee Groups are one of the strongest ways to build both safety and belonging for Jewish employees. Through the work of JewishERGs, I see every day how a network can also strengthen Jewish identity, feelings of safety and pride among colleagues. These colleagues then use that confidence to help others understand what it means to be Jewish, and/or Zionist, often for people who have never knowingly met a Jewish person before. A great deal of work remains to encourage and support employers in creating and running Jewish Employee Groups, and I hope this guide sparks a conversation to help drive meaningful cultural change,” Phillips told the Post.

title: DoorDash in Advanced Talks to Acquire Instacart in Reported $17 Billion Deal
description:
DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire grocery-delivery company Instacart in a deal valued at approximately $17 billion, Reuters reported on Oct. 26, 2026.
Acquiring Instacart would give DoorDash access to an established grocery marketplace and the retailer partnerships that come with it.
The two companies reportedly held advanced talks to acquire discussions in 2021, but antitrust concerns contributed to those talks collapsing, according to Reuters.
A combined DoorDash and Instacart would overlap across restaurant, convenience, and grocery delivery.
Consumers could benefit from a single membership covering both restaurant and grocery delivery, and broader merchant relationships could expand your available selection.
text:
DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire grocery-delivery company Instacart in a deal valued at approximately $17 billion, Reuters reported on Oct. 26, 2026. No agreement has been confirmed, and sources cautioned that negotiations could still fall apart.

The reported deal would mark a significant consolidation in online delivery, arriving as both companies face intensifying competition from Amazon and Walmart. It also revives a pairing that collapsed once before.

The Amazon Problem Neither Company Can Solve Alone

Analysts say the proposed combination is driven by the need to compete with vertically integrated retail giants, though no deal terms have been confirmed.

Acquiring Instacart would give DoorDash access to an established grocery marketplace and the retailer partnerships that come with it. Instacart, legally incorporated as Maplebear, would gain DoorDash’s broader delivery network and its large consumer base.

Wedbush analysts described the combination as strategically useful for competing against Amazon and Walmart, according to MarketWatch. Bernstein analysts went further, characterizing the potential platform as an “indispensable solution,” per the same MarketWatch report.

Those assessments reflect analyst opinion, not confirmed company strategy. Cross-selling restaurant, grocery, and convenience orders through a single app is one possibility analysts have raised. Bundling memberships across both platforms is another. Neither company has announced either plan.

Separate delivery and restaurant memberships create real friction for users. A combined platform could, in theory, eliminate that redundancy, though no integration plan has been announced.

A Deal That’s Been Here Before

Antitrust concerns derailed earlier talks between the two companies in 2021, and regulatory risk remains a central uncertainty for any new agreement.

This is not the first time DoorDash and Instacart have explored a transaction. The two companies reportedly held advanced talks to acquire discussions in 2021, but antitrust concerns contributed to those talks collapsing, according to Reuters.

Instacart also held preliminary discussions with Uber before those conversations went inactive, Reuters reported. By the time Reuters published its Oct. 26 report, DoorDash had emerged as the active party.

A combined DoorDash and Instacart would overlap across restaurant, convenience, and grocery delivery. That broad footprint is likely to draw antitrust scrutiny. Which agencies would review the deal, and what remedies might be required, cannot be determined until a transaction is formally announced.

Investors registered the uncertainty immediately. Instacart shares closed 7.9% higher on Oct. 26 while DoorDash shares fell 6.1% during the same session, per MarketWatch. The divergence suggests investors were weighing Instacart’s takeover premium against concerns about DoorDash’s costs and regulatory exposure. Deal structure has not been disclosed. Whether it would involve cash, stock, or a combination, along with any financing terms or breakup fee, remains unknown.

What It Could Mean for You

Consumers could see real benefits from a unified platform, but consolidation also carries risks that remain unconfirmed at this stage.

Consumers could benefit from a single membership covering both restaurant and grocery delivery, and broader merchant relationships could expand your available selection. Delivery coverage could also improve if the companies’ logistics systems were integrated.

Consolidation carries real risks, though. Fewer independent platforms generally means reduced competitive pressure on pricing, and subscription costs could shift after integration. Retailers and restaurants that currently negotiate separately with each platform could face altered economics under a combined operator. None of these outcomes has been confirmed.

Watch for a formal announcement, which Reuters indicated could come within days, though timing remains uncertain. How both companies address the 2021 antitrust history will likely determine whether this deal closes at all.

text:
Dive Brief:

Eli Lilly’s triple-acting metabolic drug retatrutide bested Novo’s Ozempic in a head-to-head Phase 3 trial, with the highest dose tested beating Novo’s drug on measures of blood sugar and weight loss, the company said Wednesday.

After 80 weeks of treatment, a 12 milligram weekly dose of retatrutide lowered blood sugar by an average of 2.2 percentage points, significantly more than Ozempic’s 1.8 percentage points, Lilly said. A 9 mg dose of retatrutide also lowered blood sugar by 2.2 percentage points, but the difference when compared to Ozempic was statistically “nominal,” the company said.

The results confirm earlier findings suggesting retatrutide — which acts on three metabolic pathways versus one for Ozempic — could be a differentiated diabetes and weight loss medicine. In an obesity trial, this “triple-G” drug stimulated weight loss that rivaled results seen in bariatric surgery.

Dive Insight:

Should retatrutide go on to win approval, Lilly may further cement its place atop metabolic medicine. The ascent of its already-marketed Zepbound and Mounjaro have propelled Lilly’s market value far beyond that of its pharmaceutical peers. And the buzz surrounding retatrutide is so strong that many people have resorted to a nebulous “black market” to get their hands on it.

Retatrutide represents the next step in a push by obesity drug developers to make therapies that can drop weight even more profoundly than existing medications. While GLP-1 medicines have been on the market for more than 20 years, for instance — Lilly was the commercial partner for the first such shot — the company has been specializing in drugs that add more metabolic targets to boost effectiveness.

Zepbound and Mounjaro modulate GLP-1 as well as a second hormone called GIP. Retatrutide acts on a third, called glucagon, too. Novo is aiming to catch up, but has yet to launch a dual acting drug, and its three-pronged candidates are in Phase 2 trials.

The latest trial result showed just how challenging a foe retatrutide might be for Novo. The highest dose lowered weight by 21% on average, while a 9 mg dose was associated with 20% weight loss. That number was 9% for Ozempic recipients.

Those benefits appear to come with a trade-off. In the study, only 3% of Ozempic recipients stopped treatment because of side effects compared with 8% of the people on the highest retatrutide dose and 5% of those in the 9 mg group.

Still, the results “strengthen the case for retatrutide’s long-term differentiation” and justify a “branded premium” ahead of the 2032 U.S. patent expiration of semaglutide, wrote Leerink analyst David Risinger in a client note.

Risinger expects annual retatrutide sales to reach $15 billion in 2032, higher than the $10 billion consensus among Wall Street analysts.

So how can grocers support shoppers after they come off the medication?
Like many grocers, Hy-Vee has implemented wellness initiatives designed for shoppers taking GLP-1s for weight management.

This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

It’s no secret GLP-1 medications are drastically changing shopping behaviors. Baskets are shrinking as people using these drugs shift away from pantry staples and “carb-centric” goods toward protein- and fiber-rich items, seafood, functional nutrition and more intentional snacking, according to Numerator’s GLP-1 usage tracker in August.

Spending from this shopper cohort — which accounts for over $660 billion in consumer spending across CPG, general merchandise and quick-service restaurants — has declined nearly 4% compared to similar households not using GLP-1 medications after one year, Numerator found.

In response, grocers are working overtime to establish themselves as GLP-1 destinations. For instance, The Giant Company offered store tours to customers this past month to help them find food that pairs well with the weight-management medications. ShopRite launched wellness kits designed for customers new to GLP-1 medications, and Costco introduced more protein-focused products to its private label line.

But GLP-1 usage for weight loss and management is only temporary. So how can grocers support shoppers after they come off the medication?

The short answer: Grocers need to play the long game.

Research shows consumers’ grocery shopping habits stay the course for the first few months after coming off GLP-1 medications, but by the six- to 11-month mark, that behavior “largely converges back toward non-user norms,” Sherry Frey, vice president of Total Wellness at NielsenIQ, said in emailed remarks.

That could mean creating dedicated protein and fiber destinations and merchandising complementary products together while also highlighting nutrient benefits on shelf, she suggested. Grocers can also offer meal solutions built around satiety and balanced nutrition and use loyalty programs to personalize recommendations, she wrote.

Like many grocers, Hy-Vee has implemented wellness initiatives designed for shoppers taking GLP-1s for weight management. However, CEO Jeremy Gosch said Hy-Vee is trying to focus on the broader picture and support shoppers once their stint on the medication ends.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Grocery Dive free daily newsletter

“We all know about GLP-1s, but the problem with GLP-1s is it’s going to help you eat less. It’s not going to change what you eat,” Gosch said during his keynote address at the Groceryshop conference in September.

With this issue in mind, Hy-Vee focuses heavily on educating customers about GLP-1s. In July, the grocer introduced a wellness program that aims to both help individuals taking the medications and also establish healthy habits they can continue practicing once they’re off the medication.

Unlike other grocers’ GLP-1 initiatives, Hy-Vee is focusing on long-term lifestyle changes. The six-week, self-guided online course it offered included one-on-one check-ins with a Hy-Vee registered dietitian, video modules and personalized goal setting. The course also helped participants establish lifelong habits such as staying hydrated; eating smaller, more frequent meals; and preparing meals ahead of time.

Gosch, like fellow food retailers, wants to cater to GLP-1 users, but he is also looking to keep this consumer cohort — as well as their new healthy eating practices — once their time on the medication ends.

text:
The Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation’s (ADDF) Diagnostics Accelerator (DxA) announces a new collaboration with Eli Lilly and Company, which has licensed the ADDF’s SpeechDx dataset, the world's largest harmonized longitudinal dataset of speech and biomarker data spanning the Alzheimer's continuum, from cognitively unimpaired individuals to Alzheimer's dementia. Lilly will use the data to investigate the utility of speech as a tool for Alzheimer's research.

“Lilly is a world leader in Alzheimer’s therapeutics and diagnostics, and their licensing of the SpeechDx data is an important recognition of the quality of this resource and the ADDF’s leadership in advancing speech-based measures,” said Isobel Coleman, Chief Executive Officer of the ADDF. “AI-driven tools have the potential to transform how we detect and monitor Alzheimer's, but they are only as good as the data behind them. Through SpeechDx, the ADDF is building one of the largest and most comprehensive datasets in this space, a unique resource designed to give researchers and industry partners what they need to develop and validate the next generation of digital markers."

SpeechDx, the ADDF's largest investment in AI to date, was launched in 2023 by the ADDF's DxA to address a critical gap in the field: the absence of datasets that track how a person's speech changes over time alongside biomarker-confirmed diagnoses and clinical outcomes. The study follows more than 2,000 participants over three years, creating a gold-standard resource that AI models can train and validate against. Speech is one of the earliest indicators of cognitive decline, and because it can be captured inexpensively through the microphones already built into smartphones and computers, it offers a highly scalable way to monitor brain health.

“For more than 35 years, Lilly has worked to advance the understanding and treatment of Alzheimer’s disease. This unique dataset pairs speech-based data with established biomarkers, supporting our efforts to make diagnosis more accurate, accessible, and less invasive across the disease continuum,” said Mark Mintun, group vice president, Neuroscience Research and Development for Eli Lilly and Company. “Earlier detection is critical, as mild symptoms are often mistaken for normal aging, delaying opportunities for intervention.”

Lilly joins Siemens Healthineers and Callyope as the third organization to license the SpeechDx dataset, underscoring the potential value of dynamic, digital measures that can be used alongside blood tests to provide additional information on a patient’s cognition and future risk.

“Speech has enormous potential as a signal of cognitive change, but potential alone is not enough,” said Niranjan Bose, Managing Director, Health and Life Sciences at Gates Ventures. “To turn that signal into a reliable digital measure, the field needs large, well-characterized datasets. That is the value of SpeechDx. We have already convened a group of high-caliber researchers alongside partners like Siemens Healthineers and Callyope. Adding Lilly brings us another step closer to establishing speech as a credible, validated tool for Alzheimer's research and drug development."

text:
Boston Scientific (BSX) lowered its full-year financial outlook amid the impact of a cybersecurity incident earlier this year, while the medical device maker's third-quarter earnings fell year over year.

The company now expects full-year adjusted earnings of $3.16 to $3.18 per share and net sales growth of about 4.25%. It previously projected adjusted EPS of $3.28 to $3.32 and net sales growth of 5.5% to 6.5% for the year. Analysts in a FactSet survey are looking for EPS of $3.22 and revenue of $21.16 billion, which would indicate a year-over-year growth of 5.4%.

Shares of the company were down 9.9% intraday, taking the stock's year-to-date losses to 57%.

"Our (third-quarter) results were impacted by our previously reported cybersecurity incident, which we estimate reduced our sales growth by approximately 300 basis points and adjusted EPS by $0.07 in the quarter," Chief Executive Mike Mahoney said during an earnings conference call, according to a FactSet transcript.

Last month, Boston Scientific flagged its inability to meet its near-term financial outlook amid a "material impact" from a recent cybersecurity incident. The incident, which the company identified on Aug. 25, affected some of its information technology systems and caused a network outage that impacted its ability to manufacture, process and ship customer orders.

Boston Scientific has seen three estimate resets this year, Truist Securities said in a note, adding that the latest reduction may not yet get full credit as a "clearing event" among investors. The brokerage said Boston Scientific's stock could recover in the second half of 2027 and into 2028 if the company can demonstrate that growth is accelerating again.

For the September quarter, adjusted EPS fell to $0.73 from $0.75 a year earlier, slightly ahead of the consensus of $0.72 but below the company's guidance of $0.80 to $0.82. Net sales rose 1.5% to $5.14 billion, which exceeded analysts' $5.06 billion estimate.

The impact from the cyberattack is expected to persist in the current quarter, Mahoney said.

"We anticipate that it will be a 200 basis points or 300 basis points of impact from the cyber incident as we work through elevated customer orders at the end of (the third quarter) to replenish inventory levels," he told analysts.

For the December quarter, Boston Scientific expects adjusted EPS of $0.77 to $0.79 and net sales to decline by 1% to 3% year over year. Analysts are looking for EPS of $0.83 and revenue growth of 2.6% to $5.42 billion.

Third-quarter sales in the cardiovascular business increased 1.9% year over year to $3.41 billion. The MedSurg division delivered a 0.6% growth to $1.73 billion, as a double-digit gain in neuromodulation was offset by weakness in urology and endoscopy.

"We anticipate continued top line pressure into 2027, which we expect will make it challenging to grow revenue and adjusted earnings per share, excluding Penumbra," Chief Financial Officer Jonathan Monson told analysts.

Earlier this year, Boston Scientific agreed to acquire medical device company Penumbra (PEN) in a cash-and-stock deal with an enterprise value of about $14.5 billion in a bid to strengthen its cardiovascular portfolio.

"We expect our underlying business dynamics in (the ongoing quarter) to persist into 2027, and believe our fourth quarter guidance provides a reasonable baseline for next year's revenue and adjusted earnings per share outlook," Monson said.

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) recently raised its full-year outlook even though the upgraded midpoints missed Wall Street's estimates.

Q3 Results and 2026 Outlook Boston Scientific reported $5.14 billion in third-quarter 2026 sales, up 1.5% from the same period last year, as a cybersecurity incident disrupted operations and weighed on results.

text:
Boston Scientific and Heartflow have announced a strategic collaboration to advance CT-guided planning for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients with coronary artery disease.

The companies will evaluate compatibility between Heartflow’s AI-powered PCI Navigator platform, which creates patient-specific 3D coronary models for preprocedural planning, and Boston Scientific’s AVVIGO+ multi-modality guidance system, which supports intravascular imaging and physiology assessment during procedures. They’ll also explore ways to integrate the technologies to help physicians plan and perform PCI with greater precision and efficiency.

“Through this collaboration, we aim to support more informed clinical decision-making and advance a more personalized approach to care for patients with coronary artery disease, from diagnosis through treatment,” Heartflow said in an X post announcing the partnership.

The collaboration was also revealed in Boston Scientific’s Q3 earnings release.

Q3 Results and 2026 Outlook

Boston Scientific reported $5.14 billion in third-quarter 2026 sales, up 1.5% from the same period last year, as a cybersecurity incident disrupted operations and weighed on results.

The company lowered its full-year 2026 sales growth outlook to about 4.25% on a reported basis and 3.75% organically. It expects fourth-quarter sales to decline 1% to 3% year over year, and forecasts adjusted earnings of $0.77 to $0.79 per share.

The company posted adjusted earnings of $0.73 per share, down from $0.75 a year earlier. The company estimated the cyber incident stifled organic sales growth by approximately 300 basis points, following an eight-business-day disruption that halted manufacturing and shipments across its global network.

Cardiovascular sales grew 1.9% to $3.41 billion, while MedSurg sales increased 0.6% to $1.73 billion. Neuromodulation led growth within MedSurg, with sales rising 13% to $331 million. Endoscopy sales declined 0.6% to $741 million, and Urology sales fell 3.1% to $661 million.

During the quarter, Boston Scientific received FDA 510(k) clearance for two technologies in its StoneSmart kidney stone treatment portfolio: the Navigator Flex ureteral access sheath set, which uses suction to remove stone debris, and the LithoVue Elite single-use digital flexible ureteroscope, which adds real-time fluid temperature monitoring. The company also received clearance for an expanded size offering of its SEISMIQ intravascular lithotripsy catheter for treating severely calcified peripheral artery disease.

text:
Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting.

The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020, aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050.

But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in.

Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase.

This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025.

However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons.

The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024.

Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8.

In an SEC filing, the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually.

The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan.

It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt.

In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending.

On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth.

We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance.

Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks.

The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

name: Air Liquide
title: Three things Europe needs to turn hydrogen ambition into industrial reality | Werner Ponikwar
description:
The hydrogen industry has never suffered from a shortage of ambition.
For Europe to turn its hydrogen ambitions into industrial reality, I am convinced that three things must come together: Let me explain why.
Competitive energy: Europe needs it at scale – electrolysis can make it possible You cannot produce competitive hydrogen with uncompetitive electricity.
We must also ask a second question: Where will the technologies and industrial capabilities we depend on come from?
Without competitive, secure electricity, Europe cannot build a competitive green hydrogen industry.
text:
An electrolyser is not something you buy for next year. You buy it for the next 20 or 30 years. That is a long time in business – and an even longer time in politics.

When our customers invest in an electrolyser, they are making a bet on the future: On energy prices, demand and infrastructure. And on the technology and industrial capabilities they will be able to rely on for decades. At Thyssenkrupp Nucera, we take that responsibility seriously. We develop and deliver large-scale electrolysis technology.

Three things Europe needs

We know what it takes to turn engineering into industrial reality. And we know that technology alone is not enough. The hydrogen industry has never suffered from a shortage of ambition. What we need now are more projects. At some point, potential needs to become a purchase order. For Europe to turn its hydrogen ambitions into industrial reality, I am convinced that three things must come together:

Let me explain why.

Competitive energy: Europe needs it at scale – electrolysis can make it possible

You cannot produce competitive hydrogen with uncompetitive electricity. Let me put this into perspective: Producing one kilogram of hydrogen takes roughly 50 to 55 kilowatt-hours of electricity. At €0.04 per kilowatt-hour, that means at least €2 ($2.22) in electricity costs alone. At €0.10, the bill rises to more than €5. Same technology. Same kilogram of hydrogen. More than twice the electricity cost. And that is before you pay for the electrolyser, financing and operation. That is why electricity prices matter so much. They are the biggest single cost driver in renewable hydrogen production.

This is where electrolysis comes in. It connects renewable electricity with industrial value creation. It turns electricity into molecules that can be stored, transported and used where direct electrification is not enough. It can also help the power system become more flexible.

Electrolysers can adjust their operation to electricity availability. Where the economics and system conditions allow, they can use renewable power. Power that would otherwise go unused. In other words: electrolysis can help connect Europe’s renewable energy potential with the needs of its industry.

But we must look at the whole system:

Strategic choice: Europe needs a strong base and partnerships abroad

But competitive energy is only part of the story. We must also ask a second question: Where will the technologies and industrial capabilities we depend on come from? An electrolyser is a long-term investment. Its true cost is not determined by the initial purchase price alone. Performance, efficiency, availability, service and reliability matter over the entire life of the plant. That is why we need to look beyond the cheapest initial offer. A piece of technology can look inexpensive on day one — and become very expensive if critical components, services or supplies are no longer available when you need them.

That is why we are investing in our own industrial capabilities: In Portugal, we are establishing our first company-operated Assembly Hub for electrolyser cells. It will centralise and semi-automate assembly, strengthen our European value chain, and bring manufacturing and service closer together. This is what industrial resilience looks like in practice. A real investment in manufacturing capacity, industrial skills, and project execution.

At the same time, we are building partnerships beyond Europe: In India, we are working with Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited to support local manufacturing capabilities and project delivery. And to help develop the hydrogen ecosystem.

These are two sides of the same strategy. We strengthen industrial capabilities in Europe while building partnerships that create value in other markets. It is not a contradiction. It is how international industry works.

Industrial execution: Public money should unlock private capital

Europe has spent years setting hydrogen targets, developing strategies and establishing rules. Of course, we need rules. But they should help make industrial projects possible, not make them harder to deliver. And projects only move forward when customers and investors can build a credible business case.

Investors cannot make a long-term commitment if the underlying market conditions remain fundamentally uncertain. We have done our part. At Thyssenkrupp Nucera, we have developed competitive technology, industrialised our products and built the capacity to deliver at scale.

Our responsibility is clear: deliver technology that performs, reliably and efficiently, over the lifetime of a plant. But we cannot create the entire market ourselves. We cannot build the necessary infrastructure on our own. And we cannot eliminate uncertainty about public policy.

We need reliable demand, infrastructure that develops alongside production, and rules that investors can plan around. Not because industry wants to avoid risk. Investors need to understand the risks they are taking. And they need to know which conditions they can rely on.

But it also reminds us how much further we need to go. Projects of this scale must become more than exceptions. They must become repeatable. The real test is not whether we can deliver one large project. It is whether we can make projects like this the basis for an entire market. That means learning from each project, improving technology, reducing costs, and building the conditions for the next investment.

We need to change how we measure success

Let me bring these three points together. First, competitiveness starts with energy. Without competitive, secure electricity, Europe cannot build a competitive green hydrogen industry.

Second, resilience means choice. Europe must remain capable of developing, producing and choosing the technologies on which its industrial future depends.

Third, we know how to build it. Now we need to scale it.

These three challenges are connected: Competitive energy creates the economic foundation. Industrial capabilities preserve strategic choice. And execution turns both into results.

Europe has important technological capabilities. Companies are investing. Projects are moving forward. Now we need to bring the pieces together. Industry must deliver. Europe must enable.

Success should not be measured by how many targets we announce. It should be measured by the investments we unlock, the plants we build and the industrial value we create.

The technology is here. Industrial capabilities are here. Now, let’s turn Europe’s ambition into industrial reality.

text:
Microsoft on Monday announced a new voluntary buyout program that will cover about 60,000 eligible employees who can choose to leave the company with financial support and other career planning resources.

The buyout program covers more than a quarter of Microsoft's global workforce, as the company said it had about 223,000 full-time employees around the world as of June 30, 2026, in its annual filing. The voluntary exit program was first reported by Business Insider and follows Microsoft's rollout of a voluntary retirement program earlier this year.

Amy Coleman, Microsoft EVP and chief people officer, said in a memo posted on the official Microsoft blog that the buyout program "reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter."

The company's voluntary exit program is time-limited and available to eligible employees at level 70 and below. Microsoft's announcement indicated that eligible employees would be notified via email about the details of their voluntary exit offer within a few hours of the announcement.

MICROSOFT PRESIDENT SAYS AI FACES FEWER SAFETY RULES THAN MILK IN CALL FOR GLOBAL REGULATION

Some organizations within Microsoft are participating in the program, which covers eligible employees in the U.S., the United Kingdom, Canada and India.

Microsoft indicated that the participation of different organizations within the company is based on each business unit's priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.

Coleman added that the voluntary exit offer is new to Microsoft and that the company will learn from it and added, "At the same time, we'll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft."

MICROSOFT CEO SAYS SUPERINTELLIGENCE MUST REMAIN 'UNDER HUMAN CONTROL'

"There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee," Coleman said. "These are a few of the ways we're trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute."

"My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving," she added.

Earlier this year, Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 7% of its U.S. workforce, or about 9,000 employees.

MICROSOFT SAYS ITS AI TOOL OUTPERFORMS GENERALIST DOCTORS IN COMPLEX DIAGNOSES

It also announced cuts affecting about 4,800 jobs in July, or about 2.1% of the global workforce, as it overhauled its Xbox gaming business and divested up to five studios to boost returns in the division.

Microsoft and other tech giants are facing costly investments in the buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure like data centers and in the chips that are used to train models, which have prompted moves to cut costs in other areas of their operations.

title: How AI, Quantum, and Web3 Are Quietly Rewriting the Rules of Capital
description:
Crypto was for day-traders, AI wrote quirky poems, and quantum computing was a sci-fi trope.
Programmable Cash: Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and institutional deposit tokens (like JPM Coin) moving fiat money natively on-chain.
When AI Agents Get Their Own Bank Accounts The bigger shift isn't chatbots, it's agentic AI: software with direct financial execution authority.
Quantum computing changes that: 1,000 Steps Instead of 1,000,000: using Quantum Amplitude Estimation, quantum processors can process millions of risk paths simultaneously.
Europe's MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) framework established standardised rules for digital assets across 27 member states.
text:
By Artjoms Asatrjans, Board Member at Latvian Blockchain Association (LBAA); Founder at ArtEstate

Imagine trying to explain email to a bank manager in 1985. You'd mention protocols and packet switching, and their eyes would glaze over. But if you said, "It's a letter that arrives anywhere on Earth instantly, for free," they'd get it immediately.

In his book Blockchain Banking, tech investor Monty C. M. Metzger captured this shift well: "Blockchain is to money what email was to letters."

For a decade, the public treated high-tech finance as a novelty. Crypto was for day-traders, AI wrote quirky poems, and quantum computing was a sci-fi trope. But while attention stayed on the hype, institutional finance quietly began building the infrastructure behind it.

Set aside speculative tokens. Three forces are reshaping how capital actually moves.

1. Capital at the Speed of Light (T+0)

Traditional finance settles slowly. When a $100 million bond trade happens, the cash and asset sit in a two-day settlement window (T+2) while clearinghouses process the paperwork.

Tokenisation turns capital into programmable code:

Real-World Assets (RWA): bonds, commercial real estate, and credit converted into smart-contract tokens.

Programmable Cash: Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and institutional deposit tokens (like JPM Coin) moving fiat money natively on-chain.

When both the asset and the cash sit on the same ledger, settlement can happen in milliseconds (T+0). According to analytics from RWA.xyz, institutions have already moved over roughly $15 billion in US Treasuries on-chain, pushing total tokenised assets past $35 billion.

Real-World Example: Siemens & Franklin Templeton

In one of the earlier examples of this shift, Siemens issued a €60 million digital bond on a public blockchain in 2023, selling directly to institutional investors without a bank intermediary. Franklin Templeton's BENJI fund now allows investors to trade tokenised money-market funds on-chain around the clock.

2. When AI Agents Get Their Own Bank Accounts

The bigger shift isn't chatbots, it's agentic AI: software with direct financial execution authority.

An AI managing a corporate treasury doesn't just write a report for a human to review. It can hold a cryptographic wallet on a secure blockchain, scan global yield curves, evaluate credit risk, and execute micro-transactions in real time to optimise yields.

Instead of waiting for delayed quarterly balance sheets, this kind of system can continuously calculate credit scores from live trade data and supply-chain telemetry.

3. Quantum Computing: Faster Risk, Stronger Encryption

Pricing complex derivatives requires Monte Carlo simulations, running millions of scenarios. Classical supercomputers can take hours to do this.

Quantum computing changes that:

1,000 Steps Instead of 1,000,000: using Quantum Amplitude Estimation, quantum processors can process millions of risk paths simultaneously. Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase are actively testing these algorithms for real-time risk hedging.

Post-Quantum Protection: banks are already building Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) into their digital vaults, to prevent future quantum hardware from cracking standard encryption.

Real-World Example: BNY Mellon

BNY Mellon (roughly $60 trillion in assets under custody) deploys quantum-inspired algorithms to optimise international collateral allocation across clearinghouses in fractions of a second during simulated panics.

The Regulatory Foundation: MiCA

None of this would be possible at scale without clear legal rules. Europe's MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) framework established standardised rules for digital assets across 27 member states. Combined with permissioned smart contracts, which embed Know-Your-Customer (KYC) rules directly into token code, banks can transact on-chain knowing compliance is built in by design.

How the New Stack Fits Together:

The Takeaway

Web3 was never meant to be a digital casino. Strip away the noise, and it is simply a genuine upgrade for global capital: instant settlement, AI-assisted execution, and quantum-enhanced risk modelling.

description:

DTC Participants can register selected third party wallets for their clients via a user interface.
Twenty DTC Participants have signed up so far.
Alpaca is among the launch participants and Ondo is named as a collaborator, which points toward wrapped tokens.
Trading could happen via ATS venues or tokenized securities venues that are subject to the SEC’s innovation exemption.
text:
Today the DTCC launched its Tokenization Service after the SEC granted a no-action letter in December 2025. At launch just 34 securities are eligible, a mix of equities, Treasuries and ETFs. The SEC’s no-action letter covers a far broader set, the full Russell 1000, US Treasuries and major index ETFs, worth roughly $30 trillion of the more than $114 trillion DTC holds in custody. These are tokenized entitlements that carry the same ownership rights as conventional securities held in street name at DTC and share the same CUSIP.

A key goal is 24/7 transfers. When a tokenized position moves between registered wallets, that is the settlement, so there is no T+1 wait. However, there are limits in the early period. Moving a token between chains goes through DTC’s conversion service, which runs from 2am to 6pm ET on business days, so round the clock transfers are intrachain only. The same service converts positions between conventional and tokenized form. Transfers can only be made between registered wallets. DTC Participants can register selected third party wallets for their clients via a user interface.

Twenty DTC Participants have signed up so far. They include global banks and custodians such as JP Morgan, Citi, Bank of America, Barclays, BNP Paribas, UBS, Morgan Stanley and State Street, retail and clearing brokers including Fidelity, Edward Jones, Apex, DriveWealth and Clear Street, and crypto adjacent firms Alpaca and Velocity Capital. Notable absences are BNY, the largest custodian, and Goldman Sachs, which took part in the July live trials. Future users will be onboarded on a rolling basis.

There’s a misconception that tokenization is only happening on the Canton Network. DTC’s Besu-based private distributed ledger is also available at launch and provides the foundation for the DTCC Collateral AppChain due early next year. By then additional networks such as Stellar and Circle’s Arc are expected to join the fray, as well as other blockchains subject to client demand.

Settlement and applications

The roadmap for 2027 and beyond includes expanding the eligible securities and asset servicing. For now settlement arrangements are up to Participants, but given the DTCC group’s critical role in securities settlement it is not surprising that it has plans in this area. Today netting via the NSCC typically reduces the settlement figure for conventional securities by around 98%, and the roadmap includes on-chain cash netting. The DTCC has previously told Ledger Insights it is exploring stablecoins and tokenized deposits for settlement. While not necessarily indicative, JPMorgan played a prominent role in the July live transactions and has said it plans to launch JPM Coin on Canton. Previous DTCC collateral simulations included Société Générale FORGE’s stablecoins and Fnality’s institutional settlement system.

It remains to be seen whether use cases will bifurcate, with traditional finance attracted to 24/7 movement of collateral and crypto natives using DTC tokens to trade or to underpin wrapped tokens. Alpaca is among the launch participants and Ondo is named as a collaborator, which points toward wrapped tokens. Trading could happen via ATS venues or tokenized securities venues that are subject to the SEC’s innovation exemption. Canton may not be known as a major DeFi trading venue, but one of the first TSVs planning to launch, TSV LLC, is on the Canton Network. That said, it only plans to support issuer-sponsored tokens rather than third party tokens such as the DTCC’s.
