text:
Highlights

Medtronic announced its intent to acquire CathWorks, a developer of technology that assesses blockages in heart arteries without placing a pressure wire inside the vessel, according to the company's release.

The company framed the move as an extension of its innovation strategy in cardiovascular care, where it already offers a broad range of catheters, stents, rhythm devices and imaging tools.

Recent Medtronic news flow has also touched its Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system, the Stealth Axis surgical system clearance and a renal denervation coverage review at the federal Medicare program.

Medtronic (NYSE:MDT) Healthcare Medtronic PLC (NYSE:MDT) 93.95 USD -0.840 ↓ 0.886% is back at the center of medical technology conversation after announcing its intent to acquire CathWorks, a company built around a technology that estimates how much a narrowing in a coronary artery restricts blood flow. According to the company's release, the planned acquisition fits within a broader effort to advance its innovation strategy in heart care, among the largest and most closely watched parts of its business. Medtronic is among the companies tracked in our Healthcare Stocks coverage.

The announcement lands in a busy stretch for the Ireland-domiciled device maker, whose shares are part of the S&P 500. Over recent months the company has also reported milestones for its Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system, a clearance for its Stealth Axis surgical system, progress on coverage for its Symplicity Spyral renal denervation system and a regulatory clearance for a diabetes product. The stock, listed on the New York Stock Exchange, sits within the S&P 500 and NYSE Composite. Each of those threads feeds into how market participants read the next quarterly update.

This article walks through what the CathWorks step is, where it fits in Medtronic's portfolio, which other product programs are moving, and which uncertainties remain. Deal terms and closing timing were not verified, and no figures are offered where the sources reviewed did not confirm them.

What did Medtronic (NYSE:MDT) Healthcare Medtronic PLC (NYSE:MDT) 93.95 USD -0.840 ↓ 0.886% say about acquiring CathWorks?

According to the company's announcement, Medtronic stated its intent to acquire CathWorks, a developer of a system that uses imaging from a standard coronary angiogram to produce a physiological assessment of heart artery narrowing. The headline of the release tied the step to the company's innovation strategy, a phrase Medtronic uses when it describes adding technologies that complement products it already offers.

The release described the transaction as an intent rather than a completed deal, which matters for how it is read. Acquisitions of this kind typically move through customary closing conditions, and the company's statement did not, in the portions reviewed for this article, give grounds to describe a completion date. Readers should treat any timing discussion as unconfirmed until Medtronic files or announces a close.

CathWorks is not a newcomer to Medtronic. That history is part of why the step reads as a deepening of an existing relationship, though the precise commercial arrangement before the announcement was not verified here and is not described in detail.

Why does a coronary assessment tool matter to the Medtronic cardiovascular franchise?

Cardiologists deciding whether to place a stent need to know whether a narrowing is actually limiting blood flow. Traditionally that judgment relied on angiographic appearance or on a pressure wire threaded across the lesion. Newer approaches compute a flow estimate from images already captured during the procedure, which can save time and avoid an extra device in the vessel.

Guidance on which lesions need treatment can influence procedure planning, and a physician comfortable with a vendor's workflow may be more open to that vendor's accompanying devices. That commercial logic is common across the sector, though it is an interpretation rather than a statement from the company.

The counterpoint is that physiological assessment is a crowded and technical field. Competing flow-estimation software and established pressure-wire systems already have physician followings, and adoption depends on clinical evidence, workflow fit and payment.

Medical device deals are also watched for what they imply about capital allocation. A company of Medtronic's scale can choose among internal research, smaller tuck-in acquisitions, larger transactions and paying out cash through dividends. Announcing a focused acquisition of a specialty technology firm signals a preference, at least for this moment, for adding a focused capability rather than a sweeping combination, though the company did not frame it in those exact terms.

How does the Medtronic Hugo robotic system fit alongside the CathWorks news?

Medtronic has also announced a first surgery using its Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system in a new setting, according to a company release listed in recent press coverage. Hugo is the company's entry in soft-tissue robotics, a category long led by Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci platform, and its rollout is among the more closely tracked product stories at Medtronic.

It brings a recurring stream of instruments, accessories and service, and it can anchor relationships with hospital systems. At the same time, building a credible second platform in a field with a dominant incumbent is a long process that depends on regulatory clearances, surgeon training and clinical results.

What the company has and has not disclosed about Hugo utilization was not verified for this article. Market participants therefore tend to watch how often management mentions procedure counts, new indications and installed systems in its quarterly commentary, since those details indicate whether the platform is moving from introduction toward routine use.

What does the Stealth Axis clearance add to Medtronic neuroscience and spine offerings?

A recent company announcement said Medtronic received FDA clearance for its Stealth Axis surgical system, described in coverage as a first for a new approach to spine and cranial navigation. The Stealth family of navigation products has long been part of the company's surgical technologies group, which sits within its neuroscience business.

Navigation and imaging systems matter because they guide placement of implants and instruments in procedures where precision is critical.

Clearance is a necessary step, not a revenue statement. The pace at which hospitals install new capital equipment depends on budgets and competing priorities, and the company did not, in the materials reviewed, provide a verified estimate of how quickly Stealth Axis would contribute to results. That absence is worth noting when the product is discussed as a growth driver.

Where do Medtronic renal denervation and the Medicare coverage review stand?

Renal denervation is a catheter-based procedure intended to lower blood pressure in patients whose hypertension is not controlled well by medication. Medtronic's Symplicity Spyral system is among the products in the category, and the company has reported multi-year clinical results showing sustained office-based blood pressure reductions, according to its published releases.

A major swing factor for this business is payment. The federal Medicare program opened a national coverage review for the procedure, a step the company announced in a release, and the eventual coverage decision is expected to shape how widely hospitals and physicians adopt it. Coverage determinations follow a defined process with comment periods, so the timeline is set by the agency rather than the company.

For market participants, the uncertainty is twofold: whether the final coverage terms prove broad or narrow, and how quickly procedure volumes build once payment is clear.

What is happening with Medtronic diabetes products and the MiniMed brand?

The product is aimed at people who manage diabetes with injections instead of an insulin pump, a large group that has historically had fewer connected-device choices.

Medtronic has previously said it intends to separate the diabetes business from the rest of the company. The current status of that separation, including timing and structure, was not verified for this article, and readers should consult the company's most recent filings for the latest description. What can be said is that new product clearances bolster the standalone story the company has told about the unit.

Diabetes technology is competitive, with several established makers of glucose sensors, pumps and software. Clearance of a new product is step in a long process of securing payer coverage, partnering with clinics and winning patients. The next quarterly report may offer more color on how the unit is performing, though no specific result is anticipated here.

What do Medtronic recent filings and quarterly rhythm tell market participants?

Medtronic reports on a fiscal year that ends in April, so its fiscal quarter covers the period ending in late October and is normally reported in November. Earlier this year the company announced the date of its fiscal quarter results in July, according to a release on its news site. A similar date announcement is typically issued a few weeks before the quarterly report.

The company has also filed a quarterly report with the Securities and Exchange Commission, listed in recent filing summaries, which contains management's discussion of operations and the formal description of uncertainties facing the business. These documents are the authoritative source for the company's own account of its segments, and they are where details about tariffs, supply chain and regulatory matters are laid out.

Because the quarterly report has not yet been released as of this article, any commentary about it is necessarily about what readers may look for rather than what will be said. Typical items include organic growth across the cardiovascular, neuroscience, medical surgical and diabetes groups, management's updated guidance and commentary on pulsed field ablation, among the faster-growing areas in heart rhythm care.

How does Medtronic compete with Boston Scientific, Abbott and Intuitive in device markets?

Medtronic is among the largest medical device companies by revenue, but it faces strong rivals in nearly every segment. In heart rhythm care and structural heart, it competes with several large peers. In surgical robotics, Intuitive Surgical has a long head start. In diabetes, other sensor and pump suppliers are well established. That breadth is both an advantage and a burden, since management attention and capital must be divided.

Acquisitions like the CathWorks step are way the company has historically added capabilities, alongside internal development and partnerships. The approach lets the company enter or strengthen a niche without building the technology from scratch, though integration and commercial execution still determine whether the acquired product grows.

The sector backdrop adds uncertainty. Hospitals continue to manage staffing and budget pressures, device makers face tariff and supply questions, and regulators and payers scrutinize new technologies. Those factors affect all large device companies, and the specific sensitivity of Medtronic to each was not quantified in the sources reviewed for this article.

Looking ahead, the practical test for each initiative is whether it shows up in reported growth rates and in management's commentary about customer demand. Product milestones create headlines, but sustained results require adoption by hospitals, payment from insurers and public programs, and consistent supply. Medtronic's quarterly disclosures remain the most direct way to see which of these threads is gaining traction and which is still at an early stage of development.

title: Why Delta Air Lines Broke A Decade Of Airbus Widebody Loyalty To Give Boeing 1 Order

text:
Delta Air Lines sent shockwaves across the commercial aviation sector earlier this year by announcing a firm order for 30 Boeing 787-10 Dreamliners , accompanied by options for up to 30 more. The order brings with it the carrier's first direct procurement of the modern widebody family, ending an era of single-source twin-aisle orders that had long favored its European rival.

The decision to diversify its fleet shows a major pivot in capital expenditure strategy for the Atlanta-based carrier. For nearly ten years, Airbus had enjoyed a monopoly on Delta's new widebody orders, supplying highly efficient twin-engine jets to power the airline's global expansion. Reintroducing Boeing to its long-haul lineup not only mitigates supply chain risks but also provides Delta with a highly tailored, high-capacity solution to dominate premium transatlantic markets.

Strategic & Filled With Purpose

Delta's commitment to up to 60 Boeing 787-10 aircraft is a landmark acquisition for the airline, as well as for the manufacturer. This strategic deal, finalized on January 13, 2026, provides the airline with a vital counterbalance to its existing long-haul fleet structure, now splitting its future twin-aisle acquisitions between the world's two dominant aerospace manufacturers.

The balanced procurement approach will help safeguard the carrier's growth plans against sudden production delays and regulatory hurdles. For nearly ten years, Delta had banked all of its widebody investments directly on Airbus, accumulating an impressive fleet of Airbus A330-900 and Airbus A350-900 jets.

The operational concentration on Airbus was driven by highly competitive pricing, favorable maintenance packages, and the administrative simplicity of managing fewer flight-deck types. Concentrating on the European manufacturer allowed Delta to streamline its pilot training pipelines and optimize spare parts inventories across its major maintenance hubs.

However, this absolute reliance on a single manufacturer exposed the airline to escalating European assembly tariffs and aerospace supply chain delays. The decision to select the Dreamliner is a real full-circle turn for Delta's long-term planning department, returning once more to the manufacturer that still features heavily across the fleet.

Back in late 2016, the airline canceled an inherited order for 18 smaller Boeing 787-8 aircraft that it had acquired during its landmark merger with Northwest Airlines. At that point, executives determined that focusing exclusively on Airbus widebodies would deliver greater structural simplicity and superior profit margins. Returning to the Boeing widebody family ten years later demonstrates how even the most established fleet strategies can be redefined.

The operational objective of the newly ordered 787-10 fleet is to replace Delta's aging Boeing 767-300ER and Boeing 767-400ER fleets. These older twin-aisle aircraft have served as the absolute backbone of Delta's transatlantic and South American networks for over two decades.

However, with many of these aircraft approaching or exceeding their 30th anniversaries, rising maintenance expenses and outdated passenger cabins have made retirement essential. Phasing out these older airframes will significantly modernize Delta's long-haul operations, making way for the new Boeing platform.

Opting for the largest variant of the Dreamliner family, Delta is embracing a high-gauge strategy that maximizes capacity on its densest international routes. The 787-10 provides a substantial passenger capacity increase over the older 767 models while offering double the available under-floor cargo volume.

This massive cargo increase enables the carrier to capture high-yield freight opportunities on key transatlantic corridors, boosting overall route profitability. Instead of operating multiple smaller flights, the airline can use the Dreamliner's superior economics to run fewer, more lucrative frequencies. Deliveries of the 30 firm 787-10s are scheduled to begin in 2031, establishing a clear timeline for the final phase-out of the 767 fleet.

According to manufacturer specifications, the Dreamliner will deliver a spectacular 20% reduction in fuel burn per seat compared to the older twin-aisle jets it is scheduled to replace. For Delta, this is a massive operational victory that directly supports the long-term cost-reduction and sustainability targets. Curbing fuel consumption on long-haul sectors, Delta can cover its operating margins from volatile oil markets.

Why The 787 Is Perfect For Delta

Delta is planning to outfit its incoming 787-10s with an exceptionally aggressive, premium-heavy cabin configuration designed to maximize long-term passenger yields. This layout strategy reflects the carrier's ongoing effort to capture high-margin luxury travel, which has grown rapidly as a key driver of airline profitability.

Rather than focusing on maximum passenger density, the Atlanta-based carrier is choosing to allocate significant cabin real estate to high-end seating. The financial strategy underpinning this cabin configuration was highlighted by Delta's Chief Commercial Officer, Joe Esposito, during an earnings call in July of this year.

He confirmed that over 50% of the seats on the new 787-10s will consist of premium products, including Delta One Suites, Delta Premium Select, and Delta Comfort. It is an enormous shift from the outgoing 767 fleets, where premium seats typically account for only 30% of the total cabin capacity.

In addition to expanding the premium seat footprint, the Dreamliner's advanced carbon-fiber composite fuselage will offer passengers a fundamentally improved physiological experience. The aircraft is pressurized at a lower cabin altitude of 6,000 feet (1,828 meters) and maintains higher interior humidity levels compared to traditional aluminum airplanes.

These structural improvements significantly mitigate the symptoms of jet lag, dry skin, and fatigue on ultra-long-haul routes. When combined with larger, electronically dimmable passenger windows and a quieter cabin acoustic profile, the 787-10 will deliver a world-class environment that reinforces Delta's premium brand identity.

The Power Of The GEnx

A critical element of Delta's 787-10 procurement strategy is its engine selection. Alongside the airframe order, the carrier announced it had selected GEnx-1B engines from GE Aerospace to power the new widebody fleet. This propulsion choice is a major operational development for Delta, adding high-efficiency engines backed by a comprehensive long-term maintenance and services agreement.

What has become clear is that Delta is leveraging a mature engine program with more than 70 million flight hours of operational data across global airlines to go all out on proven reliability. The GEnx-1B engine is widely recognized for introducing cutting-edge materials and aerodynamic designs to commercial aviation. It is the first commercial engine to utilize both a carbon-fiber composite front fan case and composite fan blades.

Reducing the overall fan blade count from 22 to 18, GE Aerospace succeeded in cutting substantial engine weight while improving resistance to corrosion. Additionally, the low-pressure turbine incorporates titanium aluminide blades in its final stages, shaving off approximately 300 pounds (136 kilograms) compared to conventional designs and significantly boosting fuel efficiency.

These weight-saving technologies translate directly to lower operating overhead for Delta's long-haul network. The GEnx engine delivers a notable reduction in fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions compared to older propulsion systems. Furthermore, its advanced combustor system decreases nitrogen oxide emissions, helping Delta meet increasingly strict international environmental guidelines, making the GEnx an ideal match for Delta's future sustainability goals.

The Deciding Factor

The high-capacity 787-10 is expected to serve as Delta's premium workhorse across high-demand transatlantic corridors and dense South American routes, taking over from the 767. There are, of course, plenty of other aircraft that could fit the bill, and as discussed, there are plenty of reasons why Delta eventually opted for the Dreamliner.

There is, however, one key point that is often overlooked that could reveal the pivotal deciding factor. In early 2026, the FAA officially certified an increased maximum takeoff weight for the 787-10 variant. This upgrade raises the structural weight capacity of the aircraft by 14,219 pounds (6,450 kilograms), offering operators a highly lucrative choice between range and payload.

For Delta, this additional structural weight capability translates to roughly 400 nautical miles (740 kilometers) of additional flight range or five metric tons (11,023 pounds) of extra cargo capacity. The added performance envelope allows the airline to operate deep into Eastern Europe and South America with heavy passenger and freight loads, greater than what its predecessors were capable of.

The performance upgrade directly expands Delta's network options from its primary hubs in Atlanta, New York, and Minneapolis. The carrier can confidently schedule the 787-10 on long-range routes that were previously best suited to the Airbus A350-900s. Rather than being restricted to shorter transatlantic hops, the upgraded Dreamliner can easily fly deep into South American cities or premium Western European capitals while maximizing belly cargo revenue.

Balancing The Top Manufacturers

From a corporate finance perspective, the 787-10 order is designed to drive significant margin expansion across Delta’s international network. By replacing older, less efficient twin-aisle jets with a platform that burns 25% less fuel per seat, the airline is introducing a structural cost reduction that will pay dividends for decades.

In an industry where fuel remains one of the largest and most volatile operating expenses, this dramatic leap in efficiency provides a vital hedge against future energy price spikes. The financial logic extends far beyond simple fuel savings. Delta has successfully established a dual-source widebody strategy that keeps both manufacturers highly competitive, keeping both Airbus and Boeing on their toes.

This balanced fleet makeup prevents Delta from becoming captive to a single supplier's pricing power or assembly bottlenecks. It also ensures that the airline can pivot its future capital commitments to whichever manufacturer offers the most favorable pricing and delivery timelines.

Ultimately, this blockbuster procurement program marks the final step in Delta's multi-year effort to simplify and modernize its global operations. When combined with its existing orders for Airbus A350-1000s and Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft, the incoming 787-10 Dreamliners will give Delta one of the youngest, most efficient, and most premium-heavy long-haul fleets in the world.

Negative Points

Institutional & Specialty performance remained consistent but was not satisfactory, as restaurant foot traffic in North America declined mid-single digits, creating a challenging market environment.

Commodity cost inflation is expected to remain high, pressuring margins, although Ecolab Inc (NYSE:ECL) has managed to offset it through pricing and supply chain efficiency.

CoolIT is expected to be a $0.20 per quarter EPS headwind in Q3, with a larger 12% drag in Q4 due to interest and amortization, and a 5% headwind in the first half of 2027.

Q & A Highlights

Q: Tim Mulrooney (William Blair) asked about the drivers behind the 63% organic growth in Global High-Tech (legacy business plus CoolIT) and whether the 30% CAGR is still the right number to use toward the $4 billion 2030 target. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said the business is early but has the best growth potential, driven by ultrapure water improving chip performance and yields (currently 60%70% for the latest chips) and water circularity, while in data centers direct-to-chip liquid cooling is essential to extract heat. He noted Ecolab offers end-to-end "done the right way" solutions (zero water, less power) that competitors selling individual equipment cannot match, and said the targets are "more achievable than ever," with more detail to come at Investor Day.

Q: Ronan Kennedy (Barclays) asked how to think about the price/volume algorithm underpinning 2027 guidance at the upper end of the 5%7% organic growth range, including first-half versus second-half dynamics as surcharge pricing laps. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said 2027 should be stronger than 2026, with underlying earnings growth in the mid-teens. He expects roughly a 5-point EPS headwind in the first half and a 5-point tailwind in the second half from transaction costs and Nalco amortization. On the top line, he expects 1%2% volume and 5%6% pricing in the first half, shifting to 2%3% volume and lower pricing in the second half as 2026 comparisons lap.

Q: John McNulty (BMO) asked what is driving High-Tech organic growth to 63% from 29% in Q2whether it is the shift to liquid cooling or cross-selling from the CoolIT platform. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said there is no cross-selling yet, as the CoolIT and Ovivo integrations closed only in recent weeks, though cross-selling is a major future opportunity. Current growth is driven by the shift to direct-to-chip cooling, which increases demand for fluid management (3D TRASAR), coolants, and services, noting that just four minutes of cooling disruption can destroy data center chips. He cautioned 63% is not a steady-state growth rate.

Q: Vincent Andrews (Morgan Stanley) asked for detail on the new initiatives planned for the Institutional business, given tough restaurant traffic trends. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) outlined three moves: rebalancing sales and service, including doubling sales firepower in North America; serving segments (restaurants, hotels, quick-serve, retail) in an integrated rather than fragmented way to free up service efficiency for selling; and integrating the customer proposition across Hygiene, Water, Pest Intelligence, and audits, following the playbook that worked in Food & Beverage.

Q: Laurence Alexander (Jefferies) asked whether the 20% adjusted operating income margin target for 2027 is achievable even with upside surprises on inflation. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said he sees no reason not to deliver the 20% margin in 2027 despite a different path than originally planned, adding that many businesses are already above 20% and the next margin milestone will be shared at Investor Day. He reaffirmed the company's annual margin improvement commitment.

Q: Ashish Sabadra (RBC) asked about the tailwind from the new Life Sciences plant in China and whether negative mRNA vaccine headlines have affected demand. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said there has been no negative impact from the mRNA headlines. He called Life Sciences one of the best stories in company history, citing best-in-class technologies, an agile team, and the unique combination of water and contamination control. He reiterated a 10%12% top-line growth trajectory and a path to a 30% operating income margin over the next few years, noting Q3 margins were boosted by lapping a 2025 maintenance period.

Q: Michael Harrison (Seaport) asked how the CoolIT EPS headwind will track and whether Life Sciences margins should be modeled above the prior high-teens assumption. A: Scott Kirkland (CFO) said CoolIT interest and amortization was about a 10% EPS headwind in Q3 and will be about 12% in Q4 due to an extra month from international reporting lag, with a 5-point first-half headwind and 5-point second-half tailwind in 2027. On Life Sciences, he said underlying margins are similar to Q3's strong level, but Q4 margins should be in the mid- to high teens due to continued investment.

Q: Josh Spector (UBS) asked whether pricing is still accelerating into Q4 and how Water incremental margins will develop after coming in below expectations. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said Q4 should look similar to Q3, with 1%2% volume and 5%6% pricing, and that Water margins improved nicely in Q3 and will keep improving despite greater sensitivity to DPC inflation than businesses like High-Tech. He assumes DPC stays at current high levels through the end of next year, and noted Ecolab can control margins within a quarter and expand net margins after the cycle turns.

Q: Patrick Cunningham (Citi) asked how the equipment-versus-recurring mix and customization differ across hyperscaler, multi-tenant, and next-generation fab deployments in Global High-Tech. A: Christophe Beck (CEO) said both businesses are evolving toward recurring models. In data centers, faster chip generation cycles (now under a year) require full cooling system replacements, making the business more recurring and Ecolab-like, with cooling sold as an end-to-end service committing to performance, cost, and reliability. Microelectronics has a larger upfront fab build but converts to recurring 3D TRASAR service, with data center cycles measured in months to quarters and fabs in quarters to years.

text:
Your traditional grocery chain costs more than shopping at Walmart, Aldi, and Costco.

That's something we've seen doing live price comparisons at TheStreet that's backed up by a more extensive study done by Consumer Reports.

In addition, grocery giants Kroger and Albertsons both admit that they can't compete on price.

"We are not in the game of being the cheapest because we do not have the lowest costs. But we can provide the best value," Kroger CEO Gregory Foran said during his chain's second-quarter earnings call.

Albertsons CEO Susan Morris said almost exactly the same thing during her company's Q2 earnings call.

"Our goal is not to be the cheapest guy in town, but rather to have the right balanced value proposition that resonates with the customers that we serve uniquely by market," she said.

Price Chopper, a family-owned chain that shares a brand name and has no connection to the New York and New England chain of the same name. It's part of Cosentino's Food Stores, and the company has launched a new banner designed to be the cheapest option for grocery shoppers.

Price Chopper's new brand offers price transparency

Retailers rarely offer transparency when it comes to prices. That's at least partially because on many items, the markup is fairly high, or would seem high to consumers who don't understand all the costs of running a store.

Back in my retail days, for example, many products were "keystoned," which means sold at double the price we acquired them for. That's a 50% retail margin, and it helped cover the fact that some items we sold, Legos being the largest brand, were sold at manufacturer-set prices that gave us a 30% margin.

Since our operating overhead was around 40%, we actually needed to sell some items over that number to offset the ones that fell below it.

Retailers generally don't share their markup or retail margin numbers; the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIEE) publishes a study showing markup and margins for 13 national chains, with Costco and Walmart having the lowest markups.

Costco markup 14.4%, margin 3.6%

Walmart markup 32.2%, margin 4.2%

Only Kroger had a lower markup among grocery chains than Walmart, coming in at 28.6% while only showing a margin of 2.1%. Aldi and Lidl, two discount grocery chains with a national footprint were not on the list.

"Markups are calculated by subtracting the cost of goods sold from sales, then dividing the result by the cost of goods sold. Retail margins are calculated as operating income divided by sales. The markup average is 48%, and the retail margin average is 6%," according to PIIE.

Costco marks goods up less than Walmart, but only makes a slightly lower margin because of its lower operating costs and cheaper cost of acquiring goods.

Price Chopper's new store, ChopMore by Price Chopper, offers full pricing transparency.

"You pay cost plus 10% at checkout," the company shared on its website.

Price Chopper launches a discount brand

Price Chopper's ChopMore model looks a lot like the business model being used by Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drugs, which marks up all the prescriptions it fills by 15%.

"We calculate our 15% markup by multiplying the price we pay for the medication by 0.15. This gives us the markup we add to the original price. For example, if the medication costs us $50, the markup would be $50 x 0.15 = $7.50. We then add that $7.50 to the original $50, plus any pharmacy labor and shipping fees," the company shared on its website.

That's an online-only company without the costs associated with running a storefront. Operating a grocery chain that does not charge a membership fee like Costco and only marking items up 10% seems like a very challenging business model

Price Chopper's parent company, Cosentino's, said it's able to offer such ChopMore discounts by cutting expenses in other areas.

"Stack it high and sell it low. No marketing, no ads, no gimmicks, no loyalty cards," Executive Vice President John Cosentino told KCUR. "Some products are in bins. Pallet drops on the endcaps. So it's a different way of merchandising. Quicker, less labor."

More retail:

Kroger cuts discounts, promises pricing changes

Walmart gets aggressive when it comes to holiday sales

Costco copies a popular Trader Joe's collectible

The new store, which replaced a traditional Price Chopper, will operate with fewer employees.

"The former Price Chopper store in the space had about 100 employees a year ago. ChopMore now has about 60. But the company did not lay off workers. Instead, it gradually downsized through attrition," Startland News reported.

10% is a really low markup

As a former retailer, I have a hard time believing that ChopMore can operate profitably on a 10% margin.

"Look, a 10% markup sounds great until you realize that's only about a 9% gross margin. From that little slice, you've got to pay the employees, keep the lights on, cover rent, credit card fees, and pay for all the food that spoils before somebody buys it," RTM Nexus CEO Dominick Miserandino told TheStreet.

There's a reason, he noted, that retailers generally mark their prices up higher than that.

"The only way this works is by moving an enormous amount of merchandise and keeping expenses incredibly low. Costco has membership fees helping its economics," he wrote. "Price Chopper doesn't have that cushion here. They need shoppers coming back constantly, and they need those shelves turning over fast. One bad month could eat up whatever profit they've made."

TheStreet Co-Editor-in-Chief Todd Campbell spent nine years in the grocery business working for Stop & Shop, another leading supermarket chain in the Northeast, and thinks the ChopMore could work.

"Price Chopper seems to be making a market share play to gain scale. Grocery operates on razor-thin margins, which is why so many have turned to lower-cost private label, like Aldi," said Campbell. "It's tough to turn a profit on a 10% markup without cutting services and embracing a bare-bones model."

Even then, he added, with Walmart and Costco's pricing power, "ChopMore may not be the cheapest option."

text:
With just two months to go before it splits into two, the Hewlett-Packard Enterprise half could face a bumpy road.

In its second quarter results reported earlier this month, HP reported software revenues declined 6% to just $900 million, with an 11% year-over- year decline in software license revenues. Its services business fared no better, showing a 10.5% decline, with its enterprise-class server hardware, storage and networking products dropping 6.3% to $6.4 billion.

These declines are reflective of the challenge HP has faced the past few years in getting its long-time legacy users, who collectively have invested billions in the company’s on-premises products, to switch to more cloud-focused products and services for workloads such as big data. The key product that will help accomplish this transition is Helion, the company’s cloud environment, which has struggled in the face of fierce competition from a handful of competitors including Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

But HP Enterprise group’s challenges run deeper than its cloud issues. The new company has to retool its hardware, services and software organizations so they can work more closely to weave together more compelling end-to-end products that many corporate users have come to prefer, according to some analysts.

“Their history is so rooted in providing point products, they will have to evolve all aspects of their business, which will be a significant shift in their strategy,” said Stephen Belanger, an analyst at Technology Business Research, Inc. in Hampton, N.H. “For the rest of this year and into 2016, they will have some challenges as they try to realign the business to supply more end-to-end solutions.”

One corporate IT professional with an investment in HP’s higher-end servers agrees, saying he would like to see more collaboration among HP’s major product groups. He believes, for instance, that HP should push its converged infrastructure offering, the new HP ConvergedSystem 250-HC, harder because the integrated offering appears to be less expensive and easier to install and maintain than some of the standalone server offerings he’s bought in the past.

“I’m more interested in not just the integrated nature of it, but it looks like an easier solution for getting into hybrid clouds for some of the departments here,” said an IT professional with a large manufacturing company in Minneapolis.

One analyst agrees the converged infrastructure and hyper-converged infrastructure markets represent a promising opportunity for HP Enterprise. She cautions, however, that it is still a relatively nascent market that is not yet delivering the kinds of revenues HP’s x86-based servers are. The latter systems were actually a bright spot in the company’s latest revenues and earnings report.

“Converged and hyper-converged are important platforms, but in HP’s case, you have to stand back and look at the bigger picture,” said Jean Bozman, director of infrastructure research for Neuralytix Inc., IT-focused market researchers. “They will be increasingly important because it allows enterprise users to have everything all in one place, but it is a very small part of a much larger mix.”

That much larger mix HP Enterprise must deal with is its enterprise-class Superdome server line of fault-tolerant systems, which has experienced a steady sales decline; older proprietary Unix-based servers; and its two-year-old Moonshot x86 server, which is all but disappearing from view in the competitive server landscape.

Despite HP’s best efforts to market the technical advantages of Moonshot, such as its power consumption efficiencies and space-saving design, Moonshot has yet to find its raison d’etre outside of a couple of niche markets.

If [HP Enterprise] can pull it together, they could be a pretty formidable competitor.

Dana Gardner

principal analyst, Interarbor Solutions

“We have gained some traction in some markets where performance is valued, but the broader market still sees it as something of a specialty box,” said one HP executive recently. “Right now, it’s difficult to know which way to turn with it.”

Some analysts take a more optimistic view of the HP Enterprise group’s future. They contend the new company has less corporate baggage to lug around and can move faster after sales opportunities, as well as focus on offering more compelling integrated end-to-end systems.

“The net-net [of Hewlett-Packard Enterprise] is that HP can run a tighter ship and drive more profits from this business,” said Dana Gardner, principal analyst with Interarbor Solutions, LLC. in Gilford, N.H. “They can approach Global 2000 enterprises now with a more solidified enterprise package and not have to pitch them on buying printers and PCs as leverage to buy more servers and storage.”

Gardner agrees with a growing number of observers that HP needs to evolve into a better supplier of integrated systems. It has all the necessary pieces to deliver such systems, but it will have to make some organizational changes to execute that job crisply.

“Sun [Microsystems] had a lot of great pieces, too, but they couldn’t pull it all together and got bought by Oracle,” Gardner said. “HP has the same great pieces. If they can pull it together, they could be a pretty formidable competitor.”

AI is huge for all three companies, with Nvidia becoming the world's first $5 trillion company thanks to the technology, and all three companies will want to perpetuate the growth of AI for that reason.

The AI bubble hasn't burst yet, but it did see a $1 trillion decline just a few weeks ago, and the Chinese AI market lost trillions just this week. One could read further investment as a way to keep the bubble floating for a while longer, or just one in a line of many steps from all three companies to get a foot in the door once the AI boom settles. A bubble popping could help gamers eventually get lower-priced memory, but so much of the world's economy is wrapped up in it that it's hard to say just how wide the reverberations would be, for these three companies or the rest of the world. It won't be good.

The Wall Street Journal argues AI is "becoming the biggest economic bet in US history". It shows AI spending is significantly bigger, as a percentage of annual infrastructure spending, than telecom and fiber, highways, electric, railroads, and even canals way back in the 1800s. One has to wonder what would happen if that investment suddenly lost its value.

And even now, the negative impacts of AI is hitting gamers with the memory crisis, where AI is sucking up so much memory that the average gamer has to pay more and more for less capacious memory. And it doesn't just stop at memory. name: Nvidia
title: NVIDIA Is Buying a Piece of Meta: What the $3 Billion Stake Means - Yahoo Finance
description:
The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying a piece of Meta itself.
Nvidia said Tuesday that it will invest $3 billion in a stock offering from Meta Platforms.
Meta Platforms upsized the common stock part of this offering to 25 billion up from 22.5 billion originally and priced at $625 a share.
Nvidia's money goes into Meta, Meta turns around and spends more on Nvidia infrastructure.
Nvidia owns a piece of Meta.
text:
The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying a piece of Meta itself.

Nvidia said Tuesday that it will invest $3 billion in a stock offering from Meta Platforms.

So, what is that check exactly? Well, it's an equity investment. Nvidia is buying shares, which make Jensen Wong's chip giant a shareholder in one of its biggest customers.

Here's how it came together.

Meta announced the offering Monday as reported by Axios. Nvidia's stake is part of an expanded AI partnership between the two companies. And the timing tells you a lot about where the AI race stands right now.

Because Meta needs cash and lots of it. Meta Platforms upsized the common stock part of this offering to 25 billion up from 22.5 billion originally and priced at $625 a share.

That's only the start though. According to the Wall Street Journal, Meta plans to raise as much as $95 billion through a series of share sales to cover AI infrastructure spending.

The question is, why does Meta need so much money? Well, the company has guided to 2026 capital expenditures, which is the money it's putting into data s and servers of 135 to 145 billion.

In the third quarter alone, CAPEX hit 34.91 billion. Free cash flow, which is the money left over after those investments, came in negative at 2.12 billion.

That's from a company that just posted 64.6 billion in quarterly revenue. On the earnings call, Meta CFO at the time, Susan Lee said Meta wanted access to a diverse pool of funding sources.

Now, we know what she meant. So what does Nvidia get beyond the shares? The partnership expands work on Meta's Muse family of models and agents with the goal of improving inference and training performance.

Now, inference, if you're wondering what that is, it just means running a model to answer real requests. Meta plans to scale up its usage of Nvidia hardware for its next generation of AI agents, including Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs, plus Nvidia's Spectrum X Ethernet networking and Bluefield 4.

As Jensen Wong put it, AI agents represent a new computing paradigm, software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf. Mark Zuckerberg kept it even simpler. Muse is how we bring personal superintelligence to everyone.

And good for Meta shareholders, Muse is catching on. Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up Muse personal agents in about a month and a half. The catch, he admitted it's a very compute intensive service.

Which is why it hasn't launched globally yet. Wang explained the math from Nvidia's side back in August. An AI agent needs probably 15 to 100 times the compute of a human doing the same task.

Every Muse user meta adds is more demand for Nvidia Silicon. That's the loop investors need to understand. Nvidia's money goes into Meta, Meta turns around and spends more on Nvidia infrastructure. For Nvidia's shareholders, that locks in a customer already tied to a multi-year, multi-generational deals covering millions of Blackwell and Ruben GPUs.

Nvidia has already invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs and Wong has heard the criticism. In his words, we know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently. If Meta's AI products deliver, both companies will win. If they stall, Nvidia holds a stake in a customer that may slow its spending, and that's a double hit.

For Meta shareholders, the trade-off is dilution. New shares mean each existing share owns a slightly smaller piece of the company. In return, Meta gets a deep-pocketed anchor investor and the hardware pipeline to scale Muse.

So far, the market's reaction to this news is muted. In pre-market trading on Tuesday, Meta trades at 628, down just 0.41% and just above that offering price. and Nvidia is at 217.90 in pre-market, up about 0.9%.

So what should you watch? Meta says its AI businesses could start adding additional revenue in 2027 through subscriptions, commerce fees, advertising, and enterprise deals. Zuckerberg also expects to improve Muse's cost efficiency by more than 10x across the next year. Those two numbers will decide whether this spending turns into profit.

Nvidia owns a piece of Meta. It's up to Muse to prove that piece is worth the price. Thanks for tuning in. This has been 24/7 Wall Street for all your top news on finance's biggest stories. Make sure to check in with 24/7 Wall Street. Thank you.

name: Nvidia
title: Nvidia, AMD to buy $4B in Meta shares as part of expanded chip partnerships
authors: Maria Deutscher, DEVONY HOF, SLOANE KALI FAYE, RYAN STEVENS
description:
Meta Platforms Inc. today announced that Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. plan to buy $4 billion worth of its shares.
That suggests the networking chip giant will buy $1 billion in shares.
Notably, Meta plans to broaden its use of the chipmaker’s Rubin graphics processing units and Vera central processing units.
Meta also plans to buy more Nvidia networking gear.
Additionally, Meta plans to explore “collaboration opportunities” related to Nvidia’s recently introduced OpenShell Reference Architecture.
text:
Meta Platforms Inc. today announced that Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. plan to buy $4 billion worth of its shares.

The chipmakers will purchase the equity as part of an up to $95 billion stock sale that the Facebook parent intends to kick off in the near future. The fundraising initiative will also include the participation of Broadcom Inc. Meta didn’t specify how much the company is investing, but it stated on Monday that Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom together plan to invest $5 billion. That suggests the networking chip giant will buy $1 billion in shares.

Nvidia is investing $3 billion as part of a newly expanded partnership that also includes other components. Notably, Meta plans to broaden its use of the chipmaker’s Rubin graphics processing units and Vera central processing units. Companies often deploy the two chips together in Nvidia-designed DGX Vera Rubin NVL72 appliances. Each system includes 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs.

Meta also plans to buy more Nvidia networking gear. It will expand its use of the Spectrum-X Ethernet product family, which includes SuperNICs and switches. SuperNICs are chips that connect servers to a data center’s network, while switches coordinate how traffic flows through that network.

GPU clusters’ traffic patterns tend to change rapidly. As a result, connectivity bottlenecks sometimes emerge faster than the network can respond to them. Nvidia says that its Spectrum-X Ethernet product series addresses the challenge by checking GPU traffic for anomalies at sub-microsecond time intervals. A microsecond corresponds to one millionth of a second.

Another focus of Meta’s planned network investment is Nvidia’s BlueField-4 chip family. The accelerators in the series are designed to speed common networking, storage and cybersecurity tasks.

Nvidia will help Meta improve the performance and cost efficiency of its Muse large language model family. The effort will extend to the Facebook parent’s eponymous consumer AI agent.

Additionally, Meta plans to explore “collaboration opportunities” related to Nvidia’s recently introduced OpenShell Reference Architecture. It’s a collection of technical resources that makes it easier to run the chipmaker’s OpenShell toolkit. The toolkit runs AI agents in isolated sandboxes designed to mitigate cybersecurity risks.

“Nvidia and Meta are expanding our partnership to optimize the computing infrastructure end to end for capable, efficient and secure AI agents, so Muse can empower billions of people to achieve more and pursue greater ambitions,” said Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

AMD, which will invest $1 billion in Meta, today revealed that the Facebook parent has adopted its Helios rack design. Helios contains 72 GPUs much like the DGX Vera Rubin NVL72. It’s based on AMD’s latest Instinct MI450 graphics card architecture, Epyc CPUs and Pensando data processing units, which are the chipmaker’s answer to the BlueField-4.

It says Meta has deployed an “initial” set of Helios racks in its data centers and is currently testing them. The social media giant plans to deploy additional systems in the near future.

Further down the line, Meta will adopt a custom AI accelerator based on AMD’s Instinct graphics card architecture. The chipmaker, for its part, will use the technical data collected through the partnership to improve its future chip and rack designs.

“Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta’s most ambitious superintelligence models and services,” said AMD CEO Lisa Su.

INDIANAPOLIS, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY) today announced that Patrik Jonsson, executive vice president and president, Lilly International, has decided to retire at the end of 2026 after a 36-year career at Lilly.

Jonsson joined the company in 1990 as a sales representative in Sweden. He went on to lead Lilly in Sweden, Scandinavia, Italy and Japan, then served as president of Lilly Bio-Medicines and Lilly Immunology, as well as president of Lilly USA and Lilly's cardiometabolic health business, before leading Lilly International.

"For more than three decades, Patrik has dedicated his career to improving lives by bringing our medicines to people around the world," said David A. Ricks, Lilly chair and CEO. "He has held multiple executive roles in the company spanning drug development and customer operations, including head of immunology, cardiometabolic health and Lilly USA. Today he applies his deep expertise in global launches across Lilly International. Patrik is a patient-focused, engaging team leader who has mentored countless colleagues. On behalf of our Board, leadership team and thousands of employees he has worked alongside, I thank Patrik for his service to our company."

Effective Jan. 1, 2027, Lilly's U.S. and international businesses will come together as Lilly Global Markets, led by Ilya Yuffa, who will become executive vice president and president, Lilly Global Markets.

Bringing these organizations together will accelerate decision-making, increase scalability and provide a unified capability to improve human health through expanded access to medicines around the world.

Yuffa joined Lilly in 1996 as a financial analyst and has held leadership roles in finance, business development, sales and general management, including president and general manager of Lilly's Italy Hub, which covered more than 25 countries, president of Lilly Bio-Medicines, president of Lilly International and currently executive vice president and president, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities.

Ricks continued, "To build on our momentum, now is the right time to consolidate our geographies for greater impact. Ilya has run both our international and U.S. businesses, and his range of experience and commitment to excellence make him uniquely qualified to lead our customer-facing operations worldwide. He is joined by a proven team with the expertise and focus to help us reach even more people with our medicines."

The following executives will lead the company's six geographic hubs and report to Yuffa:

Laura Steele, currently group vice president, U.S. Cardiometabolic Health, will be promoted to president, Lilly USA. In 23 years at Lilly, Steele has held leadership roles in marketing, value and access, and commercial operations inside and outside the U.S., including Lilly's U.S. neuroscience business.

Elias Khalil, currently president and general manager of Lilly's Italy Hub, will be promoted to group vice president and president, Lilly Europe and Canada. In 18 years at Lilly, Khalil has held leadership roles across the Gulf region, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. neuroscience business.

Nabil Daoud will continue in his role as group vice president and president, Lilly InterContinental.

Karla Alcazar, Huzur Devletsah and Winselow Tucker will continue in their roles as president and general manager of Lilly Japan, Lilly China and Lilly India, respectively.

About Lilly

Lilly is a medicine company turning science into healing to make life better for people around the world. We've been pioneering life-changing discoveries for 150 years, and today our medicines help tens of millions of people across the globe. Harnessing the power of biotechnology, chemistry and genetic medicine, our scientists are urgently advancing new discoveries to solve some of the world's most significant health challenges: redefining diabetes care; treating obesity and curtailing its most devastating long-term effects; advancing the fight against Alzheimer's disease; providing solutions to some of the most debilitating immune system disorders; and transforming the most difficult-to-treat cancers into manageable diseases. With each step toward a healthier world, we're motivated by one thing: making life better for millions more people. That includes delivering innovative clinical trials that reflect the diversity of our world and working to ensure our medicines are accessible and affordable. To learn more, visit Lilly.com and Lilly.com/news, or follow us on Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn. C-LLY

title: Anthropic IPO Filing Reveals Looming Threat to Nvidia's Pricing Power - Business Insider
description:

text:
Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance.

The AI lab says it manages compute "as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners" — with software that can direct its work to different chips depending on where they're most productive, according to Anthropic's S-1 filing, which came out Monday as the company prepares to go public.

Anthropic says it uses hardware from four chip families: Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

That flexibility, which Anthropic said "took years and significant investment to build," could make major AI companies less dependent on Nvidia over time and give them more negotiating leverage, analysts said.

"The real exposure could be Nvidia's pricing power," said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, "because a customer that can shift work across four platforms negotiates very differently than one that can't."

Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply.

Breaking Nvidia's grip isn't easy

Although Anthropic's chip mix isn't new, the company is now pitching it as a core advantage to investors, Moorhead said.

The threat has its limits. Switching between chips is still difficult — especially when it comes to training AI models as opposed to running them, Moorhead said — and only the biggest AI companies have the resources to do it.

Anthropic also continues to spend billions on Nvidia compute, Moorhead said.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said that while other major companies like OpenAI likely take a multichip approach, it may not be worth the effort and investment for smaller players.

Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said Anthropic's strategy doesn't represent a major near-term threat. Having more chip options doesn't erase Nvidia's advantages in performance, networking, and software, he said.

There's a broader risk for Nvidia if AI compute becomes more of a commodity.

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has warned that if supply overtakes demand, it could drive down rental prices.

"GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run," he told Bloomberg last week. "The moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

title: The platform approach to becoming Frontier - The Official Microsoft Blog
description:
Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000.
By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.
To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot.
Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market.
Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale.
text:
Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There is no path where this notion of infinite cognitive compute replaces human purpose. Frontier Transformation is an opportunity for a wholesale reinvention of how you think about your unique ideas coming to life and how your organization can thrive in your industry.

Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. We are taking a platform approach toward enabling the same: Copilot as the place to call home for interacting with AI to empower human ambition; the Microsoft IQ platform to compound and amplify your intelligence from within while protecting your unique differentiation; and Agent 365 to enable Trust and Observability at every layer of the stack so that you can govern, manage, secure and get business value and return out of the capabilities you deliver.

Our latest earnings are another important marker on that journey. Behind the numbers are thousands of customers, partners, developers and employees putting AI to work in meaningful ways. We have so many inspiring stories from our customers that highlight these outcomes, and below are some of our favorites.

Empowering human ambition with Copilot

Volkswagen has scaled Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees as it expands the role of AI in decision-making and knowledge-based processes across the enterprise. Building on Copilot Chat adoption that reached more than 300,000 monthly active users, employees are now using Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced scenarios, bringing greater organizational context to decision-making and knowledge-based work. Volkswagen is also working with Microsoft to further scale its Intelligent Data Foundation on Microsoft Fabric to make data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. With this investment, Volkswagen is demonstrating how companies have evolved from using Copilot as a productivity tool to an operating system to empower human ambition.

Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000. Copilot usage has surpassed 90%, and the company is using the tool to connect employees with specialized agents and business systems. AI agents are already automating roughly 75% of initial responses and triage for a service desk that receives nearly 300,000 inquiries annually, while new agents are supporting work across sales, systems engineering, procurement, finance and accounting. As customer zero, Fujitsu is using Copilot as the front door to a multi-agent work environment and using insights from its own AI adoption to better serve its customers.

KOHLER is using GitHub Copilot to transform software development, with one organization improving code releases by 25% and reducing error defects by 75%. These engineering breakthroughs are part of a broader effort to embed AI processes across the company, spanning IT, finance, marketing, supply chain and operations. Microsoft Copilot has reached 98% adoption, saving an average of 2 to 5 hours per month as employees are making informed decisions and getting answers faster in the flow of their work. Employees across the company have also created more than 3,000 agents to date, with hundreds active daily.

At Krafton, Microsoft Security Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR are helping the security team respond to a growing volume and complexity of threats. The global gaming company automated key parts of security operations, from alerting and investigation to reporting, combining Microsoft Security solutions with its own systems and data to quickly gather context that helps distinguish real threats from false positives. This approach is having immediate results: security alert recognition time has fallen by approximately 95% to less than one minute, investigation work that previously took tens of minutes now takes about three minutes and roughly 95% of report creation has been automated. By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.

To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot. NASA employees are using Copilot to sift through massive amounts of academic literature and streamline daily tasks, and specialized assistants are helping researchers navigate complex Earth science data through natural language, extending access to information that once required significant technical expertise. Hydrology Copilot, for example, can analyze variables like precipitation and soil moisture to help communities better understand water conditions, prepare for droughts and anticipate flood risks, while automatically performing calculations and analyses.

To transform frontline work, Williams, a US natural gas company, is using Microsoft Copilot to help employees spend less time searching documents and completing manual processes, and more time on critical field operations. Copilot helps teams generate plans, interpret procedures, assess regulatory requirements, troubleshoot issues and complete safety reporting, while employees can create agents tailored to their own workflows. Demonstrating that the person closest to a problem is often the best one to solve it, one operations technician built an anomaly detector using Copilot that compares equipment data against baseline statistics and alerts teams to potential issues before they become costly or dangerous. Since deploying Copilot, AI adoption at Williams has grown from single digits to more than 90%, helping employees accelerate operations, improve reporting and compliance and identify equipment issues earlier.

Bristol Myers Squibb has rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 25,000 employees, reaching 96% adoption, and is now putting AI agents to work across everyday use cases such as document review and project management in support of the company’s mission to bring more medicines to more patients faster. One agent, called RABIT, analyzes meeting transcripts, surfaces action items and delivers insights directly within employees’ workflows.

Facing rising patient demand and financial pressures, Brown University Health is using Dragon Copilot to give clinicians more time to focus on patients. The health system adopted Dragon Copilot, and an early pilot across 420 clinicians found users spent less time on after-hours documentation and reported lower cognitive burden. Building on that experience, Brown University Health deployed Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio across departments, which led to the creation of more than 24 AI agents to support clinical workflows, hospital policies, patient access and operations. These AI solutions are not only supporting clinicians in the flow of their work but also helping to improve the patient experience and access to care.

Microsoft IQ compounds and protects your intelligence

BNY has made AI part of how its employees work through Eliza, its in-house AI platform built with Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot – with plans to add Work IQ. More than 300 solutions now run on Eliza, ranging from inquiry management to client onboarding, and 100% of employees have been trained on the platform. Across the bank, that scale is translating into meaningful results: client transaction inquiries are being resolved 80% faster and AI-assisted client onboarding is 20% faster on average. Through the Microsoft CEO Co-Innovation program, BNY also worked with Microsoft to develop an AI research capability with Foundry that investigates complex data issues, analyzes context across multiple sources, identifies likely root causes and recommends next steps, bringing AI-assisted reasoning into processes that have traditionally relied on human investigation alone.

Docusign is helping 1.9 million customers across 180 countries turn agreement data into actionable business insights. The company built an Intelligent Agreement Management platform on Microsoft Azure and used Microsoft Foundry to shift from general-purpose models to a system of task-specific models that better understand context. This change allows Docusign to process more than a million agreement documents daily with up to eightfold greater throughput and 90% lower AI processing costs. Foundry also supports a model lifecycle designed for continuous improvement, where processes are fine-tuned before deployment and monitored in production, while also providing the governance and traceability needed to meet enterprise requirements for compliance, visibility and control. Now agreement content is structured data that compounds from within, so organizations can use it to make decisions and automate workflows, knowing their IP is protected.

To help marketers create more effective content, Kantar turned decades of proprietary advertising intelligence into action with Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry. Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market. The new approach can process and score large volumes of videos 20x faster while reducing platform operating costs by 4x, helping customers move from insight to action in minutes rather than hours. By bringing its unique intelligence into a continuous loop of observation and improvement, Kantar is creating new ways to help marketers turn insight into better creative and business outcomes.

Kinaxis, a Canadian supply chain software company, runs Maestro, its AI-driven supply chain orchestration platform, on Microsoft Azure. Maestro helps businesses make better decisions faster amid constant disruption. It brings together traditionally disparate business data like sales orders, inventory and production capacity with external signals like weather, market shifts and breaking news to give planners a near real-time view of their supply chains. With this unified data foundation, planners and analysts can use predictive AI and optimization models to anticipate demand shifts, evaluate constraints and recommend action, while generative AI agents act as assistants to ask questions, explore scenarios and automate parts of the planning process. With this intelligence in one platform, businesses can understand how disruptions ripple across their interconnected operations, weigh trade-offs and adjust plans as conditions change.

Moody’s is making more than a century of credit and risk intelligence directly accessible through Microsoft Copilot, giving customers trusted, protected context for complex decisions. Through a federated connector built using Model Context Protocol, customers can access live, decision-grade Moody’s intelligence through Researcher in Copilot and within Word, Excel and Teams, without copying or exporting the underlying data. A single question can synthesize information across credit ratings, company financials, ownership information and physical risk models, helping customers reach insights in minutes instead of spending hours or days on research and analysis. This brings trusted, connected intelligence directly into workflows where customers make complex decisions.

To turn conversations into actionable intelligence at global scale, Plaud, an AI hardware and software company, is using Microsoft Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models and Azure Speech in Foundry Tools to power transcription, summarization and AI inference across long-form audio and multilingual scenarios. Serving more than 2 million users worldwide, Plaud increased transcription accuracy and processing speed by 35% and improved inference performance by 30%, helping professionals turn spoken content into structured outputs and insights. Even as its user base doubled, the company used Foundry’s elastic scaling and flexible deployment models to reduce overall compute costs by 35%, while strengthening its ability to meet security, privacy and compliance requirements across global markets.

Rockwell Automation built a Maintenance Copilot using Microsoft Foundry to put decades of manufacturing expertise in the hands of employees. The AI assistant brings together expert knowledge from veteran engineers, manufacturing data and machine manuals, allowing technicians to quickly identify likely causes of equipment issues, see how colleagues have solved similar problems and access step-by-step troubleshooting guidance. At its Singapore factory, the approach has helped reduce machine downtime by 33% and cut servicing and spare-part costs by about 25%. Rockwell estimates it has also reduced the time it takes new workers to learn to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three months.

With 1.5 billion passengers riding its elevators and escalators every day, TK Elevator knows that every minute of downtime affects how people move through airports, hospitals and offices. Building on a decade of connected-equipment data on Microsoft Azure, the company created AI agents with Microsoft Foundry that brief service technicians before they enter a building, telling them which elevator, which floor, what the issue is and which tools to bring. After each job, a voice agent records the technician’s account of the work in their own words, with no typing, and adds that expertise to a shared record. With 25,000 technicians caring for 1.4 million units worldwide, TK Elevator is turning each technician’s know-how into compounded intelligence every colleague can draw on.

Telstra partnered with Microsoft Frontier Company to deploy an AI-powered Migration Payment Agent that helps simplify one of the most complex aspects of customer migration: reconciling billing and payments across legacy and new platforms. The agent uses intelligence across these systems to proactively identify inconsistencies, recommend corrective actions and create enriched cases for human review, combining AI-driven insights with human-in-the-loop validation to maintain operational trust and governance. Already supporting more than 272,000 service migrations and delivering recommendations at 95%+ accuracy in production, the solution demonstrates how Telstra is applying agentic AI at enterprise scale to transform complex operations, improve customer outcomes and build reusable AI capabilities while compounding and protecting Telstra’s operational intelligence.

Agent 365 observes AI solutions across the stack

To advance its transformation into an AI-powered organization, Manulife is adopting Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite, expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 30,000 employees and leveraging Microsoft Agent 365 to govern, manage and secure AI agents at enterprise scale. With Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry supporting its global enterprise AI platform, Manulife is building a foundation for teams to develop and deploy AI and agentic solutions while maintaining standards for quality, security and cost efficiency. AI is already delivering impact across the business, from generative AI solutions supporting more than 110 million customer calls annually to developers increasing productivity by 30% with assisted and autonomous AI capabilities. With agentic solutions and AI-powered workflows already in production, Manulife is creating the foundation to scale AI responsibly across its global operations and accelerate its next phase of enterprise transformation.

Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale. As a Microsoft customer zero organization for Agent 365, Insight Enterprises is quick to adopt new capabilities internally and pass those learnings on to clients. With Microsoft engineering, it tested how Microsoft and third-party agents could be observed, managed, governed and secured through a unified control plane. To date, Insight Enterprises has discovered 9,734 agents with visibility into which are active, what data they can access and how to monitor their activity over time. The experience has helped Insight Enterprises build practical AI governance expertise it can bring to customers, including organizations in highly regulated industries.

KPMG is adopting Microsoft Agent 365 to manage and secure AI agents across its global organization, providing centralized observability and control as it scales agentic AI. Agent 365 will also strengthen KPMG Workbench, its multi-agent platform built on Microsoft Foundry that coordinates agents across client service delivery platforms. At the same time, KPMG is expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 276,000 professionals worldwide, helping embed AI more deeply across audit, tax and advisory services. Together, these capabilities are giving KPMG the confidence and security to move agents from experimentation into enterprise-wide deployment, while helping clients do the same.

Operating in one of the most highly regulated industries, where protecting sensitive customer information is essential, Truist Financial Corporation is using Agent 365 to manage, govern and observe more than 13,000 AI declarative agents across its organization. Truist manages its agent ecosystem with discipline: every agent has an accountable owner and agents are automatically disabled after 45 days of inactivity. That rigor is driving strong retention and adoption, with more than 8,000 agents active each month. Building on this trusted foundation, Truist has advanced its broader AI strategy through their investment of more than 50,000 Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite seats.

—

Every quarter gives us an opportunity to step back and look at the progress we are making with our customers and partners around the world. What continues to strike me is not simply the pace of change, but the ambition we see from organizations using technology to achieve aspirations that simply weren’t possible before. We look forward to working alongside you on the path to becoming Frontier, and we hope to see many of you at Microsoft Ignite this year in November to share the latest innovations that will enable you to reach that destination.

Judson Althoff is the chief executive officer of the commercial business at Microsoft. He is responsible for the product strategy, sales, services, support, marketing, operations and revenue growth of the company’s commercial business, which operates in more than 120 regional and national subsidiaries globally.
